text:
From director/Netflix documentarian Lucy Tabrizi (subscribe to her on Substack):
 Killing children. Controlling foreign governments. Manipulating the press. Engineering wars. Profiting from others’ suffering. Seeking world domination.
 Am I describing the accusations against Israel today, or those levelled at Jews throughout history?
 Frankly, who can tell?
 An astonishing number of people recycle centuries-old accusations against Jews, now aimed at Israel, sometimes word for word, while insisting with a straight face that none of it has anything to do with historical Jew-hatred.
 Just an extraordinary series of coincidences, then.
 Oh, but THIS time the accusations are true? It’s not Jews you hate, just Zionists? Just the Israeli government? Or perhaps you’ve finally uncovered the real villains: impostors posing as Jews and giving the real ones a bad name?
 Funny. History is full of people insisting they didn’t hate Jews, just the financiers, Christ killers, Bolsheviks, rootless cosmopolitans, racial infiltrators and enemies within.
 Every generation had its own perfectly valid justification. They weren’t persecuting Jews, merely protecting society, sometimes even saving Jews from themselves.
 Anti-Judaism, racial antisemitism and antizionism are different branches of the same poisonous tree. Each adapts to the moral values of its time, accumulating old prejudices and giving each new incarnation an ever-expanding arsenal of reasons to vilify Jews.
 Here are six reasons why today’s antizionism is not the historical departure its adherents imagine, but the latest incarnation of the world’s oldest hatred.
 1. The Contradictions
 One of the clearest giveaways that we’re dealing with prejudice is how blatantly these accusations contradict one another, and how utterly unbothered their proponents seem to be.
 Within the space of 80 years, Jews have been told to “go back to Palestine” and “go back to Poland”, which should be quite the geographical conundrum.
 Nazi racial ideology cast Jews as alien, non-Aryan “Semites” infiltrating Europe. Today, antizionists portray them as “white Europeans” masquerading as indigenous Middle Easterners, colonising the very region from which their ancestors came.
 Israel is both a weak, artificial state entirely dependent on Western support and an almost omnipotent force secretly controlling the very governments supposedly keeping it afloat.
 To anti-capitalists, Jews were the financiers exploiting the masses. To anti-communists, the revolutionaries plotting to overthrow society. To racial supremacists, an inferior people who nevertheless possessed the extraordinary power to manipulate governments and world affairs.
 Religious Jews were accused of refusing to integrate; assimilated Jews of infiltrating society.
 Too rich, too poor. Too powerful, too inferior. Too foreign, too integrated. Condemned for not having a state, condemned for having one. Not European enough, white European colonisers.
 Whatever Jews are, whatever they believe, whatever they do, the logic bends to make them the problem.
 Jew-hatred, after all, is not a phenomenon explained by the behaviour of 0.2% of humanity, let alone the 0.1% that live in Israel. It exposes the moral failures of societies that have spent centuries inventing reasons to hate them.
 2. The Moral Disguises
 One of Jew-hatred’s most extraordinary achievements is convincing generation after generation that persecuting them is an act of social justice.
 Defending the faith. Defending the nation. Defending the oppressed.
 Defending Christianity from “Jewish influence.” Defending the “Aryan race” from “racial contamination.” Defending Palestinians from the “genocidal state.”
 Some accusations are centuries old, like the blood libel that Jews murder non-Jewish children, famously associated with William of Norwich in 1144, and echoed today in portrayals of Israelis as bloodthirsty child-killers.
 Yes, children have been killed in Gaza. They’ve also been killed in staggering numbers in Syria, Yemen and Sudan. Yet the imagery of bloodthirsty child-killers is, curiously enough, reserved for the Jewish state.
 Other accusations have evolved with the times, but you hardly need a degree in history to recognise the family resemblance. Age-old tropes of Jewish control over finance and governments resurface today in claims of sinister “Zionist” control over Western institutions.
 In today’s antiracist society, Jews, or Israelis, are cast as white supremacists, colonisers and genocidaires.
 Then there’s Holocaust inversion. After centuries of persecuting Jews, European societies came to regard Nazism as the embodiment of ultimate evil. And what happened? Within less than a century, Jews went from victims of Nazism to being portrayed as its modern-day successors. Holocaust survivors and their descendants now find themselves accused of perpetuating the very ideology that sought to annihilate them.
 Beginning in the postwar decades, Soviet propaganda helped popularise comparisons between Zionism and Nazism.¹ Today, Israelis are often depicted as the “new Nazis,” with the Holocaust invoked as an indictment of the Jewish state. The Soviet Union collapsed. Its propaganda, apparently, did not.
 Since 1945, the world has witnessed no shortage of atrocities that might invite comparisons with Nazism, yet few perpetrators seem to attract that comparison with quite the same gusto as the Jewish state.
 This adaptability is what makes Jew-hatred so enduring and dangerous: Jews are repeatedly cast as the embodiment of whatever a society most fears or despises, until hostility towards them feels like a moral obligation.
 It’s also why we shouldn’t be so confident we’d have had the courage to hide Anne Frank. Defying a prejudice endorsed by the prevailing culture is far harder than condemning it eighty years later.
 And while today’s antizionist movement fancies itself a brave, countercultural rebellion, its rhetoric is practically mainstream across academia, the arts and cultural institutions. Defending Israel, on the other hand, won’t land you in prison, at least not in the West. Not yet. But it might cost you your reputation, your career, your friendships, or your place in polite society.
 3. Collective Guilt
 For centuries, Jews have been treated not as individuals, but as members of a collective whose sins belong to them all. Add to this the old accusation of dual loyalty, the suspicion that Jews can never be fully trusted as citizens of their own countries.
 Today, Israel provides the perfect cover for both.
 Jewish artists, academics, students and ordinary citizens find themselves subjected to political litmus tests, demands to denounce Israel, and exclusion from spaces supposedly dedicated to equality and inclusion.
 We don’t demand that Chinese Australians denounce the Chinese Communist Party, or Sudanese abroad disavow their government, before allowing them to participate in public life. We recognise them as individuals.
 Unless they’re Jews. Then it’s “Netanyahu and the Israeli government are endangering Jews worldwide.” One wonders what the excuse for the collective punishment of Jews was before Netanyahu, before Israel existed?
 Yet Jews are expected to prove their innocence as a condition of acceptance, and even then, it’s often not enough.
 Recently, Israeli filmmaker Moshe Rosenthal was asked to clarify his position on Israel’s government before a Swiss film festival would screen his work. His producers explained they did not represent the government and they opposed the war. The festival cancelled the screenings anyway.²
 Quite how intimidating Jews and cancelling Israeli filmmakers advances Palestinian liberation remains one of life's great mysteries.
 Almost like it’s not about Palestinians, but about repackaging the collective punishment of Jews as something virtuous.
 History offers a grim reminder of the limits of appeasement, as I’ve explored here. The Yevsektsiya, Jewish Communists who suppressed Judaism and Zionism, were later caught in Stalin’s purges, with many dying in Soviet prisons and labour camps. In Iraq, Jewish businessman Shafiq Ades, with no known Zionist affiliations, was accused of aiding Israel and publicly hanged in 1948.
 You can renounce Zionism, shun your own people and demonstrate your loyalty, and you might even earn a place in polite society. Until, one day, you don’t. Such is the cruelty of collective guilt: you can never prove yourself innocent of someone else’s sins.
 If your solidarity with Palestinians requires Jews to answer collectively for Israel’s government, or makes their safety and acceptance conditional on renouncing Israel, you might want to consider why your idea of justice bears such an uncanny resemblance to centuries of anti-Jewish persecution.
 4. Double Standards
 Consider how countries responsible for the very atrocities Israel stands accused of, often on a far greater scale, face no comparable global movement demanding their dismantling. I’ve previously examined these accusations, and where they have a far stronger basis, here.
 China’s persecution of Uyghurs. Iran’s brutal repression of dissent. Atrocities in Sudan and Syria. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
 Yet while these crimes may prompt demands for accountability, Israel faces something altogether different: a global movement that treats the state’s existence as the crime.
 Where better to witness this extraordinary double standard than at the United Nations, the world’s self-appointed guardian of international morality?
 In 2025, the UN General Assembly adopted 15 condemnatory resolutions concerning Israel, compared with just 11 concerning every other country combined.³
 Over the previous decade: 173 against Israel, 80 against everyone else combined.
 The UN Human Rights Council even has a permanent agenda item dedicated specifically to Israel. Not Iran. Not North Korea. Not Russia. Israel.
 The rank double standards could hardly be on more spectacular display.
 You’ll notice that none of what I’m saying suggests Israel should be immune from criticism. But legitimate criticism, as opposed to prejudice, requires at least some semblance of proportionality and consistency.
 5. Conspiracy Thinking
 In 1945, George Orwell put his finger on one of the most enduring features of Jew-hatred, observing something that should be painfully obvious: “One of the marks of antisemitism is an ability to believe stories that could not possibly be true.”
 He recalled how, after a deadly stampede at a London Underground station during the war, rumours spread that Jews were responsible.⁴ There was no evidence or rational explanation. Yet people believed it.
 What baffled Orwell was how otherwise sensible, educated people could abandon their critical faculties when the subject turned to Jews.
 Accusations against Jews have long operated under suspended evidentiary standards. For centuries, respected institutions, clergy, newspapers and political authorities accused Jews of poisoning wells, spreading plague, ritually murdering Christian children, manipulating economies and secretly controlling governments.
 Jew-hatred creates a kind of collective contagion in which otherwise intelligent people accept increasingly fantastical accusations as self-evidently true.
 The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, a notorious antisemitic forgery published in the early twentieth century, purported to expose a Jewish conspiracy for world domination. Thoroughly debunked, its accusations nevertheless proved remarkably resilient, with many surviving to this day.⁵
 Variations of these conspiracies became staples of antisemitic propaganda across the Arab world, reinforced by Nazi Arabic-language broadcasts during the Second World War and subsequently circulated through political speeches, television and state-controlled media.⁶
 Eighty years after Orwell’s observation, consider the accusations circulating about Israel: training dogs to rape prisoners, harvesting organs in the middle of a war zone, claims that 14,000 babies would die within 48 hours from Israel’s starvation campaign, or that Israel possesses secret weapons capable of vaporising Palestinians.
 Claims that would ordinarily invite intense scrutiny are instead granted instant credibility and spread like wildfire when Israel is the accused.
 Most insidiously, these conspiracies have found legitimacy within prestigious Western institutions. As Israel becomes the supposed root cause of virtually every global injustice, the same narratives have spread through academia, NGOs, activist movements and cultural institutions, often with little more than “Zionists” substituted for Jews. Apparently, blaming Israel for the weather is no longer the exclusive preserve of Iran’s fundamentalist mullahs or a baker in some remote Jordanian village. These days, you can do it with an Ivy League degree.
 It’s worth remembering that Jew-hatred predates the modern left-right political spectrum by centuries. It has never belonged exclusively to one political camp, and there’s some fascinating research into why.
 A 2023 British study led by Dr Daniel Allington found that belief in malevolent global conspiracies was among the strongest predictors of anti-Jewish attitudes, alongside authoritarian tendencies.⁷
 In other words, someone’s susceptibility to conspiracy theories may tell us more about their inclination towards Jew-hatred than their political allegiance. Which helps explain the exquisite irony of left-wing antizionists championing “Zio”, an antisemitic slur popularised by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke.
 But good luck convincing someone in the grip of such beliefs otherwise. The genius of conspiracy thinking is that contradictory evidence is dismissed as propaganda. A lack of evidence becomes proof of just how sophisticated the conspiracy must be. Anyone challenging the narrative has simply been bought, brainwashed or compromised.
 I think this helps explain the pervasive influence of antizionism as an international movement. At its core, it draws on one of humanity’s oldest and most enduring conspiracy narratives, with centuries of accumulated prejudice ready to be repackaged as revelation.
 6. Scapegoating
 Notice how the patterns of Jew-hatred outlined above tend to flourish in societies already gripped by crisis, decline or impending collapse. Rather than confront their own political failures, economic decay or institutional corruption, they discover a convenient culprit.
 As the Black Death ravaged medieval Europe, Jews were accused of poisoning wells and spreading the plague, triggering massacres. As the Russian Empire descended into revolutionary turmoil, Jews were scapegoated for the unrest, becoming targets of violent pogroms. When Germany’s empire collapsed following its defeat in the First World War, military leaders helped popularise the myth that the nation had been stabbed in the back, with Jews blamed for a defeat its leaders refused to own.⁸
 The modern West is grappling with a profound crisis of identity. Decades of globalisation, demographic change and fragmented cultural identities have transformed the social fabric, while preoccupations with historical guilt have further complicated questions of national identity and belonging. Add economic insecurity, political polarisation and collapsing trust in institutions, and the conditions for scapegoating are ripe. And once again, Israel, Zionists and supposed Jewish influence over world affairs provide the go-to explanation for everything that’s gone wrong.
 It’s all so… predictable.
 The psychological appeal is obvious. Why wrestle with complex economic, political or social problems when you can identify a single enemy responsible for everything?
 It’s certainly easier than doing the hard work of examining your own institutions, leaders or the choices your society has made. But societies consumed by blaming Jews for their misfortunes don’t solve their problems. It’s a familiar symptom of a society in trouble, and a dangerous distraction from the failures driving its decline.
 We should have learned from history. Instead, we’re marching towards the same abyss, led by friends, colleagues and trusted institutions, all convinced they’re acting in the name of compassion and justice.

text:
Wan Ok Phansa, also referred to as Pavarana Day in Buddhist tradition, marks the end of the three-month Buddhist Lent. During this period, monks stay in their temples during the rainy season to focus on meditation, study, and religious practice. For Thai Buddhists, this day is a special time to celebrate the monks' dedication and welcome a new season of spiritual renewal.

One of the most popular traditions is Tak Bat Devarohana, commonly known as Tak Bat Devo, a morning almsgiving ceremony. At dawn on the day following Wan Ok Phansa, people gather at the foot of hillside temples or along the streets to offer food and other necessities to monks. In some parts of Thailand, people also offer Khao Tom Luk Yon, a traditional sticky rice treat wrapped in palm leaves. The highlight of the ceremony is the peaceful procession of monks walking through the community to receive these offerings.

The ceremony is based on a famous Buddhist story. According to Buddhist teachings, Lord Buddha spent the three-month Buddhist Lent in Tavatimsa Heaven, known in Thai as Daowadueng, where he taught his deceased mother. Tak Bat Devo celebrates his return to Earth. At hillside temples, the long staircases represent the heavenly staircase he used to descend. People gathering to offer food to the monks also reflect the joyful crowds who welcomed him in the ancient story.

text:
DIOGENES REIPUBLICAE AMERICANAE

Chad Jackson is fundamentally correct in his assertion that an inability to read white newspapers never precluded the existence of highly sophisticated, operational oral communication networks among early Black Americans. The interviewer’s  assumption that a lack of literacy meant a lack of awareness ignores the entire history of how news traveled through the Black community.

 However, the ultimate failure of the Homestead Acts reflects a structural trap identical to forcing a newly freed slave to read a Chinese newspaper to exercise his right to vote. The American legal apparatus constructed a grand illusion, offering an egalitarian, colorblind right on paper while engineering localized, administrative, and economic conditions designed to ensure total exclusion.

To dissect why knowledge of the land never translated to widespread acquisition, the stark demographic reality of the Black population at the dawn of emancipation must be laid bare. In 1860, a mere 11 percent of Black Americans existed as free citizens, while a staggering 89 percent remained trapped in chattel slavery. 

For the small, urbanized minority of long standing free Black families, who had spent decades building businesses, trades, and localized stability, uprooting to brave the perilous, capital intensive Western frontier under the 1862 Act was an immense risk. They were managing survival within the conditions they knew, leaving the promise of the frontier to those with nothing left to lose.

The primary target of agrarian independence was the nearly four million newly freed slaves who possessed nothing but the clothes on their backs. Demanding that a family, freshly released from generations of unpaid labor, suddenly finance a 1,500 mile migration out West, purchase heavy oxen, wagons, steel plows, and seed was the ultimate systemic gatekeeping mechanism. It was a rigged literacy test of the highest order. The door to the West was technically unlocked by the 14th Amendment, but the entry fee was a sum of generational wealth the state had deliberately withheld. Knowledge of the opportunity flowed perfectly through church benches and traveling laborers, but the practical ability to execute the claim was a structural impossibility.

While approximately 180,000 Black Union soldiers successfully amassed a modest surplus from their military pay, that precious capital was instantly diverted to an urgent, sacred priority that preceded any desire for property: reconstructing the fractured family unit. Generations of the domestic slave trade had ruthlessly torn lineages apart. Upon mustering out, a veteran's immediate compulsion was not land speculation in Nebraska or Kansas. It was embarking on grueling journeys back into the belly of the Southern beast, placing advertisements in Black church publications, and tracing refugee lines to locate displaced wives, parents, and children. Survival and reconnection took precedence over pioneering.

When the Southern Homestead Act of 1866 was passed to offer public land closer to home across five Southern states, the "Chinese newspaper" test merely transformed into a bureaucratic gauntlet. Ex Confederate clerks weaponized parallel, hidden land ledgers, intentionally destroyed applications, and fabricated arbitrary processing fees to run out the clock on the exclusive filing window reserved for freedmen. 

Much of the 46 million acres set aside consisted of unfarmable pine barrens and malaria ridden swamplands. Chad Johnson is entirely correct that the information traveled seamlessly through the community without newspapers, but the administrative machinery was completely rigged to ensure the soil slipped through Black hands.

This specific blueprint of institutional exclusion granting a sweeping federal right but surrendering its administration to local, white dominated gatekeepers drew a straight, unbroken line directly to the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944. The G.I. Bill was celebrated as a colorblind masterpiece of American social policy, promising low-interest mortgages, business loans, and tuition free college to every veteran who survived World War II. Yet, just like the Homestead Acts, the mechanism of exclusion was engineered into the local bureaucracy. Southern segregationists in Congress explicitly mandated that the bill's benefits be processed not by Washington, but by localized Veteran Administration offices and state banks.

The tragic result was historically identical. When a Black soldier returned home to a state like South Carolina after surviving the bloody campaigns of the Pacific, the federal promise vanished the moment he crossed the threshold of the local office. Local bankers routinely denied mortgages, redlining Black veterans out of the post war suburban housing boom. White universities barred their doors, and local vocational counselors flatly refused to process paperwork for professional or technical training. 

Even in a supposedly more liberal area like the NYC/NJ area out of 67k  mortgages 1947 only 100 were awarded to blacks and when you consider the blacks were about 11% of the military.  Not a lot . A decorated Black veteran sought to build wealth or secure an education, the local authorities denied the application and told him to go right back to the field. Whether a freedman in 1866 or a soldier in 1945, the system ensured that a colorblind paper right would always be defeated by a localized reality. It is part of my family‘s lore . My paternal grandfather fought in the Pacific on New Guinea and Okinawa . My maternal grandfather fought through France, Belgium and Germany. He was in the Red Bull Express driving gas to  feed tanks . Then he volunteered to be thrown into the Hurtgen Forest  through the Battle of the Bulge and was a member of experimental fifth platoons attached to white companies. They both came back no G.I. Bill but their grandchildren did well for themselves. Their sacrifice was worth it.

text:
Clara Hale hid babies from city inspectors, because her Harlem licence covered fifteen children and she sometimes had thirty or forty in the building. The inspectors knew. She said they used to ask her not to give them any trouble.

On West 122nd Street in Harlem there is a row of brownstones that went up in 1910. Five floors each, about nineteen feet across, built as single-family houses for people who kept servants.

For more than thirty years, the entrance of one of them was lined with baby strollers.

Inside, past a room stocked with enough formula and food to feed an infant army for a week, there was a long corridor and a dining room with beveled glass panelling left over from Harlem's rich years, and in that dining room most afternoons an elegant woman in her eighties ate her lunch late.

Her name was Clara Hale, and Harlem called her Mother Hale.

That much is the story people tell. The part almost nobody tells is what her permission to do it actually rested on, and how easily it could be taken away.

Start before the brownstone, in a five-room walk-up a few blocks north.

By 1969 Hale was sixty-four and had just stopped. She had been taking in other people's children since the Depression and she had earned the right to sit down.

Her daughter Lorraine was out in the neighborhood that year when she saw a young woman on the street having trouble holding herself up, and having trouble holding on to the baby in her arms.

Lorraine stopped and talked to her. She worked out fairly quickly that heroin was going to take this child away from this woman whether either of them wanted it or not.

So she gave the woman an address. It was the address where she and her two brothers and about forty foster children had been raised, and she told the woman to go there and then go get herself into treatment.

The next day the baby was on the doorstep.

Accounts differ on the small details. Some say a park bench, some say a sidewalk on 146th Street, some say the mother came herself and slipped away while Hale was in another room on the telephone.

What nobody disputes is what Hale did. She did not call the city.

She took the child, a little girl, and stayed up with her.

A newborn in withdrawal does not cry the way other newborns cry. The body goes rigid, being held does not stop it, and it can go on for weeks before it eases.

Hale walked her through it. The mother came back later with her other children and left those too, and eventually came back well and took all of them home again.

Nobody paid Hale anything for any of it.

Word went through Harlem the way word does when something is free and nobody is filling in a form. Within two months there were twenty-two drug-exposed babies in five rooms, cribs pushed wall to wall.

For a year and a half there was no public money at all. Lorraine and her brothers Nathan and Kenneth took extra work and put their wages into formula, cribs and rent.

The woman doing this was sixty-four years old and had already done a version of it once.

Hale was born in 1905, and the record cannot agree on where. Most sources say Elizabeth City in North Carolina, one says Philadelphia, and all of them agree she was raised in Philadelphia.

Her father was gone when she was small. Her mother kept the household going by cooking for other people and taking in boarders, which is to say Hale grew up in a house that always had somebody else's life in it.

By sixteen her mother was dead too, and she finished high school with no parents left.

She married Thomas Hale and came to New York. He died of cancer when she was twenty-seven, leaving her with three young children in the Depression.

She cleaned houses in the day and theaters at night. She could not stand leaving her own children alone in the dark to do it, so she started keeping other working mothers' children at home instead and charging two dollars a week.

Some of those mothers had come north from Southern towns and the Midwest specifically to have their babies where nobody at home would know. Hale kept those children Monday to Friday, or for as long as it took the mother to work up to telling her own parents.

She became a licensed foster mother and kept seven or eight at a time for the better part of thirty years. About forty children were raised in those rooms.

Later she told Parade what that had actually produced. They were grown, they were doctors and lawyers and everything else, almost all of them still called, and she said "I have about sixty grandchildren."

Her own daughter was nearly sixteen before she worked out that all the others were not her brothers and sisters.

Hale House was a licensed operation. That needs saying plainly, because the truth of what happened to it is worse when you get it right.

New York State law had a definition for the kind of place she was running. A group home was a family-type home for not fewer than seven and not more than twelve children, and those children had to be at least five years of age.

Hale's house was full of people who were four weeks old.

So a licence alone could not hold it up. What kept the doors open was a second piece of paper, a waiver from the state regulations, and a waiver has to be signed by somebody.

Under Mayor Abraham Beame and then under Mayor Edward Koch, Hale House was granted them, over and over, year after year.

That is entirely lawful, and it is entirely conditional. The most famous children's home in America stood on an exception that officials were free to stop making.

She also went past even that exception, and said so out loud to a newspaper.

By 1984 Hale House had seven college-educated care workers on staff and a licence to house fifteen children. It also had a reputation, well earned, for never once turning a child away.

So the real number was not fifteen. She told the Los Angeles Times that sometimes there were thirty or forty children in the house.

No waiver covered that. That part was simply against her own licence, and she knew it, and every one of those extra children had come from a hospital, a police officer, a church, or a mother standing on the step with nowhere else to go.

Her answer was not to refuse the next one. Her answer, in her own three words to the Times, was that "we hide them."

She said the inspectors understood exactly what was going on. Her account of it was that they would ask her, almost fondly, not to give them any trouble.

So the record holds two things at once. A woman quietly over the limit of her own licence, and a city that had decided, unofficially and without writing anything down, to look at the wall.

There was a second thing she did outside the usual machinery, and it is the part that makes her more than a kind old woman with a full house.

The city returned a child to a parent through a judge. Hale House did not require a court's approval.

Her rule was that a mother could leave her baby, but she had to go into a rehabilitation programme, and when she came back well she got her child.

No court signed anything. Hale looked at the woman and decided.

Nor was it sentimental. A baby stayed at Hale House about eighteen months, and for every one of those months the mother was required to come once a week, without fail.

Her reason was practical to the point of being brutal. She was not going to hand a child over to a stranger at the end of eighteen months, and after a year and a half apart, a mother is a stranger unless somebody makes her turn up.

So the mothers turned up. Contemporary profiles reported that close to nine in ten of those children were eventually reunited with their families.

She went further still and opened a complex of thirty apartments so that women coming out of rehabilitation had somewhere to live while they got their children back.

The point was never the babies alone. The point was putting families back together, and she trusted addicted Black mothers to become well in a decade when almost no institution in New York would.

She knew what it cost them afterward, too. She told a reporter that the mothers did not move back to the old neighborhood, because having had your child at Hale House carried a stigma, and because they were frightened that going back would undo everything.

They came anyway, some Saturdays, to show her how the children had grown.

In the early 1970s Percy Sutton, then Manhattan borough president, looked at the same overcrowded apartment the clipboards were looking at and read it completely differently.

He helped her get public funding and a federal grant. With it she took a vacant five-story brownstone on West 122nd Street and rebuilt it.

The floors were laid out by what each child still needed. A floor for play and preschool, a nursery for the babies who had come through withdrawal, and a floor where new arrivals were kept while they went through it.

In 1975 it was licensed as a child-care facility. There were only two programmes in the entire city working on chemically dependent newborns, and Hale House was the only one that took the children in at birth and carried them the whole way.

On a Monday in February 1987, a reporter from the Christian Science Monitor came through that building at lunchtime and wrote down what a room full of these children actually looked like.

Nobody apologised to him for the doorbell that only worked sometimes, or for the smell of the nursery.

He was given a tour and could not get down the corridor because one child after another came and hugged his knees.

At the table, twelve pairs of small hands were clasped together to give thanks before the meal. A care worker called across the room to a child named Nicole to be careful, because it was hot, and because it was not on her plate yet, and to wait a minute.

There was a two-year-old there named Vernelle.

The staff told the reporter she was often withdrawn and despondent, and that they understood it as damage from the narcotics she had been born with. That day was one of her good days.

She moved around the room in a red dress with a frilly white collar, in front of adults who were plainly delighted by her.

And the reporter noticed something. The shape of her face, tilted up like that, matched the silhouette on a poster hanging in the Hale House offices a few blocks away.

The poster said "Nothing is higher than life."

That is Vernelle, aged two, in a red dress, on 2 February 1987, in a building the State of New York had no ordinary category for.

Hale ran that room on rules that would fit on an index card. Nobody who did not like children was to be employed there, and no child in that house was to be shouted at or hit, which she admitted was a hard standard to keep.

On the evening of 6 February 1985 she was in Washington, seated near Nancy Reagan in the gallery of the House chamber.

She was seventy-nine and had not been well, and said afterward that she went because she wanted the children to see it.

At the close of the State of the Union address, President Reagan introduced a West Point cadet named Jean Nguyen, and then he turned to Hale.

He told the chamber there was a woman there, born seventy-nine years ago, who cared for infants born to heroin-addicted mothers, children who were sometimes left on her doorstep.

He said that if you went to her house at night you might see her silhouette in the window, walking the floor with a child in her arms.

Then he said it plainly. "Mother Hale of Harlem, and she, too, is an American hero."

The room stood up. Members of Congress, the Supreme Court and the Cabinet, all of them on their feet for a retired cleaning woman from 122nd Street.

Nothing in the rulebook changed that night.

The regulation still said five years of age. Hale House still had newborns in it, and a licence for fifteen, and sometimes forty children inside, and it still ran on an exception that somebody had to keep signing.

By 1985 that exception came with about a hundred and ninety thousand dollars a year in public money and roughly thirty thousand more in private gifts.

Then the signatures stopped.

In 1989 the city stopped referring children to her, having decided that the worst of the epidemic had passed and that its own foster system could place these babies better than she could.

In September 1990 the New York Times put the fight on its pages under a headline saying Hale House was fighting City Hall over the care of babies.

That autumn the city moved to close the group nursery outright, and in October it stopped granting the exception and pulled the funding.

Nothing about that was improper. New York simply enforced the rule it had been waiving since Beame.

Hale was eighty-five years old.

She and Lorraine went out and raised the money themselves, from churches and neighbors and strangers, and the house stayed open.

The children came anyway. Parents brought them, police officers brought them, churches brought them, and by then it was not only babies in withdrawal but babies born with HIV and children whose mothers were dying of AIDS.

Somewhere between four and five hundred children came through during the worst of the drug years. Her obituary in the New York Times put the lifetime figure at close to a thousand infants.

Asked in 1990 what she counted as success, she said she thought all of them were success stories, and offered as her proof that she had never heard of one of her children going to jail.

She died on 18 December 1992, of complications from a stroke, at eighty-seven.

After she died, the sculptor Robert Berks was commissioned to make a bronze of her for the front of the house.

It showed her standing with a child in her arms, and it stood out on the sidewalk on West 122nd Street where anybody walking past could see it.

In October 2008 the Associated Press photographed that statue and reported, on the account of the man then running Hale House, that Clara Hale's ashes had been placed inside the bronze.

If that is right, and the organization's own director is the one who said it, then the last thing standing on that block was not a marker for her. It was her.

What happened to the organization afterward is documented and it is not hers. In 2001 the state opened an investigation into Hale House's finances, and in 2002 the attorney general brought a seventy-count indictment against Lorraine Hale and her husband over money taken from the charity.

They were removed by a new board and later pleaded guilty, nine years after Clara Hale was dead.

The children left in stages. By October 2008 the group beds were empty, the last of the thirteen remaining children having gone a few months before.

Then the buildings went.

In December 2013 Hale House put the five-story brownstone at 152 West 122nd Street on the market at two million seven hundred thousand dollars.

In June 2014 a developer bought it for two million two hundred thousand, and by the end of that July the permits were filed to cut it into four apartments, three floor-throughs and an owner's duplex, all free market.

The house next door at 154 stood empty. When it was listed in 2023, the sales copy explained that it had been vacant for more than eight years and had belonged to a nonprofit that had closed its operations.

That is how the record now describes what she built. A nonprofit which closed its operations.

Her name went somewhere else.

In 1993, the year after she died, the city renamed the bus garage up on 146th Street the Mother Clara Hale Bus Depot.

Twenty years later it knocked that garage down and built a new one on the same block. Three floors, a mezzanine, room for a hundred and fifty buses, at a construction cost put at two hundred and twenty-five million dollars and a total project figure reported at two hundred and sixty-two million.

The transit authority commissioned an artist to make a mosaic for the Lenox Avenue wall and called it Mother Hale's Garden. First graders from a school nearby drew the flowers that went into the glass.

The ribbon was cut in November 2014.

That was the same year the house sold. While the city was finishing that building with her name across the front, the rooms where Vernelle learned to walk were being measured for floor-throughs.

The bronze came off the sidewalk.

When the sculptor's own models and drawings for it were catalogued for auction, the listing noted that Hale House had ceased operations and that the sculpture had been removed. Where it went afterward has not been publicly recorded.

So here is the correction to carry, and it costs nothing. When this story comes past you, do not let it stop at the president and the standing ovation, because that is the part that cost America nothing.

Say the rest of it. Everything she built stood on an exception that somebody had to sign every year, and she spent those years with more children in the house than her licence allowed, hiding them from the people sent to count.

New York has a building with her name on the front and room inside it for a hundred and fifty buses.

It does not have her.

text:
Seven days ago he could not move his neck.

He had dived to make a tackle, and the tight end's knee caught him in the helmet. He lay on the turf for close to ten minutes while they immobilized him, then they carried him off on a stretcher and drove him to a hospital.

A few hours later reporters saw him walking around the locker room, which is the first good thing in this story.

His name is Kendal Daniels.

Today he wore the green dot, which means he was the one calling the defense. He led Atlanta in tackles with nine of his own. He intercepted Brock Purdy and ran it back to the red zone, and Atlanta kicked the field goal that made it a two score game.

On San Francisco's next drive he recovered the fumble that ended it.

Here is what he said about the thing that happened to him seven days earlier.

"I've never not walked off the field after an injury."

"It was a bad feeling, and I'm blessed to be able to play this week."

He could not turn his neck for days. He was back at practice on the Wednesday.

Now go back and look at how he got here, because it is stranger than you would think.

He grew up in Beggs, Oklahoma, a town of about 1,200 people. Basketball was his sport. At 6 foot 5, you can see why. He did not join the football team until he was a sophomore.

Two years after that he was rated the fifth best safety in America and the best recruit in his state.

Then Oklahoma pulled his offer.

So he committed to Texas A&M, changed his mind, and went to Oklahoma State instead. As a redshirt freshman he had 45 tackles and three interceptions, and he ended a 41 to 34 win over Texas with an interception in the final seconds.

He was the Big 12 Defensive Freshman of the Year.

Four years later he transferred to Oklahoma anyway, the school that had taken the offer back.

Atlanta traded down in April and took him with the 134th pick.

Here is one of his teammates on today.

"He's got whatever it is, and it's a testament to his preparation."

Be straight about where this actually sits. He was only out there calling the defense because Divine Deablo is hurt. He is a fourth round rookie with one enormous afternoon, not a settled thing. And a neck is not an ankle, so nobody should be treating last Sunday as finished business.

But a kid who could not turn his head seven days ago spent this afternoon telling ten grown men where to stand, and then he went and took the ball away twice.

When were you the most scared and went back anyway.

So upon further reflection, I'm really annoyed. 

I get offered filed passes for successful PSL referrals, as is the Panthers promotional policy.
My buddy gets four club level PSLs which isnt cheap. 

I get the call saying I'm getting sideline passes for the game this weekend so I hype it up to my 10 year old who gets to go to one game a year if he's lucky. So we choose this week to be his game, and then we get checked in and our passes are in the NE corner where only the bucs are warming up. 

So after spending the week telling my son how fun it will be to see his favorite players warming up and maybe even seeing them up close, then waking up at 6AM to drive the 3 hours to Charlotte and not getting to tailgate so we can get in as soon as doors open, so he can get a good spot at warm ups and not be behind people, we spend the morning watching the bucs warm up alongside a majority of Bucs fans and WAGs 

My son is constantly asking if any of our guys are going to be near us during warm ups and I have to be like.  "You see that little dot over there in blue, that Jalen Coker."

THANKFULLY a couple of Bucs guys and a position coach walked over and played catch with him but he finally admitted on the 3 hr drive home that it was really disappointing that we spent the entire pregame with the other team instead of the Panthers. 

I know this can come off as being unappreciative of ab experience not many people get, but seeing my kid br disappointed and let down after I hyped it up, sucks. 

I think any of the other three sideline pods would have been fine and fun but that was really disappointing. 

Partially my fault for hyping up something not knowing all the details, but man, after getting to think on it all the way home, I just needed to vent. 

Thanks to Kameron Johnson and DeMonte Capehart for showing my boy some love, congrats on the win.

Bought a good rep to see whether I like it, buy real if I do.  But once I had a rep, it was just a matter of time.

Reps, even good ones are NOT as high quality (or weren’t) as real but they look great.

His store is still there- when I was there last time, they had just a few Rolex watches, market was nuts at the time- he said that he offers the same trade in value deal too.  Owner’s son now runs the place.

Grey market inflated pricing is a new thing, I have always bought older models that look as new.

text:
Forensically who has better positioning for a moon to earth base, considering geographical landscaping and historical logistics in this

Grok:

The United States holds the stronger overall position for integrated Moon-to-Earth basing and logistics when weighing historical operational experience, recovery infrastructure, tracking networks, and industrial depth against pure geographic advantages.

China has a clear edge in Earth-side launch latitude and is closing gaps with independent relay systems, but the forensic balance favors the US for end-to-end reliability in the near-to-medium term. 

Both converge on the lunar South Pole for long-term bases, where surface landscape challenges are shared.

Earth-side geography and launch positioning

Lower-latitude sites gain a free boost from Earth’s rotation (highest at the equator), improving payload to LEO, GTO, or lunar trajectories, or reducing propellant needs. Launch azimuth options and downrange safety also matter.

China’s Wenchang (Hainan, ~19.6°N) is superior on pure latitude. It is China’s southernmost and only major coastal site, enabling sea transport of large rocket stages (critical for Long March 5/10-class vehicles used for lunar missions). 

It supports efficient paths toward lunar trajectories and has been used for Chang’e sample-return and deep-space flights. 

The US primary East Coast complex (Cape Canaveral / Kennedy Space Center, ~28.5°N) is less efficient than Wenchang but still strong, with established eastward Atlantic trajectories, extensive pads (including historical Apollo/Saturn V sites), and mature ocean recovery zones. 

Vandenberg is higher-latitude and oriented for polar/SSO work. The US compensates with scale of existing infrastructure and commercial capacity (e.g., Falcon/Starship families). 

Russia’s Baikonur (~46°N) is a clear disadvantage for efficiency to lunar paths.

Coastal access, weather resilience, and heavy-lift logistics give Wenchang a geographic edge for raw launch performance.
The US advantage is institutional maturity and recovery geography rather than latitude alone.

Lunar surface landscape and site suitability

“Landscaping” here means terrain (slope, flatness, crater density), illumination, resources (especially water ice), Earth visibility/comms line-of-sight, and accessibility for landing, surface ops, and return trajectories.

South Pole (current focus of both Artemis and ILRS): Permanently shadowed regions (PSRs) in crater floors can trap water ice; nearby elevated rims/peaks offer near-continuous or high cumulative sunlight for power.

Candidate zones (e.g., areas near Shackleton, Nobile Rim, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton, de Gerlache) are small and constrained.

Terrain is rugged—steep slopes, limited flat safe landing ellipses, extreme thermal contrasts, and complex lighting.

Earth visibility is intermittent depending on exact longitude/latitude; some sites need relays. Both programs target this region for sustainability (resources + power), accepting higher engineering risk.

Nearside equatorial/mid-latitude maria (historical Apollo preference): Broad, relatively smooth basaltic plains (e.g., Tranquillitatis, parts of Oceanus Procellarum, Insularum).

Easier landing and surface mobility, continuous or near-continuous Earth line-of-sight for direct comms, simpler free-return or lower-energy return trajectories, and access to resources such as ilmenite.

Apollo constrained sites near the equator on the nearside precisely for these operational and safety reasons (smoothness, approach path, propellant margins, free-return geometry, continuous communications).

Modern multi-factor studies still rate near-equatorial maria highly for research stations or bases when polar ice is not the overriding priority.

South Pole landscape favors long-term resource-driven bases once engineering is solved; equatorial nearside favors lower-risk initial logistics, frequent access, and simpler Moon-to-Earth traffic.

text:
🐇 THE RABBIT HOLE
The Signal That Never Returned

On August 15, 1977, a radio telescope in Ohio detected an unusually powerful signal coming from the direction of Sagittarius, and nearly 50 years later, scientists still haven’t figured out exactly what produced it. The telescope was called Big Ear, and what it recorded has become one of the most interesting mysteries in radio astronomy.

A few days after the detection, astronomer Jerry Ehman was reviewing the telescope’s computer printouts when he noticed six unusual characters. 6EQUJ5. He circled them in red ink and wrote Wow! beside them. Those characters represented the strength of the signal over six consecutive measurements, reaching about 30 times the normal background variation at its peak.

The frequency made the discovery even more interesting. The signal appeared near 1420 MHz, the natural radio frequency of neutral hydrogen, the most abundant element in the universe. Scientists had already identified that part of the radio spectrum as a promising place to search for transmissions from another civilization because hydrogen is found throughout the universe.

Big Ear was a fixed telescope that relied on Earth’s rotation to scan the sky. A distant source would normally pass through its receiving beam over about 72 seconds, gradually increasing in strength before fading away. The signal followed that pattern almost perfectly, but Big Ear had two receiving beams, and a persistent source should normally have appeared in both about three minutes apart. This signal was only detected in one, and researchers couldn’t determine which beam had received it.

Scientists searched the same region of space repeatedly over the following years without detecting the signal again. In 2024, researchers examining archived observations from the Arecibo Observatory proposed a possible explanation involving cold hydrogen clouds. A powerful event from a magnetar, an extremely magnetic neutron star, could potentially amplify the radio emissions from one of these clouds and produce a signal similar to what Big Ear recorded.

Further research in 2025 and 2026 produced additional findings. Updated calculations placed the signal’s frequency near 1420.726 MHz and its peak intensity above 300 Janskys, a measurement of radio signal strength. Researchers also identified other possible signals in archived observations, although no confirmed connection to the original event has been established.

One detail that often gets overlooked is the famous 72 seconds. That was the time Big Ear observed the signal crossing its receiving beam. It doesn’t establish when the emission actually began or ended. The source could have been active before the telescope detected it and continued after Earth’s rotation carried the beam away.

The original printout still exists, and scientists have been able to examine the recorded measurements using technology that wasn’t available in 1977. The hydrogen cloud theory offers a possible natural explanation, but nobody has confirmed what caused the original signal. Its exact source remains unidentified, and no confirmed repeat has ever been detected.

Scientists had already identified this particular region of the radio spectrum as a logical place to search for extraterrestrial intelligence. Then in 1977, an extraordinarily strong signal appeared near that very frequency, followed the expected pattern of a distant source passing through the telescope’s beam, and disappeared.

Almost 50 years later, we still don’t know what produced it, how long it was active, or whether anything like it will ever be detected again.

Treatment options for an acoustic neuroma
Yin Ren, MD, PhD, an otologist at the Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, explains the three main treatment options for an acoustic neuroma.
Tumor size, hearing ability, age and overall health are all important factors in determining the best treatment for an acoustic neuroma. Our multidisciplinary team will work with you to select the best approach and provide you with the most optimal outcomes. Management approaches include:
•Treatment through observation - If the tumor is small and you are experiencing few symptoms, you may only need to have the tumor checked annually via an MRI scan. Smaller tumors may grow very slowly or not at all over a period of time. However, your hearing may still decline over time even if the tumor doesn’t grow.
•Stereotactic radiation - Stereotactic radiation is a nonsurgical procedure usually used on a tumor that's growing (determined through multiple MRIs). The radiation, given through one or more outpatient appointments, is aimed precisely through special equipment with the patient in specific positions. This treatment does not require a long recovery and will stop the growth of the tumor in most cases; however, it could adversely affect hearing.
•Microsurgery - Some people choose surgery for their tumor management. This decision is highly individualized and dependent on various factors, including tumor size, tumor location and residual hearing. Your overall health also plays an important role in the decision-making.
At the Ohio State Wexner Medical Center, our treatment team has extensive experience in the three surgical approaches available for acoustic neuromas.
1The translabyrinthine approach is performed through an incision behind the ear. The surgeon will then remove part of the temporal bone and inner ear to access the tumor. This technique is useful for large tumors or for patients with substantial hearing loss as well as if hearing preservation is unlikely.
2The retrosigmoid approach is performed through an incision behind the ear but does not involve removal of the inner ear. This approach is useful for people with tumors of all sizes and has a potential to preserve hearing.
3The middle cranial fossa approach is performed through an incision in front of and above the ear. The inner ear parts are preserved, and the tumor is accessed from above. This surgical approach is ideal for small tumors, tumors located in the internal auditory canal and for patients with good preoperative hearing. The middle cranial fossa approach offers the highest likelihood of long-term hearing preservation.

Joe Caminiti of Bristol, Connecticut, is 101 years old. This year he flew to Washington, D.C., for the 81st Iwo Jima Reunion, one of just 15 World War II veterans there, and only six of them survived Iwo Jima.

Veterans were offered wheelchairs for the long walk into the National Museum of the United States Marine Corps. Caminiti first refused. The Bristol Edition reports a general traveling with the group ordered him: “𝘠𝘰𝘶 𝘢𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘪𝘵, 𝘔𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘦.”

He sat. But once he was inside the main hall, Caminiti rose from the wheelchair and stayed on his feet for the rest of the visit.

On the first day of the battle, he landed troops in the 10th wave. Then he spent 35 days hauling supplies and troops and evacuating the wounded. At the reunion he handed the Iwo Jima Association of America a copy of 𝘊𝘰𝘯𝘯𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘶𝘵 𝘏𝘦𝘳𝘰𝘦𝘴, which lists the 𝟏𝟎𝟎 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐭 𝐦𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐝∗𝐞𝐝 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐬𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝, four of them from Bristol.

Asked to take a bow, he wouldn't. “𝘐 𝘢𝘮 𝘯𝘰 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘰,” he said, calling the fallen “𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘦 𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘰𝘦𝘴.” Eighty-one years after the flag went up on Mount Suribachi, a man who earned every honor in the room spent it honoring someone else.

𝐄𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐲-𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫, 𝐚 𝟏𝟎𝟏-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫-𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐈𝐰𝐨 𝐉𝐢𝐦𝐚 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐯𝐨𝐫 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐨𝐧'𝐭 𝐬𝐢𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐝.

Lucas told the story incorrectly, because he needed to believe that the Empire was wrong and the Sith were evil. 

In truth, a setting involving a hegemonic and demilitarized galactic republic with no serious external challengers would have a history of constant warfare and recurring imperial consolidations, not a thousand years of stable democratic and republican government. 

Separatist movements would be endless and unstoppable without a central military. This chaos would mean dark-aligned Force sensitives would constantly rise to power, because their abilities would give them a competitive advantage over rivals, the crisis conditions would generate sufficient desperation to overlook or even favor them, and no central force would be able to stop them.

The Jedi would, therefore, either be an irrelevant or persecuted minority, or would turn into a body of power-seeking militants to suppress darkside emergence and protect themselves from persecution. Because planets and sectors would empower darksiders whenever it advanced their political interests, the Jedi would require the power to overrule them and would therefore demand centralization and formal authority. The civilian authorities would demand order, or they would be divided among multiple principalities seeking dominance and to avoid being dominated. The Sith would pursue conquest and dominion, and would be readily empowered by any coalition of interests desiring the same end.

Given this, the choice on offer is not between republican liberty and tyrannical Empire, but between a peaceful galaxy and one riven by strife. The republican form is a fleeting pause between anarchy and order, because all forces within it converge on its empowerment or its dissolution, and nothing forces their compromise. Choosing Palpatine is choosing the only way to rescue the galaxy from structural crisis; choosing the Republic is choosing to preserve the conditions that make ongoing crisis inevitable. 

Lucas is an American who wanted a galaxy of Americans; in reality, he placed Octavian and Agrippa at the helm of a dying republic, and tried to tell his audience that Brutus could have stopped the Principate.

text:
IP is Intellectual Parasitism, 
It is not surprising that proponents of this lifestyle do not want their ideas cross-examined, and try to obfuscate any analysis focusing on contradictions. 

The post I am responding to illustrates a recurring problem: people would rather express their misconceptions than engage with the actual idea. Rand and Rothbard both struggled with this reality.

"Instead of Austrianism (Austrian Economics) slotting under Objectivist ethics in the narrow scope of economics, Zulu is *subordinating* Objectivism under Austrianist philosophy."

Austrian economics integrates observations from reality in the same way Objectivism does. People act to achieve ends. Those ends may be consistent with the requirements of human life, or they may evade them. Economics describes available means. It does not prescribe ends. Objectivism supplies the normative standard. The two address different questions. They do not form a hierarchy.

Take a simple case. The judgment "I ought to survive, therefore I ought to eat" sets a condition (nourishment). Economics then identifies which methods of allocating scarce means best satisfy that condition.

"At the heart of this worldview is the idea of "scarcity." This is a post-Kantian, collectivist, materialist, anti-production, primacy of consciousness idea that negates the fundamental human problem of how to survive. It starts by assuming a static quantities premise; i.e., "the goods are here.""

This misstates the Austrian view. One of the first observations of Austrian economics is that certain actions are mutually exclusive. A physical resource cannot occupy two places or serve two incompatible uses at the same time. Using a resource for one purpose precludes using it for another. That is an opportunity cost. It follows from the law of identity (A is A).

Scarcity is an integration from observation. Within any given area, some resources are closer, easier to extract, or more suitable for a given use than others. Relative location and the physical properties of the world make rivalry possible over particular units of resources.

"But, unlike a paradise of unlimited goods, these proponents say, in real life there are only so many goods yet fewer people to have them."

This is not the claim. The observation is simply that using a particular scarce resource for one purpose excludes its simultaneous use for another purpose.

"So other people's wishes to command the scarce goods "come under conflict" with other people's wishes, and the way to resolve this conflict is to assign boundaries to these goods so we can all get along with each other."

Every system of resource allocation resolves conflicts over rivalrous uses by assigning boundaries. The distinctive claim of the Austrian school and Anarcho-Capitalist Natural Law is that the assignment can be made without logical or performative contradictions.

"Rand's philosophy takes a completely different approach."

It does not. I know of no passage in which Rand denies that physical resources are subject to opportunity costs. She must necessarily submit to the law of identity and avoid contradictions. If Rand contradicts her own foundations in a statement, that statement can be classified as an error and ignored.
This is why Objectivism should not become Randianism, even if the author erroneously claims otherwise.

"She starts with the individual and asks: what does man need in order to survive, i.e., in order to sustain himself? What she observes is that all living organisms live by a process of self-sustaining action. They act to gain values from their surroundings to maintain their lives."

This description of the end does not specify the means, except that the means must be consistent with reason and free of contradictions.

"As you can see, there are already two main differences to these approaches: Rand says that the fundamental problem is that of survival, and that values, to be gained, must be acquired through action."

This is not a difference. Praxeology describes the same mechanism of action. It simply refrains from evaluating the ends. A complete philosophy therefore requires a theory of values, which Objectivism supplies.

"By contrast, (Austrian Economics) ignores the problem of survival"

It does not. Economics is a tool for analyzing means, comparable to a measuring instrument. A tape measure reports distance. It does not tell you whether the distance is relevant to survival. Requiring a descriptive tool to supply normative conclusions confuses the two domains.

"and treats values / goods as if they are already here, with the only problem being how to distribute them."

Goods and values are distinct. Goods are physical aspects of reality. Values are judgments about what promotes or hinders a person's life. The economic value of a good depends on the actor's ranking of ends and on opportunity costs. These concepts should not be conflated.

"Note the definition that Zulu offers for property. He defines property rights by their consequence and through negation (both logical errors)."

The definition is not a logical error. It is reached by elimination. Every alternative either produces a formal contradiction or a performative contradiction in argumentation. This is the same method used to establish foundational axioms by Rand, as inspired by the arguments of Aristotle.

"He says that ownership is the right to exclude because he starts from the collectivist premise of people claiming their whims on static quantities."

This is incorrect. Ownership is the right to exclude because that is what distinguishes it from mere possession. The definition follows from the nature of rivalrous resources and from the requirement of non-contradiction.

This is an individualist principle. On an unowned island, Crusoe is the first to emborder a stick. If Friday later claims the same stick, the facts of who acted first are ascertainable. The firstcomer has a claim that does not depend on collective whim. Collective whim can ignore reality at its peril and become an engineering problem.

"This is absurd if you actually looks at reality. Simple examples of restaurant owners who invite people into their property or a person lending his book to a friend demonstrate that property is not always *literally* excluded from the use of others."

In both cases the owner voluntarily suspends the right to exclude under known conditions. The owner retains the power to reassert it ("Leave" or "Return the book"). The examples illustrate the exercise of the exclusion right, not its absence.

"Rand's definition of property is correct because she doesn't start from the false scarcity premise. Man, I believe she writes this explicitly, starts with NOTHING. Neither abundance nor scarcity, which is a false dichotomy. He starts with *zero* values and must generate action to gain values from the outside world."

The term "values" is used in more than one sense here. Man starts with no material values already in hand. He must act on existing physical resources. The phrase "generate action" adds no clarity beyond "man acts." Treating action itself as a substitute for tangible resources risks treating effort as sufficient to establish a claim over resources already owned by someone else (such as the effort of a thief).

"How does he know though which values are indeed values? How does he know how to gain values? Knowledge is not automatic, so he must think to guide his actions. This, together with action, is the primary problem of survival, which are both problems that (Austrian Economics) glosses over (because fundamentally it rejects consciousness—but that's for another time)."

Nothing in praxeology contradicts the claim that knowledge is not automatic and that thought guides action. Praxeology simply does not evaluate the ends or the methods of cognition. Those are tasks for ethics and epistemology. Requiring a descriptive science of action to supply a full theory of values confuses categories.

"Thus Rand reaches the definition of property, which is the right to use or dispose of earned things according to one's judgment. Note, it is the right to use—not the right to exclude."

The right to use is a consequence of the right to exclude. Without a justified right to exclude others, "use" collapses into mere possession.

""Use" presupposes a mind that decides how to use. You can use the object yourself or you can let someone else use it. Hence "exclusion" is not essential to the concept."

Exclusion is essential because it is the only feature that distinguishes ownership from mere possession. A thief can use and dispose of a stolen good, yet the thief cannot exclude the original owner without contradiction.

"It can be one result of how you decide to use an object, but not more than that. The essential characteristic of property is that you earn it and get to decide how to use it."

If this were sufficient, a thief could claim ownership over stolen goods on the ground that he decides how to use them. Ownership is not mere possession. The thief is a latecomer and therefore lacks the justified right to exclude the original owner.

"The idea of exclusion and scarcity, however, dispenses with the mind,"

It does not. The claim has not been demonstrated.

"and reduces the issue of property to physical distribution, as if humans are nothing but animals (or 5-year-olds) fighting over the same finite resources."

Physical resources are locally limited by the opportunity costs of their use. One cannot perform two contradictory actions with the same unit of a resource at the same time. That constraint does not eliminate the role of the mind. It is a fact the mind must take into account when choosing.

"Now because "use" is mind-dependent, the issue of property in a social context is not how to draw boundaries around goods, but whether or not *one's consent of usage is respected by others*."

This restates the problem of drawing boundaries.
Some people will have a bad philosophy, or will choose evasion over reason. Making such people respect one's boundaries is an engineering problem, not a problem of law or philosophy.

"If you physically take an object that's mine, that's not theft if I gave you my consent to use it. It is only theft if I *did not* give you my consent."

Taking an object is theft when the owner has excluded the taker and the taker proceeds anyway. 

"The implementation of property rights is an epistemological problem, not a metaphysical one."

Epistemology is downstream of metaphysics. The primacy of existence entails that knowledge depends on the nature of what exists. The concept of ownership exists as distinct from possession via the firstcomer principle (which is derived by negating alternatives). 

"Thus physical possession cannot be the basis of property rights (this is concrete-bound and dumb, actually, with all due respect)."

The position defended here is not a possession ethic. It is an objective assignment rule based on the firstcomer principle. The person who first emborders an unowned resource acquires the right to exclude others from it, even if the resource is held for later use.

"Since this is already long, I'll offer only a brief comment on IP."

The debate concerned IP. Treating the topic as an afterthought is notable.

Interesting how by simple substitution the "brief comment" can be entirely negated. 

Intellectual Parasitism does not exist in a non-market context. If the parasite lives in a remote isolated community, they do not harm your ability to survive. But markets are a different story, once the parasite starts telling you how to use your body and your resources, at threat of violence, that is when they threaten your survival. Specialized production becomes more difficult the more Intellectual Parasites are nearby.

That is the nature of IP: intellectual parasitism. Using obfuscation, mysticism and special pleading to rule over other people and their resources.

In practice, it is one of the strongest levers of control of the State-Corporate leviathan. If the project of liberty is to have any hope, IP must be abolished.

Intellectual Parasitism Delenda Est!

text:
This debate is a perfect illustration for why I attack Austrianism.

Some Objectivists maintain that Austrian econ is compatible with Rand's philosophy. Well, here we have a case of a person, @PunishedZulu, who (somewhat) genuinely attempts to infuse Austrianism with Objectivism.

But notice what happens here. Instead of Austrianism slotting under Objectivist ethics in the narrow scope of economics, Zulu is *subordinating* Objectivism under Austrianist philosophy.

This is why I keep arguing that Austrianism is not merely economics; it is a worldview.

At the heart of this worldview is the idea of "scarcity." This is a post-Kantian, collectivist, materialist, anti-production, primacy of consciousness idea that negates the fundamental human problem of how to survive.

It starts by assuming a static quantities premise; i.e., "the goods are here." But, unlike a paradise of unlimited goods, these proponents say, in real life there are only so many goods yet fewer people to have them. So other people's wishes to command the scarce goods "come under conflict" with other people's wishes, and the way to resolve this conflict is to assign boundaries to these goods so we can all get along with each other.

Rand's philosophy takes a completely different approach. She starts with the individual and asks: what does man need in order to survive, i.e., in order to sustain himself? What she observes is that all living organisms live by a process of self-sustaining action. They act to gain values from their surroundings to maintain their lives.

As you can see, there are already two main differences to these approaches: Rand says that the fundamental problem is that of survival, and that values, to be gained, must be acquired through action.

By contrast, Austrianism ignores the problem of survival and treats values/goods as if they are already here, with the only problem being how to distribute them.

Note the definition that Zulu offers for property. He defines property rights by their consequence and through negation (both logical errors). He says that ownership is the right to exclude because he starts from the collectivist premise of people claiming their whims on static quantities.

This is absurd if you actually looks at reality. Simple examples of restaurant owners who invite people into their property or a person lending his book to a friend demonstrate that property is not always *literally* excluded from the use of others.

Rand's definition of property is correct because she doesn't start from the false scarcity premise. Man, I believe she writes this explicitly, starts with NOTHING. Neither abundance nor scarcity, which is a false dichotomy. He starts with *zero* values and must generate action to gain values from the outside world.

How does he know though which values are indeed values? How does he know how to gain values? Knowledge is not automatic, so he must think to guide his actions. This, together with action, is the primary problem of survival, which are both problems that Austrianism glosses over (because fundamentally it rejects consciousness—but that's for another time).

Thus Rand reaches the definition of property, which is the right to use or dispose of earned things according to one's judgment. Note, it is the right to use—not the right to exclude. "Use" presupposes a mind that decides how to use. You can use the object yourself or you can let someone else use it. Hence "exclusion" is not essential to the concept. It can be one result of how you decide to use an object, but not more than that. The essential characteristic of property is that you earn it and get to decide how to use it.

The idea of exclusion and scarcity, however, dispenses with the mind, and reduces the issue of property to physical distribution, as if humans are nothing but animals (or 5-year-olds) fighting over the same finite resources.

Now because "use" is mind-dependent, the issue of property in a social context is not how to draw boundaries around goods, but whether or not *one's consent of usage is respected by others*. If you physically take an object that's mine, that's not theft if I gave you my consent to use it. It is only theft if I *did not* give you my consent. The implementation of property rights is an epistemological problem, not a metaphysical one. Thus physical possession cannot be the basis of property rights (this is concrete-bound and dumb, actually, with all due respect).

Since this is already long, I'll offer only a brief comment on IP.

One does not have IP in a non-market context. If someone copies your creation and you both live in a small, isolated community, this does not harm your ability to survive. But markets are a different story. In a market context we don't self-subsist, we specialize. Specialized production becomes the method of human survival in markets.

This means that we create *in order to sell our creation on the market*. If someone physically takes our creation or copies it without our consent, he has robbed our specialized advantage, robbed our time and effort, and robbed our final product. To allow copying of property of any kind—physical or intellectual—without the creator's consent, is to advocate for the destruction of markets.

I will end here, but at some point I will flesh out this argument in more detail.
