I'm not able to meet that very well constructed post with a like minded one. Thank you for sharing all of that. God loves you as you are and I hope you feel his love for you.

I will try to say a couple of things. I think the bible's criticism about being gay came from a couple of perspectives that brought on severe condemnation. In the earlier bible, humanities population numbers were low and the population simply needed to grow. So homosexual activity was seen as taking away from humanity as a whole. Then also it seems like in Roman times where men left their wives at home and went to parties with their favorite prostitute, bi and homosexuality was part of the indulgence that brought on the moral decay of society and took all the blame, even though it wasn't exclusively the problem. I think we may be facing a similar problem now with trans leading the way. Gays overall will shoulder the blame for the really problematic people. AGP's, het sexual deviants will just go back into the shadows while gays bear the brunt of the criticism for their behavior. It's not fair. But I think it's a weak spot for exploitation from the worst people. 

I don't think God makes mistakes and so that means being born gay isn't a mistake. But you have a challenge of one sort that I don't have. In a perfect world you would have a healthier landscape to love safely and without condemnation. Heterosexual relationships are simply necessary for the survival of humanity and will always be the default. But the het sex and relationship landscape is as troubled as the gay landscape. I think we have to find a way that is dignifying, truly loving, including self love, conscientious of safety and best for a community as a whole. We live in a time where we are encouraged to think that our private and personal choices impact us alone and that isn't true. We are a part of society so what we do in it reinforces what we do for others. We create something that others inherit.

Yes, many churches are rackets. I think the mega churches with their jumbotrons, cheesy rock music and shopping mall to be ridiculous, exploitive and exactly the sort of problem Jesus had with the money lenders in the temple. Yet they are the fastest growing type of church and very popular with the younger generations. And many people find it to be what they need. I don't begrudge them that. But that is not where I feel connected to God and his teachings. Though a music ministry is an important part of a church, I'm partial to the classical music varieties. I have sorted out my preference. Every church has a baggage. But the wonderful thing is that most of the people are trying to be better. 

I think in the grand scheme of things, I've reached a place where I need that community of faith. Reading the bible now is a lot different than when I was younger. I think religion has a lot of benefits that other communities lack. The strength is greater. Even the churches I'm not fond of have a lot to offer someone who is compatible with that style of faith. We aren't meant to do this life alone. Church can be supportive for people in their weakest times. I have a hungry mind for intellectual discourse on the bible, Christ and his teachings and how it applies to humanity and I have found a place that feeds that. I used to think I didn't need religion. I used to not trust the teachings. I'm comfortable now and I trust. Trust was my biggest barrier and trusting God is the one place my trust belongs. It's kind of surprising. I'm even willing to accept the restrictions on my relationships that I am supposed to embrace because it helps me, and protects me from my less than adequate judgement at times. I always needed it. I just finally allowed it to benefit me.

text:
The Sacred Ganesha Shrine of Harishchandragad Fort, Maharashtra.🇮🇳

Nestled within the breathtaking landscape of the Sahyadri mountain range in Maharashtra, India, the small stone shrine dedicated to Lord Ganesha stands as a remarkable testament to the region’s rich spiritual heritage and ancient craftsmanship.

The shrine houses a striking orange idol of Lord Ganesha and is situated on the open plateau near the historic Harishchandreshwar Temple, renowned for its impressive architecture, and the ancient Saptatirtha Pushkarni, a series of sacred water tanks. Surrounded by rugged terrain and timeless stone monuments, this tranquil sanctuary offers visitors a glimpse into the enduring religious traditions of Harishchandragad Fort.

The structure reflects the traditional Hemadpanti architectural style, characterized by the use of precisely fitted dark basalt blocks assembled without mortar. This enduring construction technique has helped the monument withstand centuries of exposure to the region’s intense monsoon rains and changing climatic conditions.

The historical significance of Harishchandragad is associated with early medieval dynasties, including the Kalachuris. The fort’s temples, rock-cut caves, and other architectural remains represent successive phases of development, with several monuments believed to date from between the early medieval period and the eleventh century.

Today, this modest yet captivating shrine remains an integral part of Harishchandragad’s sacred landscape, where ancient architecture, devotion, and the natural grandeur of the Western Ghats come together in remarkable harmony.

text:
A few years ago: “Starlink is a stupid idea. Anyone investing in this Musk scam deserves to lose everything.”
Today: “Starlink is essential to the defense of an invaded nation. Nationalize it!”
Robert Reich (video posted today) is now calling on Democrats to turn Starlink into a public corporation. Before anyone goes along with that, look at what was actually built, and how.
What he did, much of which people don’t know about:
Rockets: Took a private company that nearly went bankrupt and made orbital flight routine. Boosters now land themselves and fly again, which has cut the cost of reaching space dramatically. American astronauts fly on American hardware again after the Shuttle era.
Starlink: A working global network, now connecting phones directly in places with no towers. For villages, clinics, schools, ships, and disaster zones, it’s often the first reliable connection they’ve ever had. I believe it will do more to reduce poverty worldwide than almost any other technology.
Electric cars and batteries: Turned EVs from a niche idea into a mainstream industry, and Model Y became the best-selling car in Europe. Megapack batteries now store power for electric grids.
Neuralink: Said in January 2026 it had 21 participants enrolled in trials worldwide. Participants use the implant to control computers and robotic arms, and one returned to college. For people with paralysis, that’s independence they didn’t have before.
Much more:  Tunneling, U.S. battery materials, and much bigger rockets are all in progress.
And he did it while creating wealth for employees, builders, and investors, and paying enormous taxes, including one of the largest single-year individual tax bills on record.
None of that changed the technology. What changed is that it became valuable.  We know he is not stopping here but just getting started.  Space data centers will reduce the electrical burden, etc. of course the same objections are here.
Why nationalization is the wrong answer:
The risk was private. Nobody offered to share the losses when rockets were exploding. Taking the company after it succeeds teaches every future builder that success is the trigger for confiscation.
The state didn’t do this. Nasa's Shuttle was painfully expensive and slow- no moon ventures since the 60's - no viable path, Nasa's engineers laughed at his ideas, and showed little support. A private company, under cost pressure, made reuse work. Public ownership removes the pressure that drove the progress.
Importance isn’t a reason to seize something. If it were, the state would take every company that matters. Dependence on one provider is solved by competition, contracts, and regulation, and rivals like Amazon’s Kuiper are already deploying.
It’s a one-way door. Once a government can take a company because it became essential, no founder or investor can treat property as secure, and capital goes elsewhere.  Innovation stops, progress stops, capital stops; our pie does not expand it collapses.
My view: no one alive has done more to move humanity forward than the people who build things that work, and Elon Musk is at the top of that list. Five years ago they called it a scam, and now they want to own it.
Entrepreneurs, pay attention. Mock it while it’s risky, resent it once it works, and steal it as yours once it’s essential. Progress distorts. The party that once cheered Silicon Valley as the engine of progress now treats its biggest successes as something to be seized. And when you punish the builders, progress doesn’t just move somewhere else. It can stop. We went to the Moon, and then for over fifty years we didn’t. Reusable rockets, satellite internet, electric vehicles, brain implants, Robotics, and AI are advancing together, each feeding the others, and that kind of convergence doesn’t come around on a whim.  Government is incapable of these types of creation. Break it up and we may not get it back and the real cost of that won’t be abstract. It will be cures, cheaper energy, and connections that never arrive for the people who needed them most.  But of course, Robert must be Reich't here.  Of course.

text:
Musk’s $4 Trillion Gamble: Genius or Financial Overreach?

Elon Musk wants to merge rockets, electric cars, and artificial intelligence into a $4 trillion empire.

The question is whether he is building the most powerful business machine in history—or asking investors to finance an extraordinarily expensive bet on his own ambitions.

Musk has confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla are exploring a merger. According to Bloomberg, the objective is to announce a deal in the first half of 2027.

If completed, the transaction could create a company valued at approximately $3.7 trillion, potentially the largest corporate merger ever attempted.

The financial figures are extraordinary. SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, up 161% year-on-year. Its artificial intelligence business generated $7.56 billion, overtaking STARLINK in revenue for the first time.

Yet Starlink remains the principal profit engine, while the group’s enormous investment requirements threaten to consume its operating cash flow.

This is the central attraction of a merger with Tesla. Tesla offers manufacturing capacity, an established commercial ecosystem, and cash generation. SpaceX needs capital to expand Starlink, develop Starship and build its AI infrastructure.

Combining the businesses could give Musk greater financial flexibility across industries that increasingly depend on computing power, energy and advanced engineering.

text:
Freedom Mud: Why Dredging the Pacific Won’t Break China’s Rare Earth Monopoly

6,000 Meters Deep, 0 Refineries: The Western Fantasy of Seabed Mining

I was reading The Diplomat this morning, and I just had to laugh. The Western policy brain trust has found its latest "China-slaying" miracle weapon. Forget industrial policy, forget STEM graduates, forget building actual factories. 

The new geopolitical silver bullet? Dredging up radioactive mud from 6,000 meter under the Pacific Ocean near Minamitorishima, where 2 tectonic plates meet, it is earthquake prone and the mud are radioactive!

You can't make this stuff up. 

The headline machine is in full hype mode: “China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea - The rise of seabed mining will add new complexity to the South China Sea disputes.!" 

The Beltway armchair strategists are practically high-fiving each other. They think rare earths are literally "rare" in the dirt, and that if Tokyo just drops a giant vacuum cleaner six kilometers down to the abyssal plain, Western supply chain independence is achieved. Freedom mud!

Let’s unpack this cope for a minute.

First of all, any metallurgical engineer in Ganzhou or Baotou will tell you: the mining was never the hard part. Rare earths are everywhere in the Earth's crust. China doesn’t dominate the market because Beijing got lucky with geology. China dominates because for forty years, while the West was financializing its economy, outsourcing heavy industry, and printing paper derivatives, Chinese state enterprises built out the entire downstream chemical infrastructure.

Extracting mixed rare earth mud from underwater at 600 atmospheres of crushing pressure—where a single mechanical failure costs millions—doesn't solve your actual problem. What are you going to do with 3,500 tons of wet, salty, iron-heavy radioactive sludge every day?

You still need massive, complex, multi-stage solvent extraction plants. You need thousands of automated mixer-settlers to separate chemically identical elements like Dysprosium and Terbium to 99.999% purity. You need acid-recovery systems, shared chemical supply networks, cheap power grids, and specialized chemical engineers. China holds over 80% of global solvent extraction patents.

And even if you magically refine the oxide, where are the metal-smelting plants? Where are the sintered NdFeB permanent magnet factories? They’re in China! If Japan actually dredges up this mud, guess where they’d ultimately have to ship the concentrate to turn it into an EV motor component? Right back to Chinese refiners!

This entire Minamitorishima narrative isn't an industrial strategy—it’s high-visibility political theater to stall the Code of Conduct for the South-China Sea which is being finalized.

It’s also an expensive PR demonstration designed to reassure Western voters that Washington and Tokyo have a plan, without doing the hard, dirty work of building real domestic industrial capacity on land.

If Japan is so good with rare earth refining, why is its doing urban mining? 

That is Recycling waste electronics:
•Air Conditioners & Compressors: Industrial and home air conditioner compressor motors (manufactured by companies like Daikin and Mitsubishi Electric) contain heavy concentrations of Neodymium (Nd), Dysprosium (DY), and Terbium (Tb).
•EV Drivetrains & Hard Disk Drives (HDDs): Old automotive electric motors and server HDDs offer predictable, high-purity magnet scrap.

It’s like trying to beat a world-class restaurant chain by collecting underwater seaweed in a storm, while having zero kitchens, zero chefs, and no idea how to turn it into a meal.

text:
NFL Week 7 Observations

Giants 27, Texans 21 OT
- Not only was this the best game I’ve seen J.J. McCarthy play as a pro, but I was surprised by how many downfield throws he made, especially considering that Houston’s pass rush was impactful.

- In one of these observations posts last year I put McCarthy in the Jaxson Dart, Tyler Shough bucket as I thought McCarthy had a few good showings down the stretch last year. Very few people were saying nice things about McCarthy last year. But this week and last week’s relief appearance against the Saints, are the two games he showed the most ceiling.

- Cam Skattebo ran for 124 yards and a score on 17 carries after seeing none last week. More interestingly, I thought Skattebo looked good on opening day, and then began to gradually look less explosive in the following weeks. Either he was playing through something, or it may be in everyone’s best interest if New York manages his workload given his extremely physical running style. 15 carries for this guy is more like 50 given the way he plays.

- Skattebo was called for a penalty for lowering his head on a run, which was a ridiculous call, to the point it sounded like the Texans’ home crowd was booing it, for quite a while. Maybe there were a ton of Giants fans there, but that really stood out to me and it was the sort of foul where it would have irked any football fan.

- Skattebo ripped off a big run in overtime for 42 yards, where later on that same drive Devin Singletary broke one for 30 for a score to win the game.

- Malik Nabers went for 7-111 on 9 targets.

- Pretty pedestrian day for C.J. Stroud, but he did lead a nice drive to tie it, including a very nice evasion throw on third and goal for what would be a game tying score.

- In overtime Houston’s play caller left their LT in a one-on-one situation with Giants edge Abdul Carter, who beat him pretty badly, moving Stroud out of the pocket immediately and basically derailing the play. Carter might be the single toughest out in a one on one, obvious passing down situation, so leaving their LT alone with him, in that spot struck me as coaching malpractice.

- Houston also attempted a 1st and goal wide receiver pass, that Hutchinson tucked and ran for a few years. I thought that was fairly inept too.

- Houston had a couple runs negated by penalty and had several lanes in this game, which I mention because the Giants are going to get steamrolled on the ground at some point this season.

Falcons 29, 49ers 20
- Bijan Robinson had 20 carries, and 5 receptions in this contest (he was more effective as a pass catcher than on the ground)

- He also saw a hook and ladder that I’d imagine Atlanta will go back to in a third and long situation this season.

- Efficient game from Michael Penix, who saw very little pressure.

- Nine different Falcons caught passes today.

- Atlanta got the Niners to jump on a 4th and 4.

- San Franciscos first drive went through their running backs, and finished on a fourth and goal over the top score from Christian McCaffrey.

- Uneven game from Brock Purdy, where he had 2 interceptions while George Kittle and running back Kaelon Black lost fumbles. Atlanta had no turnovers.

- Given the state of the 49ers wide receiver room, it would not surprise me if Jacob Cowing saw some role expansion. He had a rep late in the game where I wrote down his number.

Bengals 35, Ravens 13
- Very good game that reminded me of a college game where the better team doesn’t show up until the second half, as Baltimore, without Lamar Jackson, was up 13-0 at halftime, then in what felt like a very short period of time it was 35-13, with the Bengals on top.

- One of the Bengals scoring drives came off an interception, but four of their five scoring drives were 6 plays or fewer.

- Zay Flowers busted a screen and scored on the first drive, after he was open downfield for a potential long score, but missed. This is the third time this season that I have wondered aloud if Flowers is a fringe top 5 receiver in the league.

- Tee Higgins went 6-148-1 while Ja’Marr Chase went 5-62-1. Joe Burrow was 22 of 30 for 292 yards and 4 scores. All of Cincinnati’s scoring came in the second half.

- Cincinnati’s pass rush was impactful.

Dolphins 28, Jets 25
- Dolphins scored on their first drive, which was apparently their first lead of the season.

- The Jets responded with a four play scoring drive

- Geno Smith had a very nice game, 23/30 for 287 and 3 TDs, but his interception came just outside the redzone on a likely Jets scoring drive.

- Omar Cooper Jr. went for 5-111-1 on 5 targets, including a 60-yard reception. Jets TE Mason Taylor also went 5-62-2, where I’d frame him as the Jets 7thbest skill player. New York has a very good looking, young skill group with two good running backs, 3 talented receivers, with Taylor serving as a more traditional tight end versus matchup nightmare Kenyon Sadiq.

- This was easily Malik Willis’s best game as a Dolphin.

- Ollie Gordon went for 103 yards and a score on 25 carries, he’s been much better than I was expecting in the wake of Devon Achane’s injury.

- Caleb Douglas had a 63 yard score, and Greg Dulchich finally had a good looking game with 86 receiving yards on 5 catches.

- The Jets missed a 40-yard field goal on the first drive of the second half.

Vikings 16, Colts 10
- Jonathan Taylor broke a run for a long score, putting the Colts up 7-0 early.

- The Vikings pass rush was very impactful in this game, and Daniel Jones was a liability that did virtually nothing to help his team win.

- The Colts missed two field goals, while Minnesota missed one.

- Minnesota linebacker Blake Cashman had kind of a monster game.

- Kyler Murray broke a 30-something yard run, but otherwise had a game manager type of outing.

- Murray threw a pick in the endzone, that was either overturned on review or negated by penalty.

- It looked like Jordan Mason had significantly more carries than Aaron Jones (looked like Jones may have had an injury)

Browns 27, Titans 24
- Both running backs had very good games. Quinshon Junkins ran for 96 yards and 2 scores on 27 carries, while Tony Pollard blew up for 129 and 3 scores on 25 carries.

- Another better than he’s been in previous seasons Deshaun Watson type of game.

- Cam Ward did very little, until the late game drive that tied the score. He missed a tight end wide open in the seam, but a play or two later hit on another chunk play that more or less made up for it.

- Both quarterbacks threw interceptions, and neither pass rush was as impactful as I’d have expected.

- KC Concepion went 8-129 on 10 targets, while Harold Fanin went 6-91. When I list a player’s production during a game it’s because I made a note while watching to check it, and both of these Browns young pass catchers got one of those notes in game.

- Browns kicked a short field goal to win as time expired

Steelers 16, Saints 10 (Paris)
- Another solid game from Aaron Rodgers, but running backs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle accounted for a ton of the Steelers offense in this game.

- I love that monster tight end Darnell Washington continues to see purposeful looks in the scoring zone, as he caught a 4 yard touchdown against what looked like a small Saints DB.

- Tyler Shough looked like he had a better game than one that would have led to a 10 point output, but I’m not sure New Orleans had 20 yards rushing in this game.

- Both pass rushes had what I’ll call decent games, but Saints Edge Chase Young has surprised me a few times this year.

Buccaneers 43, Panthers 13
- Tampa ran for over 250 yards as a team with 3 rushing touchdowns on 49 total carries versus just 11 Baker Mayfield throws.

- Bryce Young threw 2 interceptions, while the Panthers also lost 2 fumbles.

- Tampa’s pass rush was impactful, with edge Yaya Diaby having a big day.

- Young made a great throw to Darren Waller for a 50ish yard score on a deep post.

- Tampa scored two points on a blocked extra point that they returned for a score in what was a sequence I rarely see.

- The best way I could describe this game was that it was over before halftime, and it struck me as a regression (for both teams, positive for Tampa, negative for Carolina) buzz saw kind of game.

Broncos 30, Cardinals 16
- Bo Nix busted a 70ish yard run for a score, but he had another pedestrian game as a passer.

- Jonah Coleman looked like the team’s best runner today.

- Denver tried to get Jaylen Waddle involved (looked like he left with an injury), but he had a middling game with right around 50 receiving yards.

- Denver’s pass rush derailed this game.

- Trey McBride went 10-111-1

- Bam Knight for the second week in a row not only looked good, but had a couple of physical runs that really surprised me.

- This was a game where it’s obvious that Denver could be a contender if Bo Nix was playing at a higher level.

Rams 35, Raiders 21
- I thought this was Sean McVay’s best called game of the year.

- A handful of really good looking play designs to manufacture touches for tight ends.

- The Rams running game lead the charge, where both Kyren Williams and Blake Corum had nearly 100 yards a piece on the ground.

- Puka Nacua didn’t have a monster stat line, but he might be the most physical receiver I’ve ever seen on a week in and week out basis.

- I was very surprised at how impactful the Rams pass rush was given their injures to their front.

- I would guess that Kirk Cousins had a solid box score, but a lot of it came when this game was already over.

- Cousins threw a dropped pick six on the first drive.

- The Raiders had no running game, again, where I noted a few plays where their RBs were hit in the backfield, on one occasion Ashton Jeanty was hit basically as soon as he was given a hand off.

- Jeanty had a better game as a pass catcher than a runner

- Tre Tucker had another good showing.

- I thought there was a chance Fernando Mendoza would take over at halftime, and I’m pretty surprised he didn’t play at all.

Lions 20, Packers 17
- Weird game as it looked like it would shoot out early, especially on the Lions end as their first drive was just chunk play after chunk play and you can usually tell when Jared Goff is going to play well from the jump (and he did)

- Spike game from Amon-Ra St. Brown 9-153

- Jahmyr Gibbs had 29 carries and 5 receptions. He also lost a fumble in the redzone.

- The Lions went for it in their own end late, failed, then Green Bay missed what was basically a free field goal attempt.

- Detroit came back down, kicked a very short field goal as time expired to win after a 70ish yard drive.

- The Lions secondary is a mess. There was a call on 3rd and roughly 4, where Tucker Kraft caught a 5ish yard sit down, where he was all by himself to the point he ran for another 20ish yards after the catch. The call itself looked like it offered the enormous void.

- Confusion when the Packers showed motion, enormous voids in coverage, I’m not sure what’s going on there defensively but it’s a miracle Green Bay only scored 17 points.

- The Packers threw 45 passes to 19 runs, even with Josh Jacobs back. Jordan Love played well for the most part, at least early, and the Packers were simply not having much success on the ground, but that’s a very wide disparity.

Seahawks 20, Chiefs 3
- Seattle’s defense showed tonight why they remain a very dangerous team, as they shut down the undefeated Chiefs in both phases.

- This was a game where I left questioning if the Chiefs have a “gotta have it” pass catcher. That’s a question I’ve pondered for a few years now in truth, but it really showed up tonight.

- Kansas City missed two field goals.

- Kansas City did not generate much pressure.

- Jaxon Smith-Njigba: 9-150-1. Guy is unreal.

- Emanuel Wilson ran for 100 yards and a score on 24 carries.

- The Chiefs, similar to the 49ers, were “due” for a down performance, but I wouldn’t just pin this result on that notion, as Seattle’s defense forced a number of misfires and they really did an outstanding job limiting Kenneth Walker in his return to Seattle.

To be clear, I do zero editing on these so I can get them out fast.

text:
From 1914 to 1940, anyone applying for a federal civil service job had to attach a photograph of their face to the form, and the government said it was to stop cheating on the exams. That first year, across every civil service examination held in the country, the record shows fourteen cases of somebody impersonating an applicant.

Fourteen, against a rule that let the hiring clerk see a Black applicant's face before he looked at the score.

Somebody sit down and tell me that rule was about cheating.

In 1949 the post office in San Jose, California hired a woman who had taught mathematics for fifteen years. There is no record that she ever taught school again.

That was the good outcome. That was her winning.

Five years earlier she had walked into the San Jose school district office with a teaching certificate from Langston University and fifteen years of algebra behind her. She was thirty-seven years old.

She had six children and a husband already out at the Oakland shipyards, and she had come two thousand miles on the understanding that California schools were integrated. She was told the district did not hire Black teachers.

Then she was offered a job as a cleaner.

Understand what that is. It is not a slammed door, it is not a slur, and there is no shouting in the room.

It is somebody looking at a certificate and a record of fifteen years in a classroom and deciding which of the building's jobs the woman holding them is shaped for. Offered the way you would offer a chair.

She said no.

She went to an employment agency next, and the agency told her that what was available for her was domestic service. She had gone to college for the specific purpose of never doing that work.

Her mother's generation had done that work. So she said no again, and she went out to a cannery and picked fruit.

San Jose in the mid-1940s had about eighty thousand people in it. Five hundred and fifteen of them were Black.

Her name was Inez Jackson.

She was born Inez Young in Kaufman County, Texas in 1907, to a farmer and his wife. The family moved to Terrell, where the Black high school was run by a jazz musician named William Henry Burnett, who spent forty-four years as the main person in that town arguing that Black children should be educated.

He got her to 1925, and she graduated second in her class. She went straight up into Oklahoma, to Shawnee, at eighteen.

By nineteen she was president of the local YWCA, and her name turned up in the Shawnee column of Roscoe Dunjee's Black Dispatch out of Oklahoma City. She took her teaching certificate at Langston University, Oklahoma's state-supported college for Black students.

In 1929 she married a barber named Leon Jackson in Shawnee, and she went into the segregated schools there and taught mathematics. Fifteen years of it, with six children in the house.

She was raised inside a promise, the one every Black family in Oklahoma was making to its children in the twenties, which was that the paper you earn is the one thing nobody can take back off you. In 1944 the Selective Service came for Leon.

He chose the Oakland shipyards over the war, and she finished out the school year in Shawnee. Then she loaded up the children and went west to a state that turned out to have its own arrangements.

To understand why the post office was the door she ended up walking through, you have to know that for more than sixty years, federal law barred Black people from carrying the United States mail along its post roads. Congress passed the act on the third of May, 1802.

After the first of November that year, nobody but a free white person could be hired to carry the mail on a post road, as a rider or as a driver of a mail coach. The Postmaster General had requested it, and he put his reasoning in writing to Senator James Jackson of Georgia, who chaired the Senate's post office committee.

Gideon Granger explained that the most capable enslaved men were the ones being used as post riders, and that traveling day after day and mixing with people, they would pick things up. Then he wrote the sentence that gives the whole century away.

They will learn that a man's rights do not depend on his color.

He was not afraid of theft. He was afraid of a Black man who moved paper for a living reading the country off it and going home to teach his brother.

In 1828 they tightened it further. If Black hands were needed to lift the mail down off a coach and carry it inside, the lifting had to happen in front of the white man who had custody of it, under his immediate direction.

He could hold the sack. He could not be trusted with it alone for the length of a corridor.

Congress reaffirmed that rule in 1810 and again in 1825, and did not repeal it until the third of March, 1865.

Reconstruction pried the doors back open, and for the rest of that century there were Black postmasters and clerks and city carriers. The post office became one of the only federal rooms in America where a Black person stood on level ground with the man beside him.

Then, on the thirty-first of May, 1913, the seven Black clerks at postal headquarters in Washington were screened off from their white coworkers. Not a memo.

Screens, physical ones, standing in the room.

By every account that survives, not one of their white coworkers had asked for this. The order came down from above them, from a department run by a new Postmaster General from Texas who had complained in cabinet that Black and white railway clerks were working elbow to elbow in the mail cars.

Now think about the rest of that day. There is a lunchroom in that building and they are not allowed in it, and there is nowhere else, because no restaurant in Washington will serve them either.

Somebody eventually asked the building superintendent why the government did not just open a second lunchroom. He answered that since the restaurants of Washington were closed to Black people, the government could hardly be expected to feed them.

Out on the railway lines it was worse than screens. Men who had spent years working a run near their own homes were reassigned onto all-Black crews on distant lines, far enough that the job took a father out of his house.

Here is the part that should stop you. No general segregation order is known to have been issued.

Officials out on the lines simply began separating crews, apparently with the department's blessing. Which meant there was no order anywhere to appeal against.

Others were dismissed on charges that would not stand up.

Roosevelt finally took the photograph off the federal application in November of 1940. Inez Jackson walked into that San Jose school district office four years later.

The school district was not the federal government. It did not need a photograph to know.

And here is the part that will not lie down flat. Even with the screens, even with the photograph, even with a procedure called the rule of three that let an appointing officer choose any one of the top three scorers, which meant a Black man could finish first and be passed over, finish first and be passed over, finish first and be passed over, and no line of the file would ever have to say why, the post office was still the steadiest and best-protected wage work a Black American could get in this country.

Because every other door in America was worse.

In 1939 somebody surveyed Black teenage boys in New York City about what they wanted to be. Post office clerk came first on a list of twenty-two jobs, and mail carrier came sixth.

Not doctor, not lawyer. Clerk.

Men with law degrees threw mail on the night shift because no white firm in their city would take them, then went and argued their cases in the morning. Medical students worked the cases between classes, and one study counted at least half a dozen Black postal employees in Chicago writing books in a single year.

Richard Wright clerked in the Chicago post office before he wrote Native Son.

Say that plainly, because it is the part nobody ever finishes. America did not lose those men, it used them.

It took a lawyer and had him sort envelopes. It took a woman who could teach a room of children how numbers behave and put her in front of a sorting case.

It got its mail delivered on time, and it called that opportunity.

Which brings us back to Oklahoma, and to a man who came home from the Marines in December of 1945 and decided to attack that wall with envelopes. James Edward Stewart was born in Plano, Texas in 1912 and carried up to Oklahoma City as a small boy.

His father died in 1920, and his biographers record that his mother held the family together on thirty-five cents a day. He went through Douglass High School alongside Ralph Ellison.

He started at Oklahoma Natural Gas in 1937 as a janitor, and by September 1940 he was running the company's east side office. He also wrote a column in Dunjee's Black Dispatch called Jimmy Says.

When he volunteered for the Marine Corps during the war his acceptance sat in a drawer while somebody investigated that column, because it had gotten him written down as a troublemaker. They took him in the end.

He served in the 51st Defense Battalion, the first Black battalion in the Marines, and was discharged on the sixth of December, 1945. He came home, took back the presidency of the Oklahoma City NAACP branch, and went looking for jobs for other people.

His biographers record that the first place he went was the post office, and that the campaign he ran there was a letter-writing campaign.

Sit with the shape of that for a second. To get Black Oklahomans hired inside the one building in the city whose entire purpose is handling letters, ordinary people sat at their kitchen tables and mailed letters into it.

It worked because it was the only address in Oklahoma City obligated to open the envelope. That building had a complaint procedure, a fair employment officer, an appeals board, a civil service commission, and a congressman who wanted to be re-elected.

And what those jobs bought was not a wage. It was a wage that was very hard for anybody in Oklahoma City to take away.

A schoolteacher could be fired over a petition. A maid, a porter, a driver, a cook, a clerk in a white-owned store, any of them could be gone by Friday on one telephone call from downtown.

A federal clerk could be reached too, but only the long way round. When a Savannah letter carrier named Westley Law, who ran that city's NAACP branch, was fired in September of 1961 after a congressman campaigned on firing him, Kennedy had him put back on his route the following month.

That is the whole difference, and it is not immunity. It is that for the first time there was somewhere above the men downtown to appeal to.

Willenhem Castilla, a postal worker over in Jackson, Mississippi, told the historian Philip Rubio that men like him were "the backbone" of the NAACP in that state, and he gave the reason without dressing it up. The local officials could not fire them so easily.

Herbert Hill ran labor for the NAACP from 1951 to 1977, and he said that when he came into a town hunting for somebody willing to lead, the ones who stood up were the minister, the undertaker, the lawyer and the man who worked at the post office. Three of those four were paid by Black people.

The fourth was paid by the United States government, and that is exactly why he could afford to stand. In July of 1958, in remarks the New York Times carried, Hill said that in the whole American South the Post Office Department was the only federal agency employing Black people above the level of janitor.

The only one. In 1958.

And in 1958 there was a branch post office on the northeast side of Oklahoma City with Black men working the cases inside it, throwing the city's mail into the slots, twelve years after those letters started going in. That is the same year those children walked into Katz.

A month before Katz, up in Wichita, Ron Walters and his cousin Carol Parks had filled the stools at the Dockum Drug Store and held them from the nineteenth of July to the eleventh of August, when the owner finally told his staff to serve them because he was losing money. Parks explained later what she had been sitting there for, which was that Black customers had to order at the end of the counter and carry it out in a paper container, and "We never knew what it was to just sit there."

The Oklahoma City young people had been in contact with Walters. Clara Luper had been writing to the Katz Drug Store for more than fifteen months by then.

She was the first Black student in the University of Oklahoma's history department, and she advised the NAACP Youth Council. All she was asking for was the downtown lunch counter opened to the children she taught.

Katz never wrote back. There is no fair employment officer at a drugstore.

So on the nineteenth of August, 1958, thirteen children walked in with three adults and sat down, and the youngest of them was six years old.

They ordered Cokes and were refused. They sat there from opening to closing, and they had brought their schoolbooks and studied at the counter while it went on around them.

Marilyn Luper Hildreth was one of those children, and looking back on the sit-in years she has listed what it cost them. Being spat on, kicked, talked about, ridiculed and abused.

They came back the next day and the day after. On the twenty-first they were served, and the company's head office in Kansas City opened its counters across three states.

Now ask the question the photograph of that lunch counter cannot answer. Who feeds thirteen children's families while their mothers spend August downtown being spat on, and who can put his own name on a bail bond, and whose job survives the reprisal.

Jimmy Stewart, the man who had opened the post office with envelopes, helped organize those sit-ins.

Now go back ten years, and two thousand miles west.

In 1948 Truman signed the order on fair employment in the federal service, and Inez Jackson sat the civil service examination. She passed it.

The San Jose post office would not hire her.

She had the certificate and she had the fifteen years. She had now also sat the federal government's own examination and cleared the federal government's own bar, and a man in a building in San Jose still said no.

So people mailed it. They wrote to that post office, they telephoned it, and they walked in the door in person, over and over, until in 1949 Inez Jackson became the first Black postal clerk San Jose had ever had.

She was in her forties. The country that had offered her a mop had to be buried under its own mail before it would let her sort letters.

She did not go quiet after that.

She and Leon eventually bought a house from a white seller who agreed to the sale mainly to spite the neighbor next door, and the neighbor next door was her supervisor at the post office. In 1951 she pushed the San Jose police department into hiring its first Black officer.

She talked a fellow postal clerk, Mary Anne Smith, into becoming the city's first Black real estate agent. Smith, another agent named Berthina Nelson and a white broker named J. S. Williams who hired them both spent the next two decades walking Black families into neighborhoods that had been closed.

She held meetings in her own front room three and four nights a week.

And in the 1960s, when she wanted San Jose State students to go and sit down at the Kress and the Woolworth downtown, the two models she reached for were Greensboro and Oklahoma City. So it went out and it came all the way back.

A woman who had taught school in Shawnee got inside a federal building because strangers mailed letters. Then she used a sit-in out of her own home state to crack open a lunch counter in California.

She was president of the San Jose NAACP from 1969 to 1973 and ran the local YWCA from 1973 to 1976, where she opened a rape crisis center. In 1978 she talked the city into renting her an empty fire station for a dollar a year and started a community agency in it.

She died in 1993, at eighty-six.

There is no number for what this cost. Nobody has ever counted how many Black teachers and lawyers and engineers this country parked behind a sorting case for forty years because the classroom and the firm and the laboratory were shut, and nobody was ever paid a cent for the career they did not get to have.

There is no claim you can file for that. There is no docket.

What there is, in San Jose, California, is a small library inside a community center, with her papers in it, and her name on the door.

Inez C. Jackson, mother of six. One certificate, one cannery, one examination she passed and was refused on anyway, and a working life spent handling everybody else's mail.

When we write, we never fully know where the words will travel or whose hands will hold them.

Seeing Mfanelo Sphelele Calvin Ndlela standing in Washington with a copy of Betting on a Darkie moved me more than I expected. In front of those grand buildings, he carried a book that tells the story of lifting one’s game - in the boardroom, in leadership, and in life. That image captures something powerful: the moment a story leaves the page and becomes part of someone else’s journey.

We write hoping our words will shift people into action and offer them hope when they need it most. We rarely get to see that hope take shape. Mfanelo’s post showed me that it does. It reminded me why the work of writing matters, and it gave me fresh energy to keep going.

Thank you, Mfanelo, for carrying the book so far and for sharing the moment. It inspired me to make more time to write.

🇷🇺 🇺🇦 FT: a New York lawyer, a banker and Putin's ex-Stasi friend ran a secret 2022-23 channel; a Ukrainian MP now says the peace plan was real, and a former Biden official disputes a key claim

A Financial Times Magazine cover story by Moscow bureau chief Max Seddon is drawing new reactions. Seddon reports that Richard Conn, a former Latham and Watkins lawyer, and Bob Foresman, an American investment banker, used Matthias Warnig, a former East German Stasi officer and longtime Putin friend, to open an unofficial channel to the Kremlin in late 2022. According to the FT, Conn relayed messages from Eric Green, then the National Security Council's senior director for Russia, which Warnig delivered to Putin as nuclear fears peaked that October. Green disputes parts of Conn's account and calls a channel run through "a former GDR spy talking to a New York lawyer" a "real bass-ackwards approach."

The story's core claim concerns a peace draft. Per the FT, the group met on Gran Canaria in January 2023 and sketched a deal: Russia would pull back to roughly the lines it held in Crimea and parts of Donbas before the full-scale invasion, Ukraine would accept Russian control of Crimea and a land corridor, and NATO states would back the ceasefire. Warnig told the group Putin went through the text "line by line" and agreed on the front line while rejecting NATO membership. Zelensky and then chief of staff Andriy Yermak refused territorial concessions, the FT reports; their office did not comment.

On Sunday, Ukrainian MP Oleksiy Goncharenko wrote that "the 2023 peace treaty plan leaked to the FT did indeed exist", adding that Roman Abramovich was "the key figure" and that Russia would have handed back Melitopol and the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant. The FT does not name Abramovich. 

Thomas Wright, a former senior official on Biden's National Security Council, pushed back on another part of the story, the account that Ushakov asked Jake Sullivan about the channel and was told Washington did not need it: "The part about Ushakov asking Sullivan about the Warnig channel is false. Did not happen". The FT itself reports that former US officials say Ushakov never raised the channel.

The piece lands as Witkoff carries a new US paper and Kyiv again rules out land swaps. Its participants argue the US and Ukraine missed a chance at better terms than Putin offers now. Former US officials quoted by Seddon think Putin wanted to win outright, and one asks of the nuclear threats, "Who was deterring whom?" The story is a rare look at how freelance diplomacy brushed against the White House at the war's most dangerous moment.

📸 Prayer as a Photo-Op: An #OvertPsyops Readout on the Bishops' "Public Apology"

Twelve bishops walk into the White House expecting a "private discussion" and "an opportunity to pray privately with the president." Within hours, photos and video of the prayer are posted publicly, less than two weeks before the midterm elections. Now two of them say they were used.

The real lesson isn't just that a political office used clergy. Prayer staged for cameras was never what Χριστός (Christ) taught in the first place.

 Ἰησοῦς (Jesus) Already Ruled on Camera-Ready Prayer

Ματθαῖος (Matthew) 6:5-6: And when you pray, do not be like the ὑποκριταί (hypocrites/actors), for they love to stand and pray in the συναγωγαί (synagogues) and on the corners of the streets, so that they may be seen by ἄνθρωποι (men). Truly I say to you, they have their μισθός (reward). But you, when you pray, enter into your ταμεῖον (inner room), and having shut your door, pray to your Πατήρ (Father) who is in secret, and your Πατήρ (Father) who sees in secret will reward you.

The word ὑποκριτής (hypocrite) literally means a stage actor. A prayer circle in the most photographed building on earth, with officials present, is a stage, whatever anyone promised beforehand. The ταμεῖον (inner room) is not the Oval Office.

    Bishop Grob admits, "I did not go without reservations."
    The meeting was set up in September, scheduled weeks before a national election.
    Agenda items included tax credits and visas, things the bishops' institutions want from government.

A meeting where an institution seeks policy favors from a politician, near an election, ending in a group prayer, is political by its very structure. φρόνησις (prudence) would have seen that before walking in. The "apology" is about being photographed, not about the arrangement itself.

The Older Pattern: Kingdoms and Thrones

The relationship between Rome's hierarchy and the White House is not new, and it crosses party lines. 

Tommy's archive documents it:

🔹 Cardinal Pietro Parolin assured Trump of prayers after the 2016 election. 🔹 Cardinal Timothy Dolan met privately with Trump. 🔹 Fortune reported on how Catholic support helped Trump's 2016 victory. 🔹 Daniel Burke's Washington Post piece called George W. Bush possibly "the nation's first Catholic president," with Catholic advisors shaping policy.

Both sides use each other. Politicians want the image of blessing; the hierarchy wants access and policy. Ἰησοῦς (Jesus) refused that whole trade:

Ἰωάννης (John) 18:36: My βασιλεία (kingdom) is not of this κόσμος (world).

Full Greek text: ἡ βασιλεία ἡ ἐμὴ οὐκ ἔστιν ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.

When Σατανᾶς (Satan) offered all the kingdoms of the world (Ματθαῖος (Matthew) 4:8-10), Χριστός (Christ) said no. Clergy lining up for access to power are taking a meeting Ἰησοῦς (Jesus) declined.

The White House Non-Answer

Asked plainly whether consent was given, the spokeswoman answered a different question: "There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans." That is a classic deflection: replace a factual question with a slogan. Λόγος (logic) notes what was not said.

The bishops are sorry the camera caught it; the deeper issue is that the arrangement treated προσευχή (prayer) as part of a transaction between two worldly power structures. Ikhwan Attempt to Destroy the Trump-Haftar Partnership Foiled

In a single day, the Muslim Brotherhood attempted to undermine Libyan-US relations, fracture the Trump-Haftar alliance, and push all of Libya into the Ikhwan militias’ camp. However, a statement issued tonight by President Donald Trump appears to have defused the situation, at least for now.

It all began with frustration expressed by President Trump during an election rally last night, when he criticized three extremist forces in Somalia, Haiti, and Libya for turning these countries into what he described as “s.. countries.” He was apparently referring to Al-Shabaab in Somalia, which has been associated with terrorism and regional instability; the powerful gangs in Haiti, responsible for widespread violence, drug trafficking, and hostage-taking; and the jihadist militias in western Libya, which have been accused of facilitating the movement of illegal migrants toward Europe. Trump has increasingly appeared frustrated with the Ikhwan-affiliated militias that wield influence over the government in Tripoli.

Less than three hours after Trump's remarks, the Muslim Brotherhood's formidable propaganda machine launched a wave of personal attacks against the US president, demanding that he apologize. His critics accused him of insulting the Libyan people and attempted to associate him with Jeffrey Epstein. The apparent objective of this campaign was to undermine the strong relationship between the Trump administration and Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army (LNA), as well as his son, Major Saddam Haftar, the LNA's deputy commander and a potential presidential contender.

The Ikhwan campaign escalated into a barrage of insults directed at the US president, with criticism also coming from figures associated with the Tripoli-based government.

President Trump, however, subsequently issued a strong statement clarifying his position. He portrayed the Libyan people, who have suffered enormously from jihadist violence since 2011, as partners in the fight against terrorism.

Trump's relationship with Haftar dates back to 2019, when the US president spoke with the field marshal and expressed support for counterterrorism efforts against al-Qaeda, ISIS, and other armed groups, including those affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood, as the LNA conducted military operations near Tripoli.

Trump's latest statement offers a significant indication that the White House is not prepared to allow this controversy to derail US relations with Libya or undermine its relationship with Haftar and the LNA. For the Ikhwan, the attempt to exploit Trump's remarks to drive a wedge between Washington and Haftar may have backfired.

text:
Global trade is not disappearing but shifting toward regional agreements and trusted partners as the multilateral trading system weakens. So, what should we expect for the next two or three years? Arturo Bris, Director of the IMD World Competitiveness Center, offers some advice. 

“First, the turbulence will stay in prices, freight, and currencies, not in who leads. The countries at the top have survived a pandemic, a supply-chain meltdown, two wars, and a tariff war, because their strengths are the kind that do not change overnight.

Second, the real race will be among what I call the connector economies, such as Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia, India, and Mexico, that are absorbing the factories leaving China. Those that turn that investment into better institutions and better skills will climb. Those that simply relabel goods will end up in the crosshairs of both Washington and Beijing.

Third, proof will become the new currency of trade. Access to the largest markets will increasingly be paid for in verifiable data on carbon, forests, and labor, and the countries and companies that can produce that data cheaply will win.

In a fractured world, the countries that trade best are the ones that do their homework at home.”

Live Updates: Polls Close in Brazil as Presidential Race Comes to Chaotic Close

Brasília8:57 p.m. Oct. 25
LiveUpdated 
Oct. 25, 2026, 7:41 p.m. ET15 minutes ago
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/KNr87Dz4cF

The leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, accused officials in some areas of slowing transit. His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, said flooding was hampering his voters. Polling places were kept open an extra two hours.

Updated 
Oct. 25, 2026, 7:03 p.m. ET54 minutes ago
Adam B. Ellick and Ana Ionova
Here’s the latest.

Brazil’s fiercely contested presidential race came to a chaotic conclusion on Sunday as transportation delays and inclement weather forced polls to stay open an additional two hours and raised the prospect of a contested result.

Counting is underway, with a winner expected to be declared within hours. The announcement of extended polling hours came right as voting was set to conclude, and risked undermining faith in the electoral system during a contest that will either extend the presidency of a prominent leftist or return to power a right-wing family with close ties to President Trump.

The 80-year-old leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, accused public officials of purposefully slowing down public transportation in areas where he won in an earlier round of voting. He said he had “never complained about an election,” but added that “this time, something abominable is happening.”

His right-wing opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, also sought an extension of voting, saying that flooding in part of the country where he held electoral advantages would unfairly hurt him.

In response, a judge on Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered polls to stay open — but the ballot count was already underway in some areas. And, in some parts of Brazil, local electoral authorities refused to comply with the court order, raising questions over whether all voters would be allowed to cast their ballots.

Mr. Lula is trying to fight off a hard-right challenge from a son of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro. The vote will not only determine who leads Latin America’s largest nation for the next four years, but also provides the biggest test yet for an ascendant right-wing movement that has been capturing presidencies across the region.

The outcome carries major implications for Mr. Trump’s ambition to assert political and economic hegemony in the Western Hemisphere. Mr. Lula has defied Mr. Trump on several fronts and sought closer ties with China, while Mr. Bolsonaro is aligned with Washington on many issues, including using lethal force to fight drug gangs.

Looming over the contest is an epic political struggle that has roiled and defined Brazilian politics for more than a decade. Mr. Bolsonaro is running in lieu of his father, who could not stand for office because he was convicted of attempting a coup against Mr. Lula after losing the last election. He was sentenced to 27 years in prison and is serving his sentence at home because of health reasons.

The candidates have offered starkly different visions on issues that include fighting organized crime and revitalizing a sluggish economy. The outcome could also reshape Brazil’s trajectory on many divisive issues for years to come, because the next president will fill four open seats on the country’s powerful Supreme Court, which has 11 seats in total.

Mr. Bolsonaro won more ballots than Mr. Lula in the first round of voting on Oct. 4, though not enough to avoid a runoff. Mr. Lula’s campaign desperately scrambled to overhaul its leadership and strategy after the demoralizing result.

Heading into the final weekend, the race was a statistical tie, according to most polls.

Here’s what else to know:
•Quick results expected: Brazilians cast their votes using electronic voting machines, and they have one of the fastest and most secure electoral systems in the world. The electoral authority has started reporting votes, and a final tally will most likely be announced a few hours later. The count can be followed in real time here.

•One town’s story: Nanuque, about 500 miles north of Rio de Janeiro, is a cattle-raising, churchgoing town where crowds turn out on foot for an annual march for Jesus and on horseback for the nation’s independence day. It is a microcosm of Brazil, offering clues to Mr. Lula’s lackluster showing in the first round and Mr. Bolsonaro’s rise. Read more ›

•An ally to Trump: Over the last 18 months, right-wing candidates have won the last seven presidential elections in Latin America. Mr. Bolsonaro, if he wins, would be the eighth, giving the American president another ally in his effort to wage war on drug cartels. Read more ›

text:
Jalen Williams got a needle in his wrist before every single playoff game for two months, kept it quiet, and won Oklahoma City a championship.

Tonight, three games into the comeback, he got wheeled off on a stretcher while Shai hid his face in his jersey.

The wrist went on April 9, 2025, in a regular season game against Phoenix. He tore the ligament that holds two of the small bones in his wrist together, and he said it sounded like paper ripping. He put off surgery and decided to play through it, which meant figuring out how to shoot a basketball with a wrist that felt like it was on fire.

A normal jump shot ends with your wrist snapping forward, every single time. So right before the playoffs, he rebuilt his shot to come off his fingertips with barely any follow-through. The tape stayed hidden under his shooting sleeve. By his count he took 28 or 29 shots in that wrist over the playoffs, a numbing shot before every game.

He played all 23 games. There was a stretch against Denver where he went 10 for 43 and got killed for it by people who had no idea what was going on. He answered with 24 in Game 7 of that series, then 40 in Game 5 of the Finals, and OKC won it all in seven.

Then it all caught up with him.

Surgery a week after the parade. A second procedure to pull a screw out of the wrist, which pushed his return back. Then a hamstring that kept going on him. He missed 49 games last season, played in only 5 of OKC's 15 playoff games, and watched the Thunder lose the West finals to San Antonio in seven.

So this season was the do-over. It's the first year of the five-year deal worth up to $287 million he signed in July 2025, which is a lot of money for a kid who left high school in Gilbert, Arizona, with three Division I offers and ended up at Santa Clara.

He had 8 points, 5 assists and 2 steals tonight when he drove with 1:14 left, got fouled, and came down on his left leg.

The training staff had a towel over it within seconds. They called for the stretcher almost right away, the game stopped for about five minutes, and guys on both teams just stood there in shock. Shai went to the line and shot the free throws for him. After the game he tried to talk about it on TV and only got as far as "Just feel bad for him. Nothing more than that."

There's no word yet on what it is. Daigneault said the team gets briefed tomorrow morning, and that they're not doing great.

On his way out, in an air cast, he turned to the crowd and gave them two thumbs up while the whole building chanted J-Dub.

Same guy who took a needle before every playoff game and never said a word, still trying to make everybody else feel better on the way out.

text:
▫️⛳ Dustin Johnson Among LIV Golf Stars Demanding Over $100 Million From Saudi Arabia’s PIF▫️

🏌️ More Than $100 Million in Disputed Payments: Two time major champion Dustin Johnson is among more than 10 LIV Golf players seeking a combined total exceeding $100 million from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF). The golfers claim they are owed money under their original contracts or deserve severance settlements following the league’s financial collapse.

💰 Saudi Arabia Withdraws Financial Support: The PIF, which invested more than $5 billion in LIV Golf, announced in April that it would stop financing the league. LIV subsequently filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September, leaving substantial contractual obligations unresolved.

⚖️ Players Reject Initial Settlement Offer: According to reports, the PIF initially offered settlements worth approximately two cents for every dollar owed. That would translate into just $2 million for every $100 million in outstanding contractual claims. The players are seeking substantially better compensation.

🏆 Major Champions Join Financial Dispute: Former Masters champion Bubba Watson and Belgian golfer Thomas Detry are reportedly among those seeking payments alongside Johnson. Attorney David Cornwell represents the group and argues that the golfers made major career decisions based on financial commitments associated with LIV Golf.

🚨 LIV Golf Faces Growing Player Departures: Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton, Ian Poulter and several other prominent golfers have announced they will not participate in LIV's proposed successor league. The departures threaten the competition's ability to retain recognizable stars and attract commercial investment.

🏦 New Investors Offer $300 Million Lifeline: BC Partners Credit has proposed financing of up to $300 million to support a restructured competition known as LIV 2.0. However, the investment depends partly on securing enough player commitments, and unresolved financial claims are complicating negotiations.

📉 Executives Received Millions Before Bankruptcy: Court records reveal that LIV Golf paid approximately $15.6 million in executive retention awards before filing for bankruptcy. CEO Scott O'Neil received $6.375 million in retention compensation, raising additional scrutiny as players, vendors and other creditors pursue outstanding payments.

🌍 Potential Consequences Beyond Professional Golf: Johnson's attorney has warned that the dispute could affect how athletes and sporting organizations evaluate future financial commitments from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund. The outcome could influence LIV Golf's restructuring and the broader reputation of the PIF as a sports investor.

text:
The drought lesson Revanth needs today!

By Pendyala Mangala Devi

A government’s leadership is tested not when the rains are plentiful and circumstances are favourable, but when people face hardship and uncertainty. In such moments, citizens expect decisive action, visible leadership and the assurance that their government is working to protect them.

Yet the Congress government in Telangana increasingly appears to have made blaming K Chandrashekhar Rao (KCR) a political strategy in itself. Every problem becomes an occasion to revisit the previous government’s record, while the more pressing question — what is the government doing about the problem today? — often takes a back seat. Criticising a predecessor is easy; governing a State is not.

Telangana’s experience during the severe 2015–16 El Niño drought offers a useful benchmark for examining how a government responds when rainfall fails, groundwater declines, crops suffer and drinking-water supplies come under pressure. The KCR-led government faced a serious crisis through a combination of emergency water arrangements, financial assistance, agricultural support and longer-term infrastructure initiatives.

Severe Water Stress

The 2015 southwest monsoon recorded a rainfall deficit of 15%, while the northeast monsoon suffered a shortfall of 76%. Groundwater levels fell by 2.78 metres, placing additional pressure on drinking-water supplies and agriculture. Through GO Ms No 6, Revenue (Disaster Management) Department, dated November 24, 2015, the government declared 231 mandals across seven districts drought-affected: Mahabubnagar: 64 mandals, Medak: 46, Nizamabad: 36, Ranga Reddy: 33, Nalgonda: 33, Warangal: 22 and Karimnagar: 19.

These figures establish the scale of the emergency. The State faced simultaneous pressure on drinking water, agricultural production and rural livelihoods. The administration had to respond quickly rather than wait for the drought to ease. The then KCR-led government responded effectively, instilling confidence among the people.

Taking Water to People

One of the most immediate challenges was ensuring that people did not go without drinking water. Where existing sources were inadequate, emergency measures were needed to bridge the gap.

Under GO Ms No 2, Revenue (DM-II) Department, dated June 15, 2015, Rs 55 crore was provided as revolving funds to district Collectors to meet urgent drought-related requirements. An additional contingency allocation exceeding Rs 100 crore was made through PR-RWS and Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).

District administrations were authorised to arrange private borewells on hire, deploy water tankers, repair pumps, deepen tubewells, and lay HDPE pipelines to supply drinking water to people in affected areas. Hiring private borewells was an important emergency option where public sources could not meet local demand: it allowed administrations to draw on available water sources while longer-term arrangements were pursued.

These measures were necessarily local and practical. A village facing an immediate shortage could not wait for a major irrigation project to be completed. It needed water from the nearest viable source, transport where necessary, functioning pumps and officials empowered to act.

The response also illustrates the importance of decentralised administration. District Collectors and local bodies had to identify shortages, mobilise available resources and arrange supplies according to local needs.

Emergency borewells and tankers were not permanent answers to drought. They were measures to prevent an immediate crisis from becoming a humanitarian disaster. Effective governance requires both: relief that reaches people today and infrastructure that reduces their vulnerability tomorrow.

Securing Hyderabad, Districts

Hyderabad’s drinking-water security was a major concern during the drought. The city’s dependence on water sources outside its immediate boundaries made reliable supplies especially important.

The Godavari Drinking Water Supply Project, drawing water from the Sripada Yellampalli Barrage, formed a significant part of the response. KCR inaugurated the project at Ghanpur and Shamirpet on November 24 and25, 2015. Its operating stages were reported to provide approximately 86–172 million gallons per day (MGD).

Emergency arrangements were also made to draw water from Nagarjuna Sagar and Akkampally to meet the city’s requirements. District-level measures were adapted to local water resources.

Credit, Crops and Electricity

The drought’s effects on agriculture were severe. The government pursued several measures to ease the pressure on farmers. Under GO Ms No 69, Agriculture and Cooperation (Agri II) Department, dated August 13, 2014, the second instalment of the farm-loan waiver involved approximately Rs 2,019 crore.

The government also sought to maintain nine hours of free three-phase electricity for agricultural connections and promoted subsidised short-duration crops, including pulses, bajra, castor and sunflower, as alternatives suited to difficult conditions.
Employment support complemented these measures. On September 14, 2015, the Ministry of Rural Development announced an increase in the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme entitlement from 100 to 150 days per rural household in designated drought-affected areas.

No single intervention could erase the consequences of a failed monsoon. However, credit relief, agricultural power, alternative crop options and supplementary employment addressed different dimensions of rural distress.

Protecting Livestock, Rural Livelihoods
Drought also threatens livestock through shortages of fodder and water. For rural households, cattle, sheep and other animals are productive assets, sources of income and a form of financial security.

The relief measures included cattle feed at a 50% subsidy, with an initial allocation of 50 tonnes per drought-affected mandal. More than 490 tonnes of silage bales were supplied, alongside fodder seeds and the promotion of neeti thotlu (water troughs) for livestock. Veterinary interventions included vaccination against enterotoxaemia, sheep pox and foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), while livestock markets were monitored.

From Emergency Relief to Long-Term Water Security

Immediate relief can manage a crisis, but recurring water scarcity requires structural solutions. The drought reinforced the need to restore local water bodies, improve storage and strengthen drinking-water infrastructure.

Through GO Ms No 44, Irrigation and CAD Department, dated March 13, 2015, the government advanced Mission Kakatiya. Its first phase covered 9,306 tanks, with the objective of restoring traditional water bodies and improving their storage and irrigation potential.

Mission Bhagiratha, launched by KCR at Medak on August 7, 2016, represented another major initiative towards household drinking-water security. It envisaged a pipeline network of approximately 1.3 lakh kilometres to provide treated drinking water across the State.

At the inter-State level, Telangana and Maharashtra entered into an agreement on irrigation projects on March 8, 2016. Subsequent redesign placed the proposed Kaleshwaram Lift Irrigation Project’s intake at Medigadda, downstream of the confluence of the Pranahita and Godavari rivers.

These initiatives, their implementation and their outcomes must be assessed on the evidence. No infrastructure project should be exempt from technical, financial or performance scrutiny. But equally, long-term water security cannot be built through emergency tankers alone. It requires planning, investment, coordination and sustained execution.

KCR faced the crisis; Congress must stop evading its own

The defining difference in a crisis is not whether a government faces criticism. Every administration does. It is whether the leadership confronts the situation, mobilises the machinery of government and gives people confidence that their problems are being addressed.

During the 2015–16 drought, the KCR-led government responded with emergency funds, he could successfully secure Rs 791.21 crore in assistance from the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF), hired private borewells, tanker supplies, local water arrangements, agricultural assistance, livestock relief and longer-term water initiatives.

For people struggling to find irrigation and drinking water, reassurance matters when it is backed by action. Leadership means showing people that the administration is responding, resources are being mobilised and solutions are being pursued. It means confronting the crisis rather than allowing uncertainty to become despair.

That is the standard against which the Congress government should now be measured. The Congress inherited a State with excellent infrastructure for water and electricity. Its responsibility is to deliver better outcomes. It cannot govern by remaining permanently in campaign mode against its predecessor.

KCR faced a crisis and sought to give people confidence through emergency action and longer-term measures. The Congress must now demonstrate that same sense of responsibility, not by repeating its accusations, but by solving the problems people face today.

Blaming KCR will not fill a dry borewell, bring water to a village, irrigate a farmer’s field or protect a rural family’s livelihood. People do not need an endless political argument about yesterday; they need a government that works for them today. Telangana’s people deserve solutions, not excuses, blame games or another accusation that the previous government is responsible for the State’s problems.

text:
“You can’t go home again.” - Thomas Wolfe … or maybe you can? Had a fabulous experience earlier tonight participating in a Zoom reading of a brilliant new play in development from my Wabash College classmate JS Simpson. It was fun to dust off acting skills I haven’t much used since before the pandemic, but more significantly it was a delight to hear Simpson’s sharp character development come to life alongside fellow Wabash grads, friends, and readers Scott Smalstig, Ken Ogorek, Hugh Vandivier, and Jason Strasser as well as newly adopted honorary Wabash fellow Mark Holley.

Without spoiling anything, in “Indiana Beta,” Simpson (always a bright, incisive, witty voice and observer) deftly captures perfectly and poignantly a unique moment in time: the early 90s with its intersection (and conflict) of much-vaunted collegiate tradition with a sociocultural milieu that was evolving rapidly, progressively. And what that now means in 2026 for the (cough) fifty-something men looking back on those formative moments with nostalgia and regret, wondering how decades of arguably arrested development have flashed by in the blink of an eye.

In the process, Simpson offers a provocative, thorny critique of our collective assumptions around race, gender, ethnicity, sexuality, class, while still embracing the flawed humanity that ultimately unites us. Can’t wait to see where he goes next with this, and honored tonight to have been part of the piece’s ongoing development.

@WabashCollege
