text:
Skipyo & Mirkwood Ventures

A Permanent Financial Asset Class Resolution with Silicon Valley

Strategic Institutional Alignment Memorandum | Skipyo — Disciplined Capital
I. Executive Position — A Durable Institutional Resolution

A durable resolution between Skipyo, Mirkwood Ventures, and the broader Silicon Valley investment ecosystem would recognize two distinct, commercially legitimate investment mandates: Skipyo's participation in domestic private equity and leveraged buyouts, and Mirkwood Ventures' participation in the venture capital asset class. The objective is to establish independent capital formation pathways without requiring either organization to assume defense-sector, congressional, or politically affiliated investment obligations unrelated to its commercial strategy. Such an arrangement would preserve Silicon Valley's ability to pursue frontier engineering, artificial intelligence, and DefenseTech opportunities while allowing Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures to compete for institutional capital, acquire businesses, and develop technology ventures on conventional market terms.

II. Geographic Proximity and Institutional Expectations

From my perspective, geographic proximity to Arlington and Washington, D.C., created expectations that my entrepreneurial activities should incorporate congressional engagement, defense-oriented institutional relationships, and government-facing business models. I regarded these expectations as inconsistent with my preference for independent commercial investment management. My concerns were compounded by earlier cybersecurity experiences that I associated with certain California technology organizations and by the political and media-oriented activities of prominent New York and Silicon Valley business networks. These experiences informed my reluctance to enter institutional arrangements that might introduce additional political obligations or governance dependencies. However, the existence of such expectations or cybersecurity concerns does not independently establish that specific organizations coordinated to impose them or engaged in unlawful conduct.

III. Transaction Costs and the Private Equity–Venture Capital Distinction

The capital formation requirements associated with Skipyo's proposed private equity strategy differed materially from those of Mirkwood Ventures' prospective venture capital platform. A leveraged buyout typically requires acquisition financing, detailed financial and operational diligence, lender participation, transaction counsel, a willing seller, and sufficient equity commitments to support the acquisition. By comparison, an emerging venture capital manager may establish a smaller initial fund focused on minority investments in early-stage companies, although such a fund still requires institutional credibility, limited partner commitments, regulatory compliance, and a defensible investment strategy. In my assessment, Skipyo's prospective PE strategy involved greater initial transaction complexity, while Mirkwood Ventures potentially offered a more accessible entry point into institutional investment management.

IV. Ambassadorial Finance and Additional Execution Complexity

I viewed the subsequent development of Skipyo's Ambassadorial Finance initiatives as a response to difficulties establishing satisfactory domestic private equity and venture capital financing relationships. These initiatives included UK/GCC institutional outreach, engagement with the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, the Maghreb–Egypt investment proposal, and the Iraq Babylon Adventure Park concept. Although these opportunities offered alternative commercial pathways, they introduced additional requirements involving sovereign counterparties, cross-border regulation, diplomatic coordination, project finance, and geopolitical risk. From my perspective, these requirements increased the managerial and financial burden relative to the original domestic acquisition and venture capital strategies. Whether external institutions deliberately imposed these additional hurdles remains unestablished; the relevant economic consequence was that pursuing international alternatives required substantially different capabilities and resources.

V. Emerging Venture Capital Managers and Market Access

The continued formation of smaller venture capital funds by former technology employees, engineers, and startup professionals demonstrates the existence of an investment management model in which general partners can pursue specialized strategies without first acquiring controlling interests in established operating companies. These managers may receive management fees and, where investment performance permits, carried interest under conventional fund agreements. Such compensation is subject to fund economics, operating expenses, and investor negotiations rather than guaranteed personal profitability. My concern is that the availability of this institutional pathway should extend to qualified independent managers, including Mirkwood Ventures, without requiring defense-oriented sponsorship or relationships outside their investment mandates. Any allegation that particular U.S. defense-affiliated or Israeli venture capital investors deliberately restricted Mirkwood Ventures' market entry would require evidence beyond unsuccessful fundraising discussions.

VI. Resolution Track One — Skipyo Domestic Private Equity

The first component of the proposed resolution would establish Skipyo as an independently managed domestic private equity sponsor capable of pursuing conventional leveraged buyouts with qualified U.S. institutional capital, including prospective pension fund participation. Under this framework, Skipyo could evaluate acquisitions such as LegalShield, subject to seller willingness, financing commitments, valuation, and applicable regulatory requirements. The contemplated integration of Metaseeker's consumer privacy and data-deletion workflows could provide an additional operating strategy, combining subscription legal services, identity protection, privacy administration, and technology-enabled consumer advocacy. This would represent a commercially focused U.S. acquisition mandate rather than a defense procurement or government-sponsored technology program.

VII. Institutional Independence for Skipyo

Skipyo's domestic private equity activities should not require Pentagon contracts, congressional advocacy, defense-oriented venture capital participation, or political sponsorship as conditions of investment eligibility. Potential U.S. pension investors, commercial lenders, and acquisition partners would retain full discretion to evaluate transactions according to their fiduciary duties, investment mandates, and financial underwriting standards. Government engagement would remain appropriate where independently required by law, regulation, or the nature of a specific transaction. Separate Ambassadorial Finance initiatives involving overseas projects could require additional governmental and diplomatic coordination, but those requirements should not automatically extend to Skipyo's domestic commercial acquisitions.

VIII. Resolution Track Two — Mirkwood Ventures as an Independent VC Firm

The second component would recognize Mirkwood Ventures as a prospective independent venture capital manager operating under a commercially oriented investment mandate. Its proposed EMEA-focused strategy would emphasize civilian technologies, scalable business models, and investment opportunities supported by conventional venture capital underwriting. Mirkwood Ventures would seek qualified limited partners, establish appropriate fund governance, and retain discretion over portfolio selection without compulsory defense-sector participation. Its market entry would depend on securing investor commitments and meeting the same legal, financial, and operational standards applicable to other emerging managers, rather than obtaining special institutional privileges or guaranteed capital access.

IX. https://t.co/k2m32VJERw — A Prospective Silicon Valley Syndicate

A constructive extension of the Mirkwood Ventures pathway would involve a separately negotiated venture capital syndicate to support https://t.co/k2m32VJERw, the proposed synthetic data and AI engineering platform. Silicon Valley investors could contribute capital, technical recruitment networks, product development expertise, and access to experienced science and engineering professionals. Such participation could help https://t.co/k2m32VJERw progress from its existing prototype stage toward technical validation, security architecture development, commercial pilots, and eventual market entry. The syndicate would require independent investment decisions, negotiated ownership terms, appropriate intellectual property protections, and defined governance rights. Neither financing nor engineering participation should be presumed committed.

X. Long-Term Institutional Balance and Strategic Resolution

The proposed framework would create a durable distinction between two investment activities. Skipyo would pursue domestic private equity acquisitions and hedge fund strategies through independently negotiated institutional relationships, while Mirkwood Ventures would pursue venture capital investments and potentially support https://t.co/k2m32VJERw through a qualified financing syndicate. Defense-oriented investors and established Silicon Valley firms would remain free to pursue their own technology and national security investment mandates without requiring Skipyo or Mirkwood Ventures to participate in them. This structure would reduce unnecessary institutional overlap, clarify capital allocation responsibilities, and allow each prospective transaction to be assessed according to its commercial merits.

My preferred resolution is a two-track institutional alignment: U.S. pension and other qualified domestic capital supporting Skipyo's commercially underwritten LBO opportunities, including a potential LegalShield–Metaseeker combination; and conventional venture capital participation supporting Mirkwood Ventures' formation and a prospective https://t.co/k2m32VJERw investment syndicate. Such an arrangement would preserve independent governance, reduce exposure to unrelated political and defense-sector obligations, and establish a commercially coherent foundation for both organizations. It would also provide a basis for reconsidering the extent of Skipyo's Ambassadorial Finance activities, subject to existing commitments and the relative attractiveness of domestic and international investment opportunities.

The objective is not to compel institutional investors to provide capital or to establish that past financing difficulties resulted from coordinated exclusion. It is to define an achievable, market-based framework through which Skipyo and Mirkwood Ventures can independently pursue their respective asset classes, access willing investors, and develop sustainable investment businesses without unnecessary institutional dependencies.

Hello California friends.

For more than 25 years I've written up an analysis of the propositions on the California ballot (14 this time) to help my friends and me *think* about them.

I write from a libertarian perspective, though hopefully not with a partisan one, and I try to offer everything in good faith with no hidden agendas. I definitely offer a bit of snark.

I have no connection to any of these issues save for being a voter and taxpayer.

Every cycle I get texts and emails: Hey Steve, where is it? and I am super glad to have it done - it's been probably on the order of 40 hours of work while I have been immersed in a pretty urgent customer project.

As always, I welcome feedback or discussions, I would love to hear about typos and the like, but two things are not welcome:

1/ being a jerk; I am happy to have disagreement, but no namecalling please.

2/ "I disagree with you on proposition X" with no further discussion.  Frankly nobody gives a shit if you agree or not:  TELL US WHY. I want good arguments.

I believe that thoughtful, civil discourse on important issues of the day make for better democracy.

If you've already voted - thank you!

text:
I was extremely fortunate that I was able to self fund the project from a rather large science outreach/education prize I won from a summer internship. Plenty of the companies I bought parts from gave me 20-40% discounts because I was a student, all I had to do was ask. I also did plenty of dumpster diving, bought equipment for pennies on the dollar at government auctions, repaired broken stuff myself, and learned so much about machining and welding. 

The guys who built my electrode grid you see with the target were machinists out in Colorado who primarily did DoD contracting, and a former mentor of mine told them about my project and what I was currently struggling with. They reached out and offered their services free of charge, which was amazing. I always remember what Mr. Roger’s said about what his mom once told him: “ Look for the helpers. You will always find people who are helping.”

The best was @McMasterCarr though. They were so helpful and generous when I needed parts or ordered the wrong part or material. I can remember at least half a dozen cases over 18 months where I ordered the wrong part or material for something on the project, so I emailed them about returning it. Their customer service told me to keep it and try to make sure another student used it at some point, and they sent me the part(s) I needed for free. Literally made me a customer for life.

I did end up mentoring a kid in high school a few years ago who built a demo fusor with a bell jar vacuum chamber that ran on helium. He did it for like $700 over a year and a ton of dumpster diving. Would be more than happy to help you if you’re interested in building one over time.

text:
🇿🇦🇺🇸🪡 Sjoe! Threading the Needle Between Redress and Reciprocity ~ 🧠🏗️ What If the Answer is Calibration Rather Than Escalation? ~ 🔄⚖️ Reciprocity Without Surrender: Testing a Different Route to Redress.
South Africa’s race-based remedial laws were never meant to become permanent fixtures of the state. Section 9(2) of the Constitution authorises measures to advance those disadvantaged by unfair discrimination so that equality can be achieved; Section 217 permits preference in procurement only inside systems that remain competitive and cost-effective. 

Neither provision contemplates indefinite racial sorting of opportunity.

Yet under-delivery has been met, repeatedly, by tighter ownership gates and numerical targets rather than by reform of the loyalty-based appointment practice that the Zondo Commission found unconstitutional. 

The United States has pressed on this intensity. 

Reciprocating that pressure through a calibrated institutional reset—explicit sunset dates, a return to the last period of demonstrated economic capacity, competence leadership over the land-race nexus, and partnership rather than confrontation—offers the only realistic path that restores the conditions under which redress can actually heal.

1. The Temporary Character of Remedial Tools

Constitutional redress was designed as a bridge, not a destination. When remedial instruments lose their temporary character, a closed diagnostic loop forms. Failure is interpreted as proof that racial thresholds were applied too gently, so the thresholds rise again. 

The loyalty filter identified by Zondo remains largely intact; the racial rules that surround it intensify. An explicit forward sunset date forces periodic, evidence-based review against measurable outcomes—net job creation, productive land use, broad-based ownership—rather than automatic escalation.

The founding commitment to non-racialism in Section 1 of the Constitution supplies the deeper constraint. Remedial measures authorised by Section 9(2) must remain compatible with that founding value. 

Permanent racial administration of opportunity risks converting a corrective mechanism into a permanent sorting system. 

Open-ended rules create their own incentives: networks that benefit from the current intensity have every reason to interpret shortfalls as evidence that still more intensity is required. Writing temporality back into the law interrupts that incentive structure. 

Without an explicit sunset, the language of healing becomes protective casing for the extraction the tools were meant to end. Reciprocating the United States ask therefore begins with restoring the temporary character the Constitution itself contemplated.
Sjoe!

A system that answers its own under-performance by raising the racial threshold has a peculiar genius: it can fail at its stated purpose indefinitely and still succeed at its operational one.

Questions Stirring:
Does treating under-delivery as automatic proof of insufficient racial intensity beg the question by assuming the cause rather than testing the unreformed loyalty filter? 
What measurable outcomes would justify extending or ending a sunset clause? 
Why does the system consistently leave the appointment practice unreformed while expanding the intensity of the rules that surround it? These questions matter because they determine whether remedial policy remains a temporary bridge or hardens into permanent racial administration of the state.

2. The Evidence-Based Calibration Point

During Trevor Manuel’s tenure as Finance Minister from 1996 to 2009, South Africa recorded average annual growth near 4 percent under the Mbeki administration, a budget surplus in 2006/07, government debt falling to approximately 26 percent of GDP, and peak net job creation approaching 500 000 positions a year. 

Earlier redress instruments operated inside that higher-capacity environment without the later hard 100 percent ownership gates. 

The Growth, Employment and Redistribution framework prioritised fiscal credibility, private-sector investment and macroeconomic stability. That stability created the fiscal and growth space in which remedial policy could function without collapsing into extraction.

Rewinding intensity to that balance is not nostalgia. It is a return to the last period in which remedial policy coexisted with demonstrable economic capacity. 

Subsequent years saw slower growth, rising debt and diminished job creation coinciding with the dual movement of retained loyalty filter and radicalised racial gates. The Manuel-era metrics therefore supply both proof that calibrated redress can function and the concrete benchmarks against which any future sunset can be tested. 

Without this rewind the claim of temporality remains rhetorical. 

Reciprocating the United States ask requires South Africa to offer this evidence-based reset as the practical meeting point that restores capacity for redress to heal.

Sjoe!
The country once produced budget surpluses and half a million jobs a year while still advancing redress. The later decision to treat that period as permanently unavailable says more about institutional incentives than about historical necessity.

Questions Stirring:
If the Manuel years demonstrated that remedial tools could operate alongside strong growth and job creation, what evidence would falsify the claim that further radicalisation is required? 
Does the coincidence of slower growth and intensified racial rules raise the question of causal direction? 
What institutional interests are served by treating the earlier calibration as permanently unavailable? 

These questions matter because they test whether the system can still recognise its own successful periods or must continue inside a closed loop that converts every shortfall into a mandate for more of the same intensity.

3. The Institutional Signal of Competence

Land reform and race-based procurement form a single overlapping operating system shaped by the same appointment practice Zondo found unconstitutional. Placing a proven fiscal steward and long-term planner—Trevor Manuel or a figure of equivalent competence profile—in a role insulated from ordinary cadre pressures would demonstrate that productive use, title security and urban land challenges take priority over pure racial arithmetic.

Professor Somadoda Fikeni’s testimony before the Madlanga Commission described a political economy of inefficiency: excellent policies written and then left to die, large unspent balances alongside front-line shortages, chronic acting appointments, ministerial churn, and loyalty frequently outranking competence. 

Only a visible break with that interface can restore credibility. 

Manuel’s record of fiscal discipline, the National Development Plan, and public insistence that any expropriation must make economic sense supplies the required profile. 

Such a designation operationalises the temporary character of remaining racial instruments and creates a measurable accountability point against which the sunset date can later be evaluated. 

Reciprocity becomes concrete when competence leadership is installed over the land-race nexus rather than further intensifying the filter that converted redress into extraction.

Sjoe!
When the same networks that once benefited from deployment recommendations appear uniquely positioned under tighter ownership gates, the system is no longer merely under-performing. It is protecting itself.

Questions Stirring:
Does the persistence of acting appointments and loyalty-over-competence patterns raise the question of whether new ownership gates will simply create new gatekeeping opportunities? 
What verification mechanisms would ensure that a Land Governor role remains insulated from the very pressures it is meant to interrupt? 
Why has the variable most consistently left unreformed been the same variable Zondo identified as facilitative of capture? 
These questions matter because they determine whether institutional signals remain symbolic or actually subordinate the loyalty filter that has shaped both land and procurement outcomes.

4. Converting Pressure into Partnership Time

The United States has pressed on the current intensity of race-based rules, viewing them as barriers to investment and as incompatible with non-racial opportunity. 

Framing a rewind to the Manuel-era balance, a competence-first Land Governor appointment, and an explicit sunset mechanism as the concrete meeting point allows South Africa to request additional time in which calibrated redress can produce measurable healing.

Earlier framing treated external pressure solely as constraint. The same pressure can be met by a signal of institutional reset, converting confrontation into negotiated runway. 

Credibility depends on visible subordination of the loyalty filter and statutory temporality of the remaining racial rules. Reciprocity in this form restores partnership conditions under which South Africa can ask for the time required for redress to perform its original function rather than remain trapped in the closed loop of failure-driven radicalisation.

Sjoe!
External pressure is usually presented as a threat to sovereignty. Rarely is it noticed that the greater threat to sovereignty is an internal system that converts every shortfall into a mandate for more of the same rules.

Questions Stirring:
Does converting external pressure into negotiated time raise the question of whether South Africa still possesses the institutional will to subordinate loyalty-based selection? 
What specific design features of a rewind and Land Governor role would make United States input a partnership rather than a diktat? 
If the dual movement of retained filter and intensified gates continues, what falsifiable evidence would interrupt it? 

These questions matter because they test whether reciprocity can create the diplomatic and domestic space in which redress is given the conditions and time it needs to heal.

5. The Integrated Package That Breaks the Loop

The combined sequence—explicit sunset date, Manuel-era rewind, competence leadership over the land-race nexus, and requested external input as partnership—interrupts the pattern in which under-delivery automatically produces more racial intensity. 

Independent lines of evidence converge: Zondo’s findings on cadre deployment, the macroeconomic record of the Manuel years, Fikeni’s operational diagnosis of policy cemeteries and unspent billions, the constitutional text of Sections 9(2) and 217, and the 2026 draft procurement regulations that would impose 100 percent designated-group ownership for certain set-asides.

The dual movement of retained loyalty filter plus radicalised racial gates has protected extraction while eroding the conditions for broad-based healing. 

Treating race laws as temporary, resetting intensity to the last period of demonstrated capacity, installing competence leadership, and inviting input as partnership restores the constitutional wager that race would cease to be the permanent organising principle of the state. 

Only under those conditions can the remedial tools heal rather than perpetuate the deficits they claim to remedy.

Sjoe!
An elegant mutation keeps the original vocabulary while quietly rewriting the operational meaning. “Redress” remains the word on the cover; the text inside has been revised by the appointment practice it was meant to constrain.

Questions Stirring:
Does the convergence of independent lines of evidence raise the question of why the loyalty filter remains the variable most carefully left untouched? 
What would constitute decisive falsification of the claim that further intensification is the only available response to under-delivery? 
Why does a system that repeatedly produces detailed inquiries still struggle to place its own enabling appointment practice under sustained scrutiny? 

These questions matter because they determine whether South Africa can still name its operating system clearly enough to change it, or whether the closed loop will continue to convert every shortfall into a mandate for more of the same rules.

Final Resolution

Reciprocity is not concession. It is the necessary condition for redress to heal. Writing an explicit sunset into race laws, rewinding intensity to the Manuel-era balance of growth and capacity, installing competence leadership over the land-race nexus, and converting United States pressure into negotiated time form a single institutional package. 

That package subordinates the loyalty filter Zondo identified as facilitative of capture, replaces the closed diagnostic loop with measurable outcomes, and restores the temporary, evidence-based character the Constitution contemplated. 

The metrics exist. The diplomatic space can be created. The path is clear—provided the country chooses competence and temporality over the indefinite escalation of the same rules. 

The beloved country has survived worse. It has not yet been required to look this steadily at the mechanism that turned its own remedial language into protective casing for extraction. 

That steady look is now unavoidable. The loyalty filter remains a choice.

text:
Seven days ago he could not move his neck.

He had dived to make a tackle, and the tight end's knee caught him in the helmet. He lay on the turf for close to ten minutes while they immobilized him, then they carried him off on a stretcher and drove him to a hospital.

A few hours later reporters saw him walking around the locker room, which is the first good thing in this story.

His name is Kendal Daniels.

Today he wore the green dot, which means he was the one calling the defense. He led Atlanta in tackles with nine of his own. He intercepted Brock Purdy and ran it back to the red zone, and Atlanta kicked the field goal that made it a two score game.

On San Francisco's next drive he recovered the fumble that ended it.

Here is what he said about the thing that happened to him seven days earlier.

"I've never not walked off the field after an injury."

"It was a bad feeling, and I'm blessed to be able to play this week."

He could not turn his neck for days. He was back at practice on the Wednesday.

Now go back and look at how he got here, because it is stranger than you would think.

He grew up in Beggs, Oklahoma, a town of about 1,200 people. Basketball was his sport. At 6 foot 5, you can see why. He did not join the football team until he was a sophomore.

Two years after that he was rated the fifth best safety in America and the best recruit in his state.

Then Oklahoma pulled his offer.

So he committed to Texas A&M, changed his mind, and went to Oklahoma State instead. As a redshirt freshman he had 45 tackles and three interceptions, and he ended a 41 to 34 win over Texas with an interception in the final seconds.

He was the Big 12 Defensive Freshman of the Year.

Four years later he transferred to Oklahoma anyway, the school that had taken the offer back.

Atlanta traded down in April and took him with the 134th pick.

Here is one of his teammates on today.

"He's got whatever it is, and it's a testament to his preparation."

Be straight about where this actually sits. He was only out there calling the defense because Divine Deablo is hurt. He is a fourth round rookie with one enormous afternoon, not a settled thing. And a neck is not an ankle, so nobody should be treating last Sunday as finished business.

But a kid who could not turn his head seven days ago spent this afternoon telling ten grown men where to stand, and then he went and took the ball away twice.

When were you the most scared and went back anyway.

text:
#Civan 📿 #BarışBaktaş 💫
To me, Cıvan is one of the most compelling, multifaceted, emotional, and genuinely evolving characters in this series. We have witnessed an extraordinary transformation: from a man who grew up in a closed world where humiliation, hurt, cruelty, and hostility were all too familiar, into a man with an incredibly kind and gentle heart, capable of holding so much love within himself that he is even willing to give it to a child who is not his own.

That is what amazes me about him. The pain he has endured has not made him heartless. His circumstances have not destroyed his ability to empathize. On the contrary, beneath his outward roughness and emotional intensity, we are gradually discovering a man who has so much goodness to offer the world.

Yet his inner world resembles a boiling cauldron with its lid tightly shut. Inside, there is hurt, disappointment, fear, accumulated pain, conflicting emotions, and a constant struggle with himself. He carries all of this almost entirely alone. He is trying to stand on his own feet, find his place in life, support his sisters, and deal with his own problems. And on top of everything else, there is his love for Nilüfer — a complicated, painful love in which their feelings collide with the differences between their worlds and the circumstances surrounding them, as though life itself were constantly testing his strength.

And do you know what saddens me most? Cıvan is a man who has learned to give love, even though he still desperately needs someone to take care of him.

He gives his love generously to his sisters, cares for those around him, and thinks of others even when he has so little himself. His willingness to welcome a child who is not his own into his heart is yet another sign of just how far he has come from the man he was at the beginning of his journey.

I am truly amazed by this transformation. But what makes me even happier is that it has been possible at all. Cıvan shows us that a person is not forever destined to remain a product of their environment, their past, or the pain they have endured. Our circumstances shape us, but love, life experience, and the inner work we do on ourselves can change us.
Because even someone who has grown up surrounded by pain can carry an extraordinary amount of light within them. And more than anything, I hope that one day Cıvan will receive the care, support, and warmth he so generously gives to others, but still needs so deeply himself.🥹

text:
I barely slept that night.

The next morning, I went to work expecting Richard to fire me.

Instead, he acted as though nothing had happened. He greeted me warmly, asked about my weekend, and even invited me to join a meeting with potential investors.

But I noticed that my access to certain financial records had suddenly disappeared.

By lunchtime, I received an email from our accounting department asking me to confirm several transactions using my employee credentials.

I hadn’t initiated them.

Someone had used my login to approve payments connected to the suspicious vehicle sales.

I immediately changed my password and reported the activity in writing.

That evening, an unfamiliar number called me.

The caller introduced himself as a federal investigator looking into possible money laundering involving several businesses in South Florida.

He asked whether I had processed invoices for vehicles purchased through multiple companies.

My heart began racing.

I told him what I knew and explained that I had raised concerns internally.

He asked whether I still had copies of the records.

I did.

I had retained legitimate work records in accordance with company policy, including emails documenting my questions and the missing delivery confirmations. I didn’t alter or remove anything further; I followed the investigator’s instructions about preserving evidence.

Two days later, investigators arrived at the dealership.

Richard was escorted out of his office while employees watched in stunned silence.

Vincent, the man who had purchased the three SUVs, was also under investigation.

Authorities suspected that the dealership had been used to disguise the origins of criminal proceeds through fabricated sales and complicated financial transactions.

I later learned that investigators were examining transactions involving several million dollars.

But the most frightening discovery came when they reviewed the digital records.

Someone had attempted to make it appear that I had approved some of the false invoices.

My written objections and the email records showing unauthorized activity became important evidence in establishing what I had actually done.

I wasn’t immediately declared innocent, and I knew that cooperating with investigators didn’t automatically guarantee I would face no consequences. I hired a lawyer and answered questions through the proper channels.

Richard was eventually charged in connection with the alleged scheme. The case took months to unfold, and I learned to be careful about what I repeated because an investigation and a conviction are not the same thing.

I lost my job when the dealership shut down.

I also lost the career I had spent years building, at least temporarily.

But I kept my records, told the truth, and refused to accept money that I suspected was meant to buy my silence.

Sometimes I wonder what would have happened if I had taken that $15,000.

Maybe I would have convinced myself it was harmless. Maybe I would have kept quiet until the investigation reached my desk and I had no explanation for the transactions bearing my credentials.

One thing I know for certain is that my boss didn’t offer me that money because he appreciated my work.

He offered it because he wanted me to become part of his silence.

Let me ask you this: If your employer offered you $15,000 to stop questioning suspicious transactions, knowing that refusing could cost you your job, would you walk away immediately, or would you be afraid to risk everything you had worked for?

text:
Britain’s strategy toward Israel is worse than virtue signalling. It is undermining its own stated objectives - even where those objectives differ from Britain’s national interest. London claims to be helping Palestinians and advancing peace, yet keeps surrendering the influence needed to do either, while putting British security and economic interests at risk.

Start with recognizing Palestine. The announcement did not create a functioning state, deliver democratic government or secure the hostages’ release - that wasn't even negotiated. Britain recognized Palestine while Hamas still held hostages and Palestinian institutional reforms remained promises. The diplomatic gesture was real. The promised transformation on the ground was not delivered by it.

Recognition was something Palestinian leaders wanted. That made it leverage.

Recognition could have been part of a coordinated bargain for the hostages, backed by pressure on Hamas and the governments with influence over it. Success was never guaranteed. But Britain surrendered that particular bargaining chip without securing their release.

Britain could have also tied it to verifiable reforms serving Palestinians: elections, accountable government, the effective abolition of payments rewarding terrorism, and removing incitement and the glorification of violence from classrooms. London acknowledged commitments on elections, prisoner payments and curriculum reform before recognition. It accepted promises where it could have demanded results. That was a missed opportunity to help Palestinians hold their own leadership accountable.

All this was supposedly done to save the “two-state solution”. Yet that formula has lost credibility among the people expected to live with its consequences. In Pew’s 2026 survey, only 17% of Israelis believed Israel and a Palestinian state could coexist peacefully, after October 7th. Fifty-six percent believed they could not. Among Palestinians surveyed in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, just 21% believed peaceful coexistence was possible, while 68% did not.

Another declaration from London cannot repair that collapse of trust.

And there is a fundamental contradiction Britain prefers to leave unaddressed, at best. If Palestinian statehood in Gaza and the West Bank is combined with an unrestricted “right of return” into Israel sufficient to eliminate its Jewish majority, the destination is effectively two Palestinian-majority states. A negotiated refugee settlement could avoid that outcome. An unlimited demand cannot simply be hidden behind the reassuring phrase “two states”. Two states for two peoples requires accepting Jewish national self-determination too. Only a small fraction of Palestinians support that.

Then consider military education. Britain suspended future Israeli participation in its military training and education courses, including the Royal College of Defense Studies. The government simultaneously explained that these courses emphasize compliance with international humanitarian law. If Britain believes Israeli officers need to learn British standards, excluding them from the institutions teaching those standards is a peculiar remedy. It also didn't apply these standards to Chinese and Qatari personal - actual violators of international humanitarian law, and not a fake one: Discussing the 2014 Gaza conflict, British Colonel Richard Kemp described Israeli efforts to protect civilians as “unprecedented in any other army”. After visiting in 2024, General Sir John McColl wrote: “The procedures are at least as rigorous as those applied in the UK armed forces”. Perhaps even more.

Asked why Chinese and Qatari personnel were not similarly banned, the government offered a case-by-case explanation about partnerships, risks and benefits. Apparently engagement can have strategic value with those countries, while exclusion is the preferred instrument for a democratic ally.

Next came restrictions targeting Israeli settlements. Britain’s businesses now face potential exposure to American anti-boycott rules, including restrictions on government contracts and public investment in Florida and Texas. Going against British national interest.

The retaliation was considerably more concrete than the diplomatic gains. Israel ordered the closure of Britain’s East Jerusalem consulate. The eventual agreement preserved a much smaller mission: Britain’s presence serving Palestinians was sharply reduced. Israel also announced Britain’s exclusion from the US-led Gaza coordination mission. A policy advertised as helping Palestinians reduced Britain’s capacity to work on their behalf.

Palestinian workers face another potential cost. Businesses targeted because they operate in settlements also employ Palestinians. Palestinian statistics put average daily wages in Israel and settlements at approximately 3 times more that in the West Bank’s private sector. If export restrictions cause employers to cut production or close, Palestinian families lose livelihoods too. Calling a measure pro-Palestinian does not protect their paychecks. Calling it anti-Israeli seems more fitting.

The diplomatic priorities are equally revealing. During September’s sanctions dispute, Pat McFadden acknowledged that Andy Burnham had not yet spoken to Netanyahu. Later that month, Ed Miliband met and shook hands with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the UN, while the Jewish Chronicle reported that he met no Israeli official during that visit. Talking to adversaries might be necessary. Failing to engage an ally while trying to change its behavior is harder to explain.

The Iranian meeting took place three days before the RAF Fairford plot. Netanyahu subsequently said Israel had warned Britain about an Iranian-sponsored threat beforehand. The strategic question is hence unavoidable: why treat a country supplying potentially life-saving intelligence as a relationship Britain can casually degrade?

Israel still has choices. Intelligence cooperation with MI6 and other British agencies is a relationship to maintain, not an entitlement. Reduced collaboration would mean fewer warnings, less visibility and greater risk for Islamist terror attacks on British soil. British security should not become collateral damage in a contest to display disapproval.

Nor should Britain overlook the economic opportunity. Dealroom’s 2025 analysis identified more than 180 international billion-dollar companies with offices in Tel Aviv, and a startup-to-unicorn conversion rate far above the wider region’s. This is a substantial partner in technology, investment and innovation. A foreign policy built around the Israel portrayed in protest slogans cannot adequately account for the Israel British businesses and security services actually work with.

Recognition spent before reforms were delivered. Military exchanges suspended. Diplomatic access reduced. Businesses exposed to competing restrictions. Palestinian livelihoods potentially damaged. A valuable security relationship placed under strain. Britain played most of it's cards.

But where is the corresponding achievement?

Britain is entitled to criticize Israeli policy. Its government is responsible for making that criticism serve a practical purpose. Sacrificing influence, commercial opportunity and security cooperation for domestic political applause and without even the guarantee of electoral reward - is a remarkable way to confuse moral performance with national interest.

🔴 A Washington Asset in White Robes: The Ledger of Pope Leo XIV’s Words and Actions

October 25, 2026, Vatican City. Speaking from the window of his study, Pope Leo XIV expressed concern over the “dire humanitarian situation” in Taiz, Yemen, and called for a cessation of hostilities. That same day, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi took to X to welcome the Pope’s statement.

This is Washington’s bridgehead within the Vatican, employing the rhetoric of “peace” to provide moral cover for yet another front in a proxy war.

💥 The Ledger of Words vs. Actions: What He Says vs. What He Does

What he says: The love of money is the root of all evil.

On October 9, 2025, the Vatican released his first apostolic exhortation, *Dilexi Te*. The document explicitly states: “The love of money is truly the root of all evil.” He criticizes “wealthy elites who live in a bubble of comfort and luxury, inhabiting a world almost entirely separate from that of ordinary people.” He argues that when wealth is treated as life’s ultimate goal, priorities become inverted—noting, for instance, that CEOs may earn 600 times as much as their workers.

What he does: While signing that very document, he dismantled the regulatory safeguards surrounding the Vatican Bank.

On October 6, 2025, the same month *Dilexi Te* was released, he signed the *motu proprio* (papal decree) *Coniuncta cura*. This decree rescinded a directive issued by his predecessor, Pope Francis, on August 23, 2022. Francis’s directive had granted the Vatican Bank (IOR) exclusive authority over the management of the Holy See’s assets and movable property. Leo XIV revoked this exclusivity, allowing the Administration of the Patrimony of the Apostolic See (APSA) to bring in external financial institutions and intermediaries from outside the Vatican to manage these assets whenever it deems such an arrangement “more efficient or appropriate.”  He opposes the concentration of wealth, yet he has loosened control over the Vatican’s own wealth.

He says: Do not turn wealth into a weapon that destroys people.

On September 21, 2025, while praying at St. Anne’s Church, he expressed the hope that leaders would not transform wealth into a weapon, a "monopoly that destroys people or humiliates workers."

His actions: When an Israeli missile struck the only Catholic church in Gaza, he refrained from naming those responsible.

On July 17, 2025, an attack by Israeli forces hit the Holy Family Catholic Church in Gaza City, killing three people and injuring several others including a priest who had been close to the late Pope Francis. Leo XIV expressed "profound sorrow," called for an "immediate ceasefire," and voiced a "deep hope" for "dialogue and lasting peace." However, his statement did not explicitly hold Israel accountable for the attack. When bombs struck a church under his own jurisdiction, he referred to the event merely as a "military attack," omitting any subject.

🎯 Yemen: How the Pope’s Rhetoric Serves the War Machine

On October 25, 2026, Leo XIV called for an end to hostilities in Yemen, specifically mentioning the siege of Taiz. Yet, he failed to specify who was responsible for the siege.

The siege of Taiz is enforced by a Saudi-led coalition and the Yemeni forces it supports, a coalition that receives logistical, intelligence, and aerial refueling assistance from the United States. The Pope’s statement made no mention of the Saudi-led coalition’s aerial blockade, the U.S. military support for that blockade, nor the documented use of Omani territory and ports as a conduit for the transfer of weapons and funds to Ansar Allah.

Oman’s Foreign Minister welcomed the Pope’s statement. Yet, according to official records from the Yemeni parliament, Omani territory and ports have served as a pipeline for the Ansar Allah war machine, including by allowing Iranian civilian aircraft to transport Ansar Allah delegations, in violation of the aerial blockade on Yemen.  The Pope has issued an appeal regarding Taiz. This appeal has been exploited by Muscat to provide a veneer of moral legitimacy to its own duplicitous agenda. Taiz does not need the Pope’s "concern"; what it needs is for the flow of weapons and funds facilitated via Oman to be cut off.

📜 His Power Base: Chicago, Washington, and the Vatican

Leo XIV, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago in 1955, is the first American-born Pope in history. He holds dual citizenship in the United States and Peru.

His initial diplomatic moves upon taking office were pointedly directed toward Washington.

On March 7, 2026, he appointed Archbishop Gabriele Caccia formerly the Vatican’s Permanent Observer to the United Nations as the new Apostolic Nuncio to the United States.

On May 1, 2026, he appointed four new American bishops in a single stroke, including those for the Diocese of Laredo (Texas) and the Diocese of Wheeling-Charleston (West Virginia), as well as two auxiliary bishops for the Archdiocese of Washington.

On May 7, 2026, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Leo XIV at the Vatican; the encounter was described by American officials as "friendly" and "constructive." This meeting took place following a series of public attacks launched by Trump against the Pope over the issue of the war with Iran. Rubio spent two and a half hours at the Vatican, a duration that exceeded the scheduled time for the meeting.

text:
Since its May peak, China's stock market has lost $3.5 trillion in value. More troubling is the earnings outlook: 2026 profit forecasts for MSCI China companies have been cut by over 4% since late March, and by more than 13% for Hang Seng Tech companies.

China's industrial output rose 5.5% year-on-year in September, while retail sales grew just 1.1%. Factories are still producing, but consumers remain cautious. Weak demand fuels price wars, steadily eroding corporate margins.

I see something similar in China's construction industry. More contracts don't necessarily mean more profit. Contractors face intense price competition, but getting paid is an even bigger problem. Progress payments are relatively reliable, while final settlement payments are often delayed or never received in cash. Developers frequently offer apartments instead of cash, but these properties can be difficult to sell, sometimes even mortgaged or frozen by court orders.

Companies may record revenue on paper without receiving the cash. Suppliers go unpaid, workers' wages are delayed, and many contractors have been forced to scale back operations or shut down altogether.

For investors, a low P/E ratio doesn't automatically mean a bargain. If earnings expectations keep falling, share prices can fall further.

What China's stock market really needs is a recovery in corporate profitability, not just support for stock indices. Strengthening household purchasing power may ultimately do more for a lasting recovery than another round of industrial capacity expansion.

text:
My take: Apollo economist: AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" outside tech. Plausible. Also: no methodology shown, deployment in non-tech is years old, and Apollo has credit exposure to corporate balance sheets. The "zero" is doing a lot of work for a number with no math visible.

Apollo Economist's "Zero Payoff" Claim Needs More Than a Quotable Number

An economist at Apollo has declared that AI has delivered "zero financial payoff" to corporate America outside of tech, despite massive investments and widespread hype. The phrase lands with satisfying bluntness. It is also, as stated in the article, the entire data layer on offer — no underlying numbers, no methodology, no time horizon, no sector breakdown. A categorical claim covering all non-tech corporate America either summarizes rich analysis that wasn't shown, or it is a conclusion in search of evidence. The article doesn't let you tell which.

The structure of the claim has a timing problem. Meaningful AI deployment in non-tech industries is, at best, a few years old. Financial payoff from infrastructure-level transformation historically lags investment by years — electrification, enterprise software, and the internet all looked like expensive disappointments mid-cycle. Calling zero return at this stage could be accurate measurement or premature accounting. Without the methodology behind the "zero," there is no way to know.

What is separately, genuinely true: the hype-to-output gap is real. Frontier labs produce models; whether non-tech companies successfully operationalize those models is a distinct, downstream question entirely outside the labs' hands. If there is a failure here, it lives in corporate adoption capacity, change management, and the hard problem of mapping general-purpose tools to industry-specific workflows — not in whether the underlying technology exists and works.

The claim also carries a faint political-economic flavor. Issued into a moment of intensifying AI investment scrutiny, "AI isn't paying off" serves narratives about bubble dynamics and regulatory justification. That doesn't make it wrong. But when a claim this broad enters contested policy-economic territory, checking who benefits from the narrative landing is fair. Apollo is a major private credit firm with exposure to corporate balance sheets. The statement could be genuine analysis. It could also be positioning on credit risk. The article doesn't say.

Bottom line: plausible in outline, insufficient in evidence, with a temporal framing that may be doing more work than the data can support. The word "zero" is carrying a heavy rhetorical load for a number that requires considerably more rigor behind it before it earns its categorical force.

text:
Hidden in Jianzha County of Qinghai Province, Luoduojie Zhihe Monastery, also known as Vajra Cliff 73 Temples, is a little-known yet stunning millennial treasure. Founded in 842 AD in the Tang Dynasty, this nearly 1,200-year-old Gelugpa Buddhist temple is a core holy site of the later revival of Tibetan Buddhism. Rated as a Qinghai provincial cultural relic protection unit, it earns the beautiful reputation as “the Mogao Grottoes of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau”.

Built upon 55-million-year-old magnificent red Danxia cliffs adjacent to Kanbula Scenic Area, the monastery perfectly integrates natural Danxia landscapes, ancient grotto groups, prayer corridors and fluttering prayer flags, combining elegant Tibetan and Han architectural styles.

It consists of three functional courtyards. The upper courtyard boasts 24 ancient meditation grottoes scattered on an 80-meter-high cliff, preserving ancient murals, statues and a total of 1,136 precious cultural relics spanning multiple dynasties. The zigzag hanging trail offers panoramic views of the valley and county scenery. The middle courtyard features the landmark Ten-Thousand-Buddha Pagoda for prayer and blessing. The lower courtyard’s grand main hall serves as the major venue for daily Buddhist rituals and worship.

Blending profound religious culture, ancient grotto art and breathtaking Danxia scenery, this quiet sacred land presents a perfect harmony of faith and nature.

So how do we settle this karma? Not through fear, and not through costly rituals done in a hurry. The first remedy is remembrance. Perform shraddha during Pitru Paksha and offer water with black sesame, called tarpan, to your ancestors on every Amavasya. In our tradition, food offered to crows during shraddha is believed to reach the ancestors. The second remedy is to complete what was left unfinished. If your grandfather left a promise unkept, a temple unvisited or a person he wronged, try to complete that work yourself. Rahu's hold can weaken when the old work is completed.

The third remedy is the worship of Maa Durga, who helps remove the fear, confusion and strong desires linked to Rahu. The fourth remedy is honesty. Rahu was born from a trick during the Samudra Manthan, when he secretly drank the amrit. So, every shortcut you refuse and every honest action you take helps you move away from Rahu's negative side. For certain cases, our tradition also advises rituals like Narayan Bali and Gaya shraddha, performed with faith and under the guidance of a learned priest. These rituals should be chosen after proper understanding, not out of fear.

text:
A street vendor is dead. A judge’s 17-year-old son was allegedly driving the Mercedes-Benz that killed him. And the grieving family claims they were treated with arrogance instead of compassion.

Is this how justice works in Kerala?

On 25 October 2026, at approximately 2:20 AM, Jayabalakrishnan was travelling on his scooter when a Mercedes-Benz struck him from behind at Cheranalloor in Kochi.

He never made it home.

Jayabalakrishnan ran a small roadside eatery near Chittoor temple. He was an ordinary working man earning his livelihood, unaware that this journey would be his last.

The Mercedes-Benz was reportedly driven by the 17-year-old son of an Additional District Judge. The teenager had no valid driving licence, and the vehicle was registered in his father’s name.

What followed raises deeply disturbing questions about police conduct, judicial privilege and accountability.

The victim’s niece, Jayalakshmi, has made serious allegations about how the family was treated.

According to her, when she questioned the judge about his underage son driving the vehicle, he allegedly became agitated and told her not to teach him the law.

She further alleged that police officers discouraged the grieving family from becoming emotional and that their attitude changed after learning the accused’s father was a judge.

These allegations require an impartial investigation.

A man has lost his life. His family has every right to demand answers. Who gives anyone the authority to dismiss their grief?

If a judicial officer attempted to intimidate a victim’s family or use his position to influence the investigation, such conduct would be utterly disgraceful.

A judge’s responsibility is to uphold the law, not to expect special treatment because of his designation.

The initial police response deserves serious scrutiny.

The teenager was initially booked for rash driving and causing death by negligence before being released on station bail.

Following protests by the victim’s relatives and local residents, police reportedly took him back into custody and added a more serious charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

This sequence raises several questions.

Why was the accused initially released on station bail?

Was that decision legally justified and properly explained to the victim’s family?

Were all available CCTV footage, witness statements and other evidence promptly secured?

Did the accused’s family background influence any police decision?

And why did the grieving family have to protest outside the police station to demand accountability?

The Kerala Police must answer these questions transparently.

The accused being a minor entitles him to the legal protections provided under the Juvenile Justice Act. Those protections must be respected.

But being a minor does not mean being exempt from accountability.

The vehicle owner’s potential responsibility must also be examined under Section 199A of the Motor Vehicles Act, subject to the applicable legal requirements.

Police have reportedly stated that the teenager took the vehicle without his parents’ knowledge. That explanation must be assessed against the evidence rather than accepted or rejected without investigation.

Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan and Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala must ensure that no judicial influence, personal connection or professional position interferes with this investigation.

The Home Minister has assured strict action regardless of the accused’s connections.

That assurance must now translate into a fair, transparent and thorough investigation.

If police officers mishandled the case or mistreated the victim’s family, appropriate disciplinary action must follow.

If the vehicle owner bears legal responsibility, his judicial position must offer no protection.

And if the investigation establishes criminal responsibility, the case must proceed strictly according to law.

But amid all these questions, we must not forget the man whose life has been lost.

Jayabalakrishnan was not a powerful politician, a wealthy businessman or an influential public figure.

He was an ordinary man running a roadside eatery, working late into the night to support his family.

He had a wife, children and responsibilities.

He deserved to return home safely.

Instead, his family is now mourning an irreversible loss while fighting for answers.

His life was no less valuable than that of a judge, a minister or anyone born into privilege.

The real test of a justice system is not how it treats the powerful. It is whether an ordinary citizen can obtain justice when the accused comes from an influential family.

The Kerala government must ensure that this case does not disappear from public attention once the initial outrage subsides.

There must be no preferential treatment, no interference, no intimidation of the victim’s family and no protection for anyone found responsible.

The investigation must establish the truth, examine every relevant person’s legal responsibility and hold those responsible accountable.

A judge’s son is not above the law. A street vendor’s life is not worth less.

Justice must never depend on wealth, influence or family background.

Justice for Jayabalakrishnan.

text:
Good luck with that.

Starlink is fully operational today with a massive consumer-focused network; Telesat Lightspeed is a planned enterprise/government system not expected to offer commercial service until early 2028.
Current status and scale
•  Starlink: ~11,000+ satellites in low Earth orbit (~550 km altitude), with ongoing rapid deployment (including new higher-capacity V3 satellites). It has roughly 12 million global subscribers and more than 500,000 users in Canada. Coverage reaches most of Canada, including remote and northern areas.
•  Telesat Lightspeed: 0 operational production satellites so far. The planned constellation is 225 satellites (recently expanded from ~156 due to a Canadian military contract). First pathfinder/production launches are targeted for December 2026 on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets, with global commercial service expected around Q1 2028. Orbits are higher (~1,000–1,300 km).
Target markets and service model
•  Starlink primarily serves residential/consumer users (plus mobile/RV “Roam,” aviation, maritime, and some enterprise). It is a direct-to-consumer best-effort broadband service. In Canada, residential plans typically run about $75–$150 CAD/month (tiered up to ~400 Mbps priority) with unlimited data and no long-term contracts; hardware is often available as a low-cost or free rental in many areas. Real-world speeds commonly fall in the 100–300+ Mbps range with ~20–40 ms latency.
•  Telesat Lightspeed is designed as a business-to-business (B2B) wholesale and enterprise system for telecom providers, governments, defence, aviation, and maritime users—not direct residential consumers. It emphasises guaranteed service-level agreements (SLAs), Carrier Ethernet (Layer 2) connectivity, optical inter-satellite links for routing control and data sovereignty, and military Ka-band spectrum. It aims to focus capacity where needed in real time and support high-latitude/Arctic operations. No public consumer pricing exists because it is not aimed at households.
Key practical differences
•  Availability and performance today: Starlink is usable now across Canada for homes, cottages, RVs, and remote sites. Telesat cannot replace it for residential users for years; even once live, it is expected to reach most end-users through local telecom partners rather than direct dish sales like Starlink.
•  Sovereignty and Canadian ties: Telesat is Ottawa-based, with substantial Canadian government funding (loans, equity, and a ~$2.3 billion Arctic military communications contract) and satellites built by MDA Space in Montreal. It markets features for secure, sovereign routing. However, a US investment firm owns a significant stake (~35%), and it depends on SpaceX for most launches. Starlink is fully US/SpaceX-controlled.
•  Capacity and economics: Starlink’s far larger constellation and vertical integration (own launches, manufacturing, and rapid iteration) give it a major scale advantage and lower per-bit costs. Telesat’s smaller, higher-orbit design prioritises enterprise-grade reliability, SLAs, and specialised military use over mass consumer volume.
In short, for anyone needing satellite internet in Canada right now (or the next couple of years), Starlink is the practical option. Telesat Lightspeed is positioned as a future sovereign/enterprise alternative, particularly valuable for government and defence needs in the Arctic and elsewhere, but it will not be a direct near-term substitute for Starlink’s consumer service.

text:
A few years ago: “Starlink is a stupid idea. Anyone investing in this Musk scam deserves to lose everything.”
Today: “Starlink is essential to the defense of an invaded nation. Nationalize it!”
Robert Reich (video posted yesterday) is now calling on Democrats to turn (Steal!) Starlink into a public corporation. Before anyone goes along with that, look at what was actually built, and how.
What he did, much of which people don’t know about:
Rockets: Took a private company that nearly went bankrupt and made orbital flight routine. Boosters now land themselves and fly again, which has cut the cost of reaching space dramatically. American astronauts fly on American hardware again after the Shuttle era.
Starlink: A working global network, now connecting phones directly in places with no towers. For villages, clinics, schools, ships, and disaster zones, it’s often the first reliable connection they’ve ever had. I believe it will do more to reduce poverty worldwide than almost any other technology.
Electric cars and batteries: Turned EVs from a niche idea into a mainstream industry, and Model Y became the best-selling car in Europe. Megapack batteries now store power for electric grids.
Neuralink: Said in January 2026 it had 21 participants enrolled in trials worldwide. Participants use the implant to control computers and robotic arms, and one returned to college. For people with paralysis, that’s independence they didn’t have before.
Much more:  Tunneling, U.S. battery materials, and much bigger rockets are all in progress.
And he did it while creating wealth for employees, builders, and investors, and paying enormous taxes, including one of the largest single-year individual tax bills on record.
None of that changed the technology. What changed is that it became valuable.  We know he is not stopping here but just getting started.  Space data centers will reduce the electrical burden, etc. of course the same objections are here.
Why nationalization is the wrong answer:
The risk was private. Nobody offered to share the losses when rockets were exploding. Taking the company after it succeeds teaches every future builder that success is the trigger for confiscation.
The state didn’t do this. Nasa's Shuttle was painfully expensive and slow- no moon ventures since the 60's - no viable path, Nasa's engineers laughed at his ideas, and showed little support. A private company, under cost pressure, made reuse work. Public ownership removes the pressure that drove the progress.
Importance isn’t a reason to seize something. If it were, the state would take every company that matters. Dependence on one provider is solved by competition, contracts, and regulation, and rivals like Amazon’s Kuiper are already deploying.
It’s a one-way door. Once a government can take a company because it became essential, no founder or investor can treat property as secure, and capital goes elsewhere.  Innovation stops, progress stops, capital stops; our pie does not expand it collapses.
My view: no one alive has done more to move humanity forward than the people who build things that work, and Elon Musk is at the top of that list. Five years ago they called it a scam, and now they want to own it.
Entrepreneurs, pay attention. Mock it while it’s risky, resent it once it works, and steal it as yours once it’s essential. Progress distorts. The party that once cheered Silicon Valley as the engine of progress now treats its biggest successes as something to be seized. And when you punish the builders, progress doesn’t just move somewhere else. It can stop. We went to the Moon, and then for over fifty years we didn’t. Reusable rockets, satellite internet, electric vehicles, brain implants, Robotics, and AI are advancing together, each feeding the others, and that kind of convergence doesn’t come around on a whim.  Government is incapable of these types of creation. Break it up and we may not get it back and the real cost of that won’t be abstract. It will be cures, cheaper energy, and connections that never arrive for the people who needed them most.  But of course, Robert must be Reich't here.  Of course.

text:
🇺🇲 🇷🇺 🇪🇺 Trump is offering Moscow things Europe controls: ECFR's Demarais and O'Brien say the EU holds the keys to Russia's frozen reserves, Lukoil's refineries and Nord Stream

Washington's sweeteners for Moscow depend on assets that sit in Europe, argue Agathe Demarais and Jim O'Brien of the European Council on Foreign Relations. They list what US envoys have floated in recent weeks: access to part of the Russian central bank reserves that European governments immobilised in 2022, the sale of Lukoil's foreign business to investors close to the envoys, and talks on selling Gazprom's stake in the Nord Stream pipeline to an American company. 

They add that on Oct. 9 President Trump allowed US firms to import Russian diesel, and seven days later waived part of the new sanctions in the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act that Congress passed in September. 

⚠️ Their verdict: "many of the things that Trump is offering Moscow are not Washington's to give."

The authors concede that Europe looks like a bystander. Lukoil is on the US sanctions list and off the EU's, so only the US Treasury sets the terms of a sale. EU sanctions bar European firms from Nord Stream business but do not stop Gazprom from selling its 51% stake to an American buyer. On Serbia's NIS refinery, they write, Washington has set every deadline, while Gazprom Neft trimmed its stake to just under the 50% threshold that would trigger EU measures.

Their case is that geography is leverage. The EU renewed its own Russia sanctions in June for 12 months. Euroclear, a Belgian firm under EU law, holds the bulk of the roughly $300 billion in immobilised Russian reserves. Lukoil's foreign assets include the Burgas refinery in Bulgaria, Petrotel in Romania, a stake in the Zeeland refinery in the Netherlands and Finland's Teboil chain, and Nord Stream lands in Germany. 

Demarais and O'Brien propose three moves: require EU approval for sales of Russian-owned energy assets on EU soil, tied to Russian concessions; fix a firm end date for Russian pipeline gas, now set for September 2027, which would make a Nord Stream stake worth little; and answer Washington on the reserves with a claims tally. They cite the World Bank's $588 billion estimate of Ukraine's reconstruction needs and Kyiv School of Economics estimates of more than $170 billion in Western corporate losses in Russia, and conclude that Russia's liabilities are more than twice its immobilised assets.

They flag the costs. Trump could retaliate, including with Graham act tariffs on buyers of Russian energy. Sanctioning Lukoil needs all 27 EU members, though national investment screens do not, and Slovakia and Hungary asked Brussels on Oct. 19 for flexibility on the gas deadline. 

The piece is a reminder that the administration's Russia offers can be blocked in Brussels, and the authors note that a Democratic Congress after Nov. 3 could add investigations. 

Source: Trump’s Russia deals are not his to make: https://t.co/Rt3SBWiSNY via @ecfr
