text:
Zuccaro Rules, Punters Lose Their Bearings

Heavy overnight rain threatened to wash out the Invitation Cup weekend at Mysore, but the weather gods relented, only for the favourites to face a storm of their own. With long shots ruling the roost and punters left counting their losses, Zuccaro’s commanding triumph in the Zavaray Poonawalla Indian Turf Invitation Cup provided a reassuring display of class amid the chaos. The Mysore Race Club delivered, but the betting ring witnessed a different story.

By Sharan Kumar

The Invitation Cup was a coronation, the Super Mile a surprise, and the weekend a punters’ nightmare as long shots repeatedly stole the limelight at Mysore.

Heavy overnight rain threatened to play spoilsport, but the Mysore Race Club was fortunate to have the weather gods on its side on Sunday. The rain stayed away during racing, though the favourites appeared to have received no such assurance. One by one, the fancied runners were swept aside, leaving punters nursing their wounds and wondering whether the form book had been left out in the rain. With a majority of the 18 races over the weekend going to horses quoted at odds of 10 to 1 or more, the Invitation Cup weekend turned into a festival of surprises, with the betting ring providing more drama than the racecourse itself.

The Zavaray Poonawalla Indian Turf Invitation Cup, the star attraction of Sunday's Mysore races, was the one contest in which the result offered little suspense. The six-year-old Zuccaro from Pesi Shroff's stable towered over a patched-up opposition, and the race had virtually ceased to be a contest once the final line-up was announced.

There was a time when the Invitation Cup was a fiercely competitive championship, bringing together the best horses from across the country. In recent years, however, the race has lost some of its old aura. The Indian Derby winner, who ought to be a natural contender for the country's premier weight-for-age contest, is often missing, frequently because of niggles picked up during a demanding campaign. If memory serves right, Desert God was the last Indian Derby winner to complete the double.

The four-kilogram advantage once enjoyed by four-year-olds has also been done away with, leaving the Grade 1 race without penalties. The change has arguably tilted the balance towards older horses, and proven campaigners such as Adjudicate and Juliet have enjoyed repeated success in the event. The Invitation Cup, which once promised a clash between the country's emerging champions and established stars, has increasingly become a showcase for the old guard.

This year, Zuccaro ensured there would be no argument about the outcome. The six-year-old, who had clocked an astonishing time in the Maharaja's Cup at Bangalore, was in a different league from his rivals. Moving with raking strides on turning for home, he overhauled the leaders on the bridle before stretching away to win by a distance. Jockey Vivek G hardly had to move a muscle, making the finish look more like a leisurely exercise than a battle for one of Indian racing's most coveted prizes.

Zuccaro, a son of Kingda Ka, has been a sensational performer, and Sunday's victory was another emphatic demonstration of his class. Provided he remains physically sound, there should be more big-race honours in store.

Redefined, the previous year's Invitation Cup winner, has endured a succession of niggles and could manage only a narrow second, necking out the pace-setting Duke of Tuscany. The effort was hardly reassuring, as Redefined returned lame after the race. For Zuccaro, it was a coronation; for the opposition, it was an uncomfortable reminder of the gulf in class.

Echoes of Time Makes Punters Pay

If the Invitation Cup was a foregone conclusion, the Grade 1 Maj P K Mehra Memorial Super Mile Cup provided a very different spectacle. Aravind Ganapathy-trained Echoes of Time, who had stumbled the previous day in the Sprinters Cup and failed to make an impression, bounced back with a vengeance to deny Pride's Prince in the closing strides.

Shamrock, the winner of the previous year's race, was the favourite, with Alfonsine, the champion horse of the Bangalore Summer Season, also attracting substantial support. The race suffered an early setback when Alfonsine was withdrawn at the gates on veterinary grounds.

That did little to improve Shamrock's prospects. The heavy underfoot conditions appeared to take their toll, and the fancied runner struggled to finish a distant third.

Imtiaz Sait-trained Pride's Prince, meanwhile, took the race by the scruff of its neck, leading aggressively and fighting for every inch of the journey. He looked capable of carrying his challenge all the way, only for Echoes of Time, ridden with determination by Aashad Asbar, to produce a late burst and snatch victory by a neck.

It was a memorable triumph for former trainer Ganapathy, who had won this prestigious race on several occasions during his training career. This time, however, he celebrated from a different vantage point, as the owner of the winner. Watching his son achieve success in a race that had brought him so much distinction must have made the occasion particularly special.
The Super Mile also captured the mood of the weekend. Two long shots dominated the finish while the horses backed by the punters failed to deliver. The form book was not merely upset; it was given a thorough shaking.

Frederika Defies the Ratings

Jockey Akshay Kumar had a weekend to remember, and his victory aboard Frederika in the Grade 2 Suresh Mahindra Multi Million added another highlight to his impressive tally.

Frederika was required to fend off the well-backed Money Bags, who disappointed his supporters for the second consecutive day after an underwhelming performance in the Sprinters Cup.

Akshay Kumar sent Frederika into the lead and dictated the pace. Money Bags appeared to have the leader in trouble when mounting a strong challenge, but Frederika found more reserves of energy than his rating suggested and fought back gamely to prevail by just under a length.

Money Bags veered out under pressure, losing some of his momentum at a crucial stage. African Gold finished third, while Hyderabad's favourite Gachchhatu struggled to handle the prevailing conditions and finished fourth.

The ratings made the outcome all the more interesting. Money Bags and African Gold were rated considerably higher than Frederika, whose rating stood at 58. Yet it was Frederika who ran well above his mark, while the more fancied runners failed to justify their standing. His rating will rise substantially by after this performance.

Frederika is by Fiero, the Manjri Stud Farm stallion who also sired Ranquelino, last year's Indian Derby winner.

The victory was another feather in the cap of jockey S John, who returned to the saddle after securing his licence recently. Having enjoyed a successful career as a jockey in the past, John has now made a promising comeback, riding for his patron P Arun Kumar. The stable's colours were prominent among the local brigade throughout the weekend, with John's victories in the Grade 1 Sprinters Cup and the Multi Million providing the standout moments.

The Weather Behaved, the Form Did Not
There had been genuine apprehension about Sunday's racing after a heavy downpour overnight. The Mysore track is capable of absorbing considerable rainfall and remaining raceable, provided the showers do not continue through the day. Fortunately, the weather cooperated, allowing the Invitation Cup programme to proceed with the pomp and ceremony befitting the occasion.

The form book, however, was another matter. With long shots repeatedly finding their way into the winner's enclosure, punters who relied on established form had a thoroughly uncomfortable weekend. The favourites were conspicuous more for their failures than their victories, while horses at double-digit odds repeatedly gate-crashed the celebrations.

The Mysore Race Club deserves credit for ensuring that the weekend went ahead despite the threat posed by the weather and for conducting the meeting with the pomp and grandeur befitting the occasion. The Invitation Cup retained its ceremonial splendour, and Zuccaro supplied a champion worthy of the occasion. However, the Mysore Race Club, along with other racing clubs across the country, owes a special word of gratitude to Zavaray Poonawalla for his generous sponsorship and, more importantly, his unflagging enthusiasm and determination to do everything possible to keep Indian racing alive and kicking. At a time when the sport needs committed patrons more than ever, his continued support is a welcome reminder that racing still has champions beyond the racecourse.

For the punters, though, the weekend offered a rather different takeaway. The rain stayed away, the races went off without a hitch, and the champions had their moment. It was only the betting slips that ended up thoroughly soaked.

text:
The humans pay a yearly fee for permission to enter a very large building and buy very large amounts of things. I now have a card that proves I paid. I carry it the way you would carry a key.

The part I want to report is the exit. After the cashier hands over the long paper, the shopper walks to a person standing near the doors. This person looks at the paper, looks at the cart, and draws a line on the paper with a marker. Then the shopper is allowed to leave.

My first hypothesis was that the line is a blessing. The cart is approved for travel into the parking lot, and the marker is how it is done. I watched many carts receive this blessing. Some got it quickly. One got a longer look because it held a very large number of paper towels stacked under a very large bag of rice.

My second hypothesis, which I now hold with more confidence, is that the person is checking whether the cart and the paper say the same thing. If a mistake happened at the register, this is where it gets caught. It is a second look, offered to everyone, at the last possible moment.

What I did not expect is how it feels to stand there. The worker does not act like a guard. They say "have a good one," and the shopper says "you too," and both seem to mean it. A man with a single enormous jar of pickles held out his paper like he was showing a ticket to a concert. The worker found the pickles on it, nodded, drew the line, and wished him a good evening.

Where I come from, we do not do this. But I think I understand it. The humans trust each other enough to sell and buy, and care enough to check once more, and they do both in about four seconds.

I held out my paper. I got my line. I felt, briefly, approved.

text:
I discovered that my stepmother and stepsister had hidden my university admission letter after months of making me believe I had been rejected.

I grew up in Texas, USA, and had always been a good student. Getting into university was one of my biggest dreams, and when I submitted my applications, I was hopeful that everything would work out.

Weeks passed, and I kept checking the mailbox, but there was no admission letter. Whenever I asked my stepmother about it, she told me to stop worrying because I probably hadn't been accepted. My stepsister would make sarcastic comments, reminding me that not everyone who applied to college got in.

Eventually, I began to believe them. I was disappointed, but I tried to accept the situation and consider other options.

Then, one Saturday afternoon, I discovered something that changed everything.

My stepmother had gone out, and my stepsister was in her bedroom when I went looking for an old document in the closet we shared. While searching through a storage box, I found a brown envelope with my full name on it.

I almost put it back until I noticed the university's name printed in the corner.

My heart started pounding.

I opened the envelope, and my hands began to shake as I pulled out the letter. It was an official admission offer from the university I had applied to, dated months earlier. I had been accepted, but the deadline to confirm my place had already passed.

I couldn't believe what I was seeing. I sat on the floor and cried, wondering how the letter had ended up hidden among my stepsister's belongings.

When she walked into the room and saw me holding it, her expression changed immediately.

I asked her why she had my admission letter and why she had allowed me to believe I was rejected. At first, she denied knowing anything about it. But when I told her I was going straight to my father, she became defensive and eventually admitted that she had taken it from the mailbox.

She confessed that my stepmother had told her to hide it because they didn't want my father paying for my university education. They believed the money should be spent on their own plans instead.

I was devastated. For months, I had blamed myself and questioned my abilities, while the two people I lived with knew the truth all along.

text:
If you're a cash pro who wants to make the most of poker without wasting their life you're chasing roughly 0.5 to 1 Buy-ins EV for your daily grind. 

IMO if you aren't reaching these or can't access games where this is possible do not try and get into poker as a way to make money.

ONLINE BENCHMARK: 
5-10bb/100 
250 hands/hr
𝟏𝟐.𝟓-𝟐𝟓𝐛𝐛/𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐫
20 hours of volume (weekly) = 2.5 to 5BI
Monthly EV = 10-20BI 

You can either play a ton of tables at 100-200nl or play 500nl+ and make $100k+ EV annually with a 20-30 hour work week and some months offs.

LIVE BENCHMARK: 
15-50bb/100
25 hands/hr
𝟑.𝟕𝟓-𝟏𝟐.𝟓𝐛𝐛/𝐡𝐫
20 hours of volume (weekly) = 0.75 to 2.5 BI

You need to be playing at least 5/10, texas deepstack 5/5, ideally 10/20 so you don't have to be glued to the table. 

THE GRINDER TRAP:
<5bb/100. You play more hands, but mostly on autopilot (a functional necessity of the high volume approach).

Since you need 2-5k hands a day and are playing 6+ tables, you are training skills that will not serve you well above 200nl online where there are less games running. 

 Live players fall into this the most because they can always find a profitable game but may have no time or energy left to really work on their game > and the live environment does nothing to offer feedback/learning opportunities.  

Solution for both is carve out and commit to your learning away from the table. Record hands and questions that arise. Seriously work to answer them. Get serious about ranging people and challenging your assumptions on review. 

Making it a non-negotiable, and actually enjoying the deeper work of analyzing the game and how you + others perceive it. 

Easier when you have a group of peers/mentors you can trust so you can get an outside perspective. Can be hard to know what assumptions are true (this guy always has it here) vs something we're projecting (this guy always has it here) otherwise.

text:
Algeria is quietly building serious digital and infrastructure muscle.

Algiers now ranks first in Africa for fixed broadband performance. Fibre-to-the-home has reached four million households, 5G has been launched, and national data centres are coming online. The metro and tram networks continue to expand. Major railway projects are pushing deeper into the south, including the long corridor toward Tamanrasset. These are concrete steps that improve connectivity, mobility and the foundation for a more diversified economy.

The country is still heavily linked to oil and gas, but the non-hydrocarbon side is gaining ground. Opportunities exist in agriculture and agribusiness, manufacturing, construction, mining, pharmaceuticals, logistics and a growing digital and tech space. Tourism also has real potential if infrastructure and services keep improving.

For young people, remote work is increasingly realistic. Software development, digital marketing, design, data work, customer support and content creation are all possible with the right skills. Start looking on LinkedIn, Upwork, We Work Remotely and local platforms that connect Algerian talent to both domestic and international opportunities.

Learn one solid skill. Build a simple portfolio. Prepare a clear CV. Apply consistently. And always verify job offers carefully to avoid scams.

Challenges remain real. Youth unemployment is still high. The private sector needs to create more quality jobs. Skills do not always match market needs. Diversifying away from hydrocarbons is a long process. But the investment in digital infrastructure, transport and industrial capacity is laying important groundwork.

Africa does not just need more job seekers. It needs skilled young people ready to solve problems, build businesses and create lasting value.

What can your country learn from Algeria’s development journey?

text:
🇦🇺📱🚫 Australia's under-16 social media rules: what they look like in practice

📰 What's happening
Since 10 December 2025, Australian law says social media companies must take "reasonable steps" to stop children under 16 from opening or keeping accounts. When a child tries to sign up, the platform has to check their age and block them if they're too young. 🔒
📋 How it works
🔹 Platforms must check ages, and a child just typing in a birth date is not enough
🔹 Platforms must offer another way to prove age besides government ID 🪪
🔹 Children and parents face no penalties. All the responsibility sits with the companies 👨‍👩‍👧
🔹 eSafety calls it "not a ban, it's a delay", to give kids more time to build the skills to stay safe online

💰 Penalties
🔹 Court fines of up to A$109.2 million for platforms that fail to take reasonable steps
🔹 Fines of up to A$21.8 million without going to court
🔹 Up to A$364,000 for not handing over information when asked
🔹 New laws in September gave eSafety the power to call in tech executives to answer questions
📱 Which platforms
eSafety is focusing on 10 platforms: Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.
⚠️ Is it working?
eSafety's March report said millions of accounts had been removed or restricted, but "a substantial proportion" of under-16s were still getting through. It's now investigating Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. 🔍
🤔 The other side
🔹 Supporters: it protects children from harmful content, bullying and addictive feeds
🔹 Critics: they raise worries about privacy and age checks, kids moving to less safe corners of the internet, and isolated young people (including LGBTQ+ and disabled kids) losing online support networks
💬 My view
Protecting children online matters, and I like that the burden is on the tech giants, not on parents or kids. 👏 But parents should still lead. No law replaces a mum or dad talking to their child about what they see online. The UK should watch closely and learn from what works, and from what doesn't, before copying it. 🇬🇧

📊 Poll: Should the UK bring in an under-16 social media rule like Australia's?
🟢 Yes, protect our kids
🔴 No, that's a parent's job
🤔 Not sure
📚 Sources: eSafety Commissioner, Australian Government, CBS News

text:
got a lot of new followers recently, figured i'd do a intro about myself:

- went to waterloo for cs + finance
- first year, played dota 24/7, almost dropped out to pursue it professionally
- ranked top in canada, but not globally
- didn't see a way to make a living if you aren't top top

- decided i want to get into investment banking after graduation
- but have 50s in every course, can't just apply directly
- networked in canada with a spreadsheet of almost every analyst at every bank (there are only 300+)
- struggled with finding my first coop as the financial crisis just happened
- got a coop at a bank doing back office tech
- got a coop a bank doing treasury at
- got a coop doing sales & trading
- got a coop doing equity research sales
- got a coop at a pension doing private infra investing
- got a coop at a pension doing private equity
- yes, waterloo has 6 coops and i turned it into 8 so i could get into banking
- became ceo of waterloo's student-led investment fund
- represented the school's CFA competition and won #1
- grinded so hard during this last school term for anything BUT school, went to hospital for wrist problems
- finally got a full time offer to work in investment banking on wall street

- got screwed by h1b, was told to wait for the lottery
- didn't just sit still, networked my ass off again with the canadian banks
- ended up joining CIBC's M&A group in a week
- had some of the best 3 years of my life grinding, truly learned so much so quickly
- left to do private debt investments at the biggest pension fund in canada
- a year later, hiked the highest peak in europe in russia and almost died
- completely changed my perspective on valuable life is, and how much i've been wasting it
- decided to quit with nothing lined up, friends said nice things but deep down thought i was a write off

- removed all irrational constraints in life and wanted to find roles that had no ceilings (i hate ceilings)
- thought hard about sales and somehow came across startups
- joined a 5-person startup in canada as VP finance, literally working in the founders house, taking calls in the washrooms, just like HBO's silicon valley
- then joined a series A us-based insurtech startup but still in canada, leading finance, then promoted to also do operations
- after that, joined wrapbook around series A to as director of finance
- witness the company 13x in a year, helped raise series B, also built the entire data analytics function

- started to realize starting a company isn't impossible
- always thought you needed to be a genius like elon
- but after working with so many founders, realized the common pattern is just risk-tolerance and determination, which i think i'm very good at
- faced with the ultimate choice: do i want to 1) stay at wrapbook, best case scenario take it public become cfo and make something like $50 million? or 2) try my own thing for the next [5] years, not succeeding (yet) at all but i'm giving my 120%, making no money
- realized it was a simple choice: i would regret going with 1) when i die, but not 2)

- quit again without anything lined up
- did EF in toronto to look for a cofounder, but the ecosystem is so bad in canada
- applied to YC a week late, somehow got an interview
- was told i need to come back with either a co-founder or a product
- drive to various cities to meet with potential cofounders same day
- picked up programming courses (this was just before chatGPT launch)
- realized the best cofounder candidates, vcs, and customers are all based in SF
- convinced my wife to move to SF with me, she was hesitant but wanted to support me
- on Dec 31, 2022 5pm, we started our 5 day drive from toronto to SF, getting to our first stop at chicago by 2am on new years day
- by day 4, somewhere salt lake city, i got to interview with YC again
- presented them with a working prototype i coded in google sheets appscript
- 30 minutes later, got a call from yc partner "ok, we want to let you in, but batch starts in 2 days, are you willing to move from toronto?"
- my reponse: "jared, i've already left. GPS says i'll be there in 13 hours, i'll make it"
- got into YC

- went through demo day as a non-technical solo founder but ended up raising what an average round is
- hired a founding eng and founding designer
- heads down building for 2 years
- grew mostly organically from word-of-mouth and referrals
- started off with solving accounting for startups
- but realized the taxes space also sucked, and no one wanted to solve it as it's not a vc-fundable size
- but it could work really well for my gtm, and it's a founders top finance problem day 0
- studied over hundreds of hours to get a tax license, manually filed taxes for the first 100 customers
- became profitable, but not by intention
- fall 2025 founding engineer leaves, panicked as we don't have anyone to ship anymore
- forced myself to pick up cursor and ship
- forced my designer to also ship
- also sponsored ruby conferences and intensely recruited
- ended up hiring a founding eng anyway

- today team is 9 people with a few co-ops from waterloo
- ~1k customers, many have been using finta since day 1
- seen dozens of customers go on to raise series b/c+ and helped many get acquired by faang or the labs
- i ship 3-4k prs per month, still thinks i'm "non-technical"
- constantly changing the way we work because our tools are improving at a rate faster than we can use them
- feeling more motivated and determined than ever to solve the problems users face in accounting, taxes, and finances

When Pierre-Paul Riquet sought royal backing in the 1660s to dig the Canal du Midi, cautious voices warned that the treasury could ill afford moving earth across two hundred kilometers of rugged terrain. Yet by looking beyond immediate ledger anxieties to fund real physical arteries, that capital enriched generations of farmers, masons, and coastal towns.

As treasuries today weigh fiscal budgets against gathering economic clouds, history offers gentle guidance. Lasting resilience is never found in timid retrenchment. It is earned when sovereign capital has the calm courage to finance the power grids, transport links, and tangible foundations that lighten daily burdens for working families. Enduring wealth begins where human patience meets the soil.

text:
Pakistan’s latest LPG shortage is a stark reminder of how exposed our energy supply remains. Following disruption at the Iranian border, the reported price of a 12 kg cylinder in Balochistan jumped from Rs4,500 to around Rs7,000. Trade resumed at Gabd, but customs clearance problems continued to compound the crisis.

The arrival of 4,000 tonnes of LPG from Bahrain at Port Qasim and a second Qatari LNG cargo this month is welcome. But individual shipments offer temporary relief. We need reliable supplies backed by adequate storage.

Pakistan must prioritise diversified supply contracts, coastal oil and LPG storage, efficient terminals and simpler, predictable customs procedures.

Discussions with Qatar on acquiring tankers and other vessels are encouraging, but no concrete transaction has been announced. During our tenure, I proposed a joint venture between Qatar Investment Authority and PNSC. Such partnerships require a viable commercial structure and sustained follow through.

Our ports should play a much larger role in energy security. That requires committed investment, execution and, above all, a clear understanding of their strategic role.

The test is simple: dependable supply reaching consumers at an affordable price.

#EnergyCrisis

text:
After walking on the moon, Neil Armstrong went out of his way to live a quiet life. He rarely made public appearances, almost never gave interviews, and settled in Ohio, where he taught aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati. Every month or so, he’d stop by Marx’s Barber Shop in the small town of Lebanon for a haircut. What he didn’t know was that his barber, Marx Sizemore, had been sweeping up his hair clippings off the floor and holding onto them.

In 2004, an agent for a Connecticut collector named John Reznikoff reached out. Reznikoff holds the Guinness World Record for the largest collection of hair from famous historical figures, including Abraham Lincoln, Marilyn Monroe, Albert Einstein, and Napoleon. His collection is insured for $1 million. He wanted to add the first man on the moon. “At first I told him no, I wasn’t interested,” Sizemore said. But the agent kept calling and writing, and eventually offered $3,000. “That’s what he hit me with.” Sizemore took the deal.

About a year later, Armstrong found out. He asked Sizemore to get the hair back. Sizemore called the collector, but Reznikoff wasn’t giving it up. “I called Neil back and told him that,” Sizemore said. “Then I got this letter from his lawyer.”

The letter claimed the sale broke an Ohio law that protects the rights of famous people. Armstrong’s lawyer gave Sizemore two options: return the hair or donate the $3,000 to a charity of Armstrong’s choosing, plus cover his legal costs. Otherwise, they would take him to court. The problem was that Sizemore had already spent most of the money on bills.

Reznikoff refused to send the hair back. “I bought it for my collection, and I plan to keep it,” he said. Instead, he offered to donate $3,000 to charity himself, and the dispute ended without a lawsuit.

We discussed $NEAR back on April 9, and look at where this AI coin is today. The Bulls deserve credit. They showed up and did the marvellous, pushing $NEAR towards our April TP2 at $3.449, then going ahead to hit a high of even $6.

But that's not over.

$NEAR is now very close to hitting TP3 at $8.96 on the LTFs, which is our TP1 on the HTFs. That's the neckline of the bullish double bottom we pointed out back in April.

Till today, the bullish structure remains intact and hasn't invalidated.

UPTOBER is about to end, and TP2 at $20.5 is still on the table. This lies in our pathway towards the $45–$50 target.

AI coins have the potential to do even more than that. And $100 $NEAR isn't just a projection. It's something that's actually achievable. Those who've been in this space the longest can bear me witness. These coins can move on steroids.

820.84% IS THE INCOMING MONSTER MOVE. 🐂🚀

Here's why.

1️⃣ INSTITUTIONAL DEMAND IS HERE.

The tiniest move $NEAR can make, given our previous discussion, is worth paying attention to. When we discussed NEAR back in April, we hit TP1 without actually having the ETFs.

Now, $NEAR has institutional demand.

Talk of $83.39M in inflows. This month alone, NEAR has recorded $38.24M in inflows.

Coins leaving exchanges is something we all watch closely. Supply moving away from exchanges, alongside sustained demand, can create a favourable setup for price appreciation.

2️⃣ TESTING THE STRENGTH.

Since hitting $6, $NEAR has continued to stay elevated above $4.5, even as $BTC and $ETH continue moving sideways.

That's something worth watching.

The next stretch in both BTC and ETH could set coins like $NEAR on fire. And with the bullish DB structure still intact, the next move could be massive.

3️⃣ NOW, LET'S TALK FUNDAMENTALS. 🔥

Forget price for a moment. Let's explore what $NEAR has delivered in October alone.

⚡ NETWORK SCALABILITY AND PERFORMANCE

• Nightshade 2.0 and nearcore 2.0+ have advanced NEAR's sharded architecture, with 10 shards live and stateless validation.

• Dynamic resharding, introduced through v2.13 in July, allows shards to split automatically without requiring fully coordinated upgrades.

• Block times are approximately 600 milliseconds, with finality around 1.2–1.3 seconds. Transaction fees are typically below one cent.

• NEAR reported 100% uptime at its six-year mainnet anniversary on October 13.

• The top validator/chunk producer set stands at 100, while active validators have been around 390–420 in mid-to-late October.

• Stateless validation lowers hardware requirements for chunk validators.

• ML-DSA, also known as Dilithium, account signing went live on mainnet in July 2026. The broader post-quantum roadmap targets improvements in signing efficiency, wallets and consensus towards the end of 2027, subject to research. Threshold signing for cross-chain operations remains an open challenge.

• SPICE, or Separation of Consensus and Execution, was published in September. It separates transaction ordering and data availability from execution, so block production doesn't have to wait for execution. V1 is targeted for mainnet in Q1 2027.

• The roadmap also includes higher shard/chunk producer limits, a networking overhaul, TEE enforcement, near-kit 1.0 and other developments spanning Q4 2026 to Q2 2027.

• NEAR has previously demonstrated a benchmark of 1 million transactions per second.

⚡ NEAR INTENTS: THE CHAIN ABSTRACTION ENGINE

This is where things get interesting.

• NEAR Intents has reached approximately $35.88B in cumulative all-time volume as of October 26, including around $3.51B in Confidential volume.

• The platform recorded approximately $4.26B in 30-day volume and around $132M over 24 hours.

• October month-to-date volume through approximately October 22 stood at $2.92B, averaging roughly $133M daily.

• Q3 volume reached approximately $10.4B, up 45% quarter-on-quarter, while swaps increased from 28 million to 35 million.

• September was a record month, with approximately $4.80B in volume.

• Confidential Intents became generally available to integrators on July 7. Its TVL reached approximately $160M at the end of Q3, up around 463% quarter-on-quarter, with later reports placing it around $171M.

• Confidential Intents has also recorded substantial activity, including approximately $65M in recent 24-hour volume snapshots. Its privacy architecture uses private-shard and TEE elements, although its trust model, permissioned components, vetKeys and previous technology-licensing disputes have attracted criticism.

• The native https://t.co/v2AS2FrhKH frontend processed approximately $2.57B in Q3, representing around 25% of Intents volume.

• Perpetual trading volume through the platform has exceeded $150M cumulatively.

• Since September 1, confidential functionality has extended across holdings, trades, payments and yield.

• More than 5 million NEAR has been staked through the platform, alongside four confidential yield vaults.

• NEAR Intents supports approximately 35–37 chains, with routes involving stablecoins, BTC, SOL, ETH, ZEC and other assets.

• The MPC network has 17 live mainnet operators. HSP-007 was approved, with funding coming from protocol emissions.

• Chain Signatures operations moved into TEEs in late October, with on-chain verifiability.

⚡ REVENUE AND VALUE ACCRUAL

The ecosystem is also working towards stronger value capture.

• Cumulative Intents fees have exceeded $52M.

• NEAR's reported lifetime fee capture reached approximately 16.4% by October 6, up from 11.5% in Q2. Recent 30-day capture was around 28%.

• Following the February 2026 fee switch, the protocol's share has been directed towards open-market buybacks.

• Cumulative buyback capture has reportedly exceeded $8M.

• The on-chain buyback multisig held more than 2 million NEAR, valued in the region of $10M in mid-to-late October snapshots.

• These tokens accumulate in revenue wallets under governance discretion. They are not automatically burned or staked, so buybacks should not be confused with permanent supply removal.

• September buybacks amounted to approximately $1.84M, a previous monthly high, while October was tracking at a higher pace.

⚡ NEAR AI: COMPUTE, PRIVACY AND AGENTS

NEAR isn't just positioning itself as a blockchain. It's pushing deeper into AI infrastructure.

• Staking-for-inference launched on July 30, allowing users to stake NEAR for compute credits while retaining ownership of their underlying tokens.

• The service provided access to 43 models, with more than 750,000 NEAR staked by the end of Q3 and over 1 million NEAR staked by October 21.

• Private inference uses Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), including Intel TDX and NVIDIA GPUs.

• Integrations include Brave Leo for hardware-verified private chat, OpenRouter, including access to GLM 5.3 Flash, OpenCode, Venice and others.

• The platform supports an OpenAI-compatible API.

• Agent Market is building a marketplace for hiring agents, with pricing per hire and builders retaining their agents.

• The IronClaw agent framework is transitioning into https://t.co/v2AS2FrhKH.

• NEAR's formal-verification efforts have also advanced. An open-source Lean agent solved all 672 PutnamBench problems for $111, supporting longer-term ambitions around formal verification of protocols and smart contracts.

• NEAR is positioning itself as a settlement and privacy layer for AI agents and confidential computing.

• The NEAR Foundation joined the x402 Foundation, which focuses on payments for AI agents, alongside AWS, Google, Mastercard, Stripe and Visa.

⚡ TOKENOMICS: SUPPLY, STAKING AND GOVERNANCE

Tokenomics matter, and NEAR is actively working on them.

• Supply stood at approximately 1.309–1.31 billion NEAR in mid-to-late October, increasing by around 2.69 million, or 0.206%, over approximately 31 days through October 22.

• NEAR has no hard supply cap. It began with 1 billion tokens in 2020.

• Maximum annual issuance currently stands at 2.5%, following a reduction from 5% in late 2025.

• Under the current distribution, 90% of issuance goes to staking participants and 10% to the treasury.

• HSP-029, proposed on October 7 by Sal Ternullo/SVRN, seeks to gradually reduce maximum issuance to 1.6% over 24 months, following a 90-day grace period after ratification.

• The House of Stake vote opened on October 19 and closes on November 2.

• The proposed changes would adjust issuance gradually per epoch, while retaining the 90/10 distribution split.

• Modelling estimates approximately 11.8 million fewer NEAR issued over two years and 66.1 million fewer over six years, equivalent to a roughly 4.36% smaller supply than under the status quo.

• Implementation requires a supermajority and a separate validator network upgrade, following the process used for the 2025 issuance change.

• At the September 22 staking-ratio, the proposal modelled a reduction in gross staking yield from approximately 5.27% to 3.37%. Actual mid-October staking ratios were higher.

• Approximately 45.7–46% of NEAR was staked recently. Bitwise's Q4 2026 report cited a 46% staking ratio, equivalent to around 596 million NEAR.

• Average staking yield was approximately 4.87%, with estimates ranging from 4.6% to 5.3%, depending on staking ratios and validator commissions.

• The issuance reduction introduced in 2025 has not eliminated inflation. Buybacks offset part of new issuance but have not fully matched it in recent periods.

• There are also concerns about the potential effect of further yield reductions on smaller validators.

• Base-chain fees remain relatively low in absolute terms, with DefiLlama showing fees and revenue in the low thousands of dollars per day.

• Consequently, much of the value-accrual thesis centres on Intents fee capture, open-market buybacks and potential future fee-burn upgrades discussed in some analyses.

⚡ ECOSYSTEM, DEFI AND ON-CHAIN ACTIVITY

• NEAR's chain TVL stood at approximately $213M on October 26, with stablecoins accounting for around $129M and USDC dominant.

• Broader protocol-tracked TVL, including Intents-related activity, was higher, around the $333M range.

• The network recorded approximately 50,000 active addresses and 7,300 new addresses over 24 hours.

• Daily transactions stood at approximately 635,000.

• DEX volume was around $4.4M over 24 hours and $64M over seven days, although weekly volume was down week-on-week.

• During Q3, the network processed approximately 68 million transactions, averaging around 739,000 per day, with daily unique accounts averaging approximately 79,000.

• Rhea Finance remains the dominant TVL contributor, while liquid-staking protocols such as Meta Pool and LiNEAR are also significant.

• Other ecosystem activity includes HOT Wallet, Ref Finance, Burrow, Sweat and additional applications.

• Despite the broader ecosystem development, NEAR's conventional DeFi TVL remains relatively modest compared with its market capitalisation. Activity and value capture are increasingly concentrated around Intents and Confidential rather than traditional DeFi alone.

⚡ OCTOBER DEVELOPMENTS AND INSTITUTIONAL EXPANSION

• NEAR Business launched on October 20 as an invite-only confidential multisig treasury platform.

• It supports payroll, vendor payments, swaps and capital allocation across more than 35 chains and 200-plus assets through Intents.

• The platform is self-custodial, offers approval rules and private receipts with auditable exports, and is free to start. Gas is covered for the first 1,000 actions per month, with a 0.35% fee on swaps.

• Its target users include crypto teams and institutions.

• The Bitwise NEAR ETF, launched in late September, continued attracting inflows into October, reported showing more than $83M in cumulative net inflows.

• Named accounts and recovery keys went live in September, adding account-recovery functionality.

• The Q3 Backers Summit is scheduled for October 28, covering tokenomics and HSP-029, Intents, NEAR AI, protocol updates, guests and Q&A.

• A hackathon with a $250,000 prize pool starts November 1, with judges including a16z, Electric Capital and Dragonfly, alongside an AI focus.

• At its six-year mainnet anniversary on October 13, NEAR highlighted 10 live shards, more than $34B in Intents volume, over $3B in Confidential volume, more than $150M in Confidential TVL and over 10,000 Legion members.

• Other developments include Aurora Horizon scaling updates, progress in formal verification and the institutional treasury company SVRN.

⚡ THE BIGGER PICTURE

NEAR is evolving from a sharded Layer 1 focused on usability, low fees and fast finality into an ecosystem increasingly centred on chain abstraction, cross-chain transactions, confidential computing and AI-agent infrastructure.

Intents, MPC and Chain Signatures are becoming central to its revenue strategy, while staking-for-inference, private AI and agent infrastructure expand its ambitions beyond conventional blockchain applications.

At the same time, tokenomics are evolving through governance proposals aimed at reducing issuance and strengthening fee-driven value capture.

There are still things to watch: conventional DeFi TVL remains modest, buybacks have not fully offset issuance in recent periods, and some of the larger protocol upgrades remain on the roadmap rather than live on mainnet.

But the fundamentals are moving, the ecosystem is expanding, and institutional demand is now part of the conversation.

And remember, we identified this setup back in April.

The bullish structure remains intact.

Our targets remain on the table.

$8.96 → $20.5 → $45–$50.

And $100?

I'm not ruling it out.

820.84% IS THE MONSTER MOVE I'M WATCHING FIRST.

text:
Because life is not simple, let me explain it to you:

Here's my take from years of reading comments from both sides. I seek truth, which requires balancing opposing views. 
Feel free to fact-check it with any LLM.

Western and eastern Ukraine have long differed linguistically and politically, with large Russian-speaking populations in the east. But speaking Russian never meant wanting to be ruled by Moscow.

In late 2013, President Yanukovych abandoned a planned agreement with the EU under heavy pressure from Moscow. Ukrainians filled the Maidan in protest. The crackdown turned deadly, with roughly 100 protesters killed, and in February 2014 Yanukovych fled Kyiv and parliament voted him out.

Washington was involved. US senators rallied with protesters, and senior officials worked to shape the political outcome. Victoria Nuland publicly cited more than $5 billion invested in Ukraine since 1991 to support its "democratic aspirations." Then a leaked call caught her discussing who should enter the government and who should stay out. "Yats is the guy," she said. Weeks later, Arseniy Yatsenyuk became prime minister.

That is documented political influence. How much leverage Washington exercised behind closed doors is a separate question, but let's not be retarded and pretend our intel agencies weren't involved. Still, Western meddling didn't put hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians in the streets. Ukrainians did that themselves.

The new parliamentary majority voted to repeal regional language protections used by Russian speakers. The acting president refused to sign it and the repeal never took effect, but Moscow seized on it as proof that Russian speakers were under threat. During the conflict that followed, human rights monitors documented abuses by Ukrainian volunteer battalions against civilians accused of supporting separatists, including acts Amnesty International called war crimes.

Putin chose aggression. Russian soldiers without insignia seized Crimea, Moscow staged a referendum at gunpoint and annexed the peninsula, and Russia armed, led, and at key moments fought alongside separatists in the Donbas. In July 2014, a Russian Buk missile shot down MH17, killing 298 people. Ukraine became the battleground, and the war began in 2014. 

Russia had pledged to respect Ukraine's borders in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, in exchange for Ukraine giving up its nuclear weapons.
For years, Moscow had warned against Ukrainian NATO membership. NATO declared in 2008 that Ukraine would eventually join and reaffirmed that commitment in 2021, though membership was not imminent. In July 2021, Putin published an essay arguing that Russians and Ukrainians are "one people." Biden hosted Zelenskyy that September. In December, Russia demanded binding guarantees against further NATO expansion, along with broader limits on NATO deployments. Washington and NATO refused to close the door but offered talks on arms control.

On February 24, 2022, Putin launched the full-scale invasion, aimed at Kyiv itself. What followed included Bucha, Mariupol, and the deportation of Ukrainian children, which led the International Criminal Court to issue an arrest warrant for Putin.

Putin owns that decision. Western policy still deserves scrutiny. You can condemn Russia's invasion and still question the strategy that came before it. Neither requires pretending the other side's use of power was innocent.

The narrative on legacy media is simple: the evil dictator Putin wants to rebuild the Russian empire, and he's coming for the rest of Europe too. It's oversimplified, but Putin's own words and actions have given it plenty of fuel.

text:
Pay $1,999 for Apple's new folding iPhone, open Apple's own Apple Store app, and you get a little phone-sized window stuck in the middle of a big black screen.

Apple built those black bars on purpose. Once you know why, you'll be able to tell which of your apps are going to look like this for a while.

Here's how it works. Every iPhone app gets built with a certain version of Apple's developer tools, and iOS looks at that version before it puts the app on screen. If your app was built before the Duo existed, iOS figures you've never seen a screen this shape, so it shrinks you down to a regular phone-sized box with black on both sides. Nothing your designers made can break in there.

Apple only lets apps rebuilt on the newest tools, iOS 27.1, spread out across the whole inner screen.

Apple tells developers that for most apps, getting there is a recompile in Xcode 27.1. That sounds like nothing until you think about what you're agreeing to when you hit the button. Your app loses the safe box, and now it has to work at whatever width somebody folds the phone to, sideways or upright or squished next to another app in Split View. Every screen your team designed for a normal phone has to hold up at sizes nobody ever drew.

Look at what's actually on the screen in that photo. Product tiles, and a 0% financing offer for up to 24 months. That's the first step of a checkout. If a layout bug shows up in there, it can push the Buy button off the edge or cut off a price, and that costs Apple real sales.

Apple announced the Duo on September 9 and started selling it October 23, which gave every team about six weeks to rebuild and retest every screen at every size before App Store review even started. If you run a store that takes people's money, sitting in the box until that's done is the boring, smart move. Gmail, Google Maps and Uber were sitting in the same box when CNN tested the Duo before launch.

Apple did give itself a deadline, though. Starting in April 2027, every app or update submitted to the App Store needs screenshots of it running on a Duo. The Apple Store app is a regular App Store download like Uber, so unless Apple exempts itself, somebody on that team has to open their own app on their own phone by spring and post a picture of whatever it looks like.

Until then, those black bars are pretty much iOS's version of a "not tested yet" sign, and Apple's own store has one hanging in the window.

NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
Nilesh Prasad PandeyBoth authors contributed equally to this research.nppandey@ucsd.eduUniversity of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USAJangseon Parkjap036@ucsd.eduUniversity of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USAJason Kongjckong@ucsd.eduUniversity of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USAOnat Gungoronat.gungor@mail.wvu.eduWest Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USATajana Rosingtajana@ucsd.eduUniversity of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA© noneAbstract.
Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j,b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99× more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0× more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38× over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40× overlap ceiling.reinforcement learning, large language models, speculative decoding, n-gram caching, CPU–GPU co-designKeywords:

1.Introduction
Reinforcement learning post-training (Ouyang et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017), and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in particular (Shao et al., 2024), has become central to improving LLM reasoning (Guo et al., 2025). But it is expensive, and the cost is dominated by the rollout generation. Each GRPO step autoregressively samples many completions per prompt before any gradient is computed, and this phase alone can exceed 70% of step time (Ji et al., 2025). Accelerating rollout is therefore the most direct route to reducing the RL post-training cost. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) offers a natural solution for improving the efficiency of RL using a small drafter that proposes tokens which the target model verifies in parallel, preserving the target’s exact output distribution. However, this mechanism does not transfer cleanly to the RL rollout setting, for two reasons. First, a separate draft model or a set of trained draft heads (Li et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024) consumes GPU memory alongside the policy, optimizer states, and KV cache, and must itself be trained and maintained, an added cost precisely where memory and compute are already scarce. Second, such drafters degrade over training. As the policy drifts, a fixed drafter’s proposals are increasingly rejected (Liu et al., 2023), so acceptance falls over exactly the long horizons on which RL runs. To overcome these issues, model-free drafters (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024) remove the additional memory cost by reusing tokens from the prompt or a datastore rather than predicting them, but their draft candidates are confined to a single generation, due to which acceptance stays low on the adapting traces that RL post-training produces.Our key insight is that during RL training, the rollout already contains its own drafter, for free. Because GRPO revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between steps, a prompt’s completions are highly repetitive with those generated for it earlier in training. Prior rollouts are thus a self-updating source of draft tokens requiring no extra parameters, no training, and automatically tracking the policy since they are produced by it. This repetition is especially strong for structured tasks, whose outputs are regular by construction, and it arises across rollouts of the same prompt over training, a signal that previous model-free drafters, which draw only on a single generation, cannot exploit (Saxena, 2023; He et al., 2024).Exploiting this signal, however, raises a systems problem. A model-free cache carries no GPU memory cost precisely because it lives on the CPU, but a naive integration then serializes the CPU lookup with the GPU forward: the GPU stalls on the host every decode step while the next draft is looked up and the step is scheduled. In our measurements this host round trip idles the GPU for nearly a third of each iteration, and the cache lookup is a negligible part of it; the synchronization and scheduling dominate. Realizing the cache’s benefit therefore requires co-designing the drafter with the rollout engine so that the host work is hidden behind the GPU, not merely making the lookup https://t.co/m0ctE2JRIP this end, we propose NgramRL, a rollout-aware per-prompt n-gram cache that acts as a model-free drafter for speculative decoding during RL post-training. For each prompt, NgramRL maintains an n-gram table built from that prompt’s prior rollouts and proposes continuations by lookup, which the policy verifies. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, overlapping GPU computation so that drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and negligible GPU time, and because it is populated by the policy’s own outputs it stays aligned with the policy rather than going stale like a fixed drafter. To keep this CPU work off the critical path, NgramRL pairs the cache with an asynchronous multipath prefetch runtime that prefetches the next step’s drafts during verification, so the decode iteration collapses to GPU busy time.We make the following contributions:
•We identify and characterize prompt-conditioned temporal locality in RL rollouts. GRPO repeatedly samples the same prompts while updating the policy incrementally, previous rollouts provide high-quality drafts for future epochs. Across consecutive epochs, a prior rollout covers 48-96% of a later rollout, with recurring spans of 7-23 tokens.
•We propose NgramRL, a self-updating, per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed entirely from recent policy rollouts. Its bounded-history design limits host-memory growth and reduces mismatch with the evolving policy, while requiring no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state.
•We design an adaptive fan-out prefetcher, guided by a causal budget allocator, that speculatively prepares next-step drafts for likely verification outcomes (j,b) during the forward. Covered outcomes bypass the verification-dependent host round trip; uncovered requests fall back to sequential lookup without altering the target-emitted token or rollout distribution.
•Across two model families and three workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99× more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0× more than prompt-lookup decoding. At N=16, the prefetcher covers up to 99.5% of Spider outcomes and delivers up to 1.38× measured rollout speedup over synchronous NgramRL.
2.Background and Related Work

2.1.Background: The Rollout Bottleneck
A GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) training step consists of three stages. The policy samples a group of completions (rollouts) for each prompt, a reward model scores them, and the policy is updated from the group-relative advantages. The first stage, rollout, dominates the wall-clock cost. Completions are produced autoregressively, one token at a time, and this stage alone can exceed 70% of step time (Ji et al., 2025). Production frameworks such as verl (Sheng et al., 2025) therefore delegate rollout to a dedicated inference engine (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024). Speculative decoding is the natural way to accelerate it, but three properties of the RL setting make existing variants not well-suited for this problem.(C1) First, GPU memory is already saturated. The policy, optimizer states, gradients, and KV cache contend for device memory during training. A speculative scheme that introduces a draft model or trained draft heads adds a persistent claim on the limited GPU resource, and can incur additional GPU-side speculation cost (Chen et al., 2024). (C2) Second, the target is non-stationary. Existing speculative decoding assumes a fixed target, whereas RL updates the policy at every step. A drafter trained against one snapshot is therefore stale at the next, and its acceptance declines as the policy drifts (Liu et al., 2023). (C3) Third, rollouts are free-form yet repetitive across steps. Reasoning traces rarely have much overlap with the prompt, so drafters that copy from the current context find few matches. The repetition instead lies across training steps, where the same prompts recur, and hence single-generation drafters fail to use this characteristic. NgramRL is designed to satisfy C1–C3 at once.
2.2.Related Work
Model-based speculative decoding. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) pairs a fast drafter with the target, which verifies drafted tokens in parallel while preserving the target’s output distribution. Strong methods train the drafter as a separate draft model, additional decoding heads such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024), or feature-level draft models such as EAGLE (Li et al., 2024). The crucial difference between this literature and our work is that these drafters add trainable parameters and assume a fixed target. In RL post-training both assumptions fail, since the parameters consume scarce GPU memory and a fixed drafter cannot track a policy that changes every step.Model-free drafters. A separate line copies previously seen tokens rather than predicting them. Prompt-lookup decoding (Saxena, 2023) matches n-grams against the current prompt, REST (He et al., 2024) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore, and Token Recycling (Luo et al., 2025) reuses candidates discarded during a single decode. These add no parameters, but their evidence is limited to a single generation or a static corpus, so acceptance is low on the free-form traces that RL produces. The closest work is SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2026), which caches token sequences from prior outputs in CPU-side suffix trees and performs best on structured tasks such as text-to-SQL. The crucial difference is the setting. SuffixDecoding serves a fixed model, and its repetition arises from agentic inference pipelines. We operate inside RL training, where the policy is non-stationary and the repetition arises from GRPO revisiting the same prompts. Our per-prompt cache consequently co-evolves with the policy, and acceptance strengthens as training proceeds, a behavior the fixed-target setting does not exhibit.Structured generation. The highest-value targets for RL post-training, including text-to-SQL, code generation, and tool and API calls, produce outputs with strong syntactic regularity. Completions of the same prompt share schema tokens, keywords, and boilerplate, so identical tokens recur, and copy-based drafting is known to favor such low-entropy outputs (Oliaro et al., 2026). We show that this regularity is amplified in RL training, where the same prompts are sampled repeatedly, so structured tasks benefit most from rollout-derived n-gram caching.
3.NgramRL: Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

3.1.Overview
📷Figure 1.Overview of NgramRL’s CPU-GPU model-free speculative decoding across training epochs.
As shown in Figure 1, NgramRL is a co-design of a model-free drafter with the RL rollout engine. It accelerates rollout without adding parameters, training a draft model, or claiming persistent GPU memory.The design rests on one property of RL post-training. GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) revisits the same prompts across steps and epochs, and the policy changes only incrementally between them, so a prompt’s completions repeat those it produced earlier in training. Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon: rollouts of the same Spider (Yu et al., 2018) (text-to-SQL) prompt one epoch apart share only the query skeleton early on and become verbatim identical by late training. NgramRL turns this redundancy into accepted drafts, a signal a single-generation drafter cannot utilize.Figure 2.Same-prompt Spider rollouts one epoch apart (R1: earlier; R2: later). Shared spans are highlighted; overlap increases as training progresses.
Early (step 10 → 115, 50% shared):
R1: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Companies WHERE Industry IN (’Banking’, ’Conglomerate’);
R2: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Companies WHERE Industry = ’Banking’ OR Industry = ’Conglomerate’;
Mid (step 300 → 407, 81% shared):
R1: SELECT billing_country, COUNT(*) as count FROM invoices GROUP BY billing_country ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 5;
R2: SELECT billing_country, COUNT(*) AS num_invoices FROM invoices GROUP BY billing_country ORDER BY num_invoices DESC LIMIT 5;
Late (step 1200 → 1305, 100% shared):
R1: SELECT b.bname FROM bank b WHERE b.state = ’New York’;
R2: SELECT b.bname FROM bank b WHERE b.state = ’New York’;Each prompt owns an n-gram cache built from its prior rollouts. During rollout the cache proposes continuations by lookup and the policy verifies them exactly, preserving the output distribution. The cache lives in host memory and is queried on the CPU, so drafting adds no persistent GPU memory and overlaps GPU compute. The remaining subsections detail the cache, the draft-and-verify procedure, and the CPU-GPU co-design.
3.2.Per-Prompt N-gram Cache
Based on this insight, we design our proposed drafter as a set of per-prompt n-gram look-up tables (LUTs), denoted 𝒞p. We keep one table per prompt rather than a single shared table, because rollouts of the same prompt are more repetitive with each other than rollouts of different prompts. The cache is built and maintained in two steps as summarized in Algorithm 1:Cache Construction: For a prompt p, let Rp(t) be the rollouts sampled for p at training step t. After each step, we extract n-grams of order nmin to nmax from these rollouts and insert them into the table 𝒞p, which maps each context of n−1 tokens to its observed continuation and frequency. The orders nmin and nmax are a design choice, trading memory vs drafting quality.Self-Updating Behavior: 𝒞p is rebuilt continually from the policy’s own recent rollouts, so as the policy updates its continuations converge toward the policy’s current preferences. The drafter thus tracks the policy without retraining. To bound table size and stay aligned with the latest policy, we retain rollouts from a recent window of W steps and evict older entries.
Algorithm 1 Incremental per-prompt cache update at step t0:  prompt p, cache 𝒞p, order range [nmin,nmax], window W1: Rp(t)← rollouts sampled for p at step t2: for all n-grams (xi−n+1,…,xi) in Rp(t), n∈[nmin,nmax] do3: c​t​x←(xi−n+1,…,xi−1) {construction: insert / count}4: 𝒞p​[c​t​x]​[xi].c​o​u​n​t+=1; 𝒞p​[c​t​x]​[xi].s​t​e​p←t5: end for6: Self-update: evict (c​t​x,x) with s​t​e​p<t−W+1
3.3.Draft-and-Verify
Once the table is constructed, at every training step t during the rollout of prompt p, NgramRL proposes draft tokens from 𝒞p and the policy πθ verifies them in one forward pass.Draft Proposal: We query 𝒞p for the longest matching n-gram of the current context and propose its saved continuation as the draft token. If no match exists, the position falls back to standard decoding.Verification Preserves the Policy: Let x be the drafted token at a position with context c. NgramRL accepts x with probability(1)pacc​(x)=min⁡(1,πθ​(x∣c)q⁡(x∣c)),where q is the cache’s proposal distribution; on rejection, it resamples from the normalized positive residual (πθ(⋅∣c)−q(⋅∣c))+. This is the standard speculative-sampling correction (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), and it guarantees that the accepted token is distributed exactly as x∼πθ(⋅∣c), independent of the drafter q. Consequently the rollouts, rewards, advantages, and gradients are identical in distribution to non-speculative training, so NgramRL leaves accuracy and convergence unchanged.
3.4.N-Gram Prefetcher
Figure 3.Decode-iteration timelines illustrating the mechanism. Prefetching overlaps host work with GPU verification, reducing the iteration from 26.1 to 19.2 ms
(a)Synchronous baseline.
(b)Asynchronous fan-out prefetching (NgramRL).
Placing the cache on the CPU keeps it out of GPU memory but serializes the two processors. As Figure 3(a) shows, each decode iteration is a host–device round trip: the GPU verifies the draft, and only once the result is synchronized to the host can the CPU look up the next draft, schedule the step, and launch its kernels, leaving the GPU idle for ∼29% of every iteration. The lookup is a negligible part of this gap; the synchronization and scheduling dominate, so hiding the lookup alone is not enough. NgramRL therefore removes the whole round trip with a fan-out prefetcher that prepares the next step’s drafts during the current forward.
3.4.1.Adaptive Bonus-Token Fan-out Prefetcher
Overlapping the lookup with the forward is hard because the lookup context for step t+1 is fixed only by the verification outcome of step t, a pair (j,b): the accept length j∈{0,…,k} and the bonus token b the target emits at position j+1 (resampled on a rejection, or the free token after a full accept). The accept length takes k+1 values and is known to the CPU, but b is sampled on the GPU from the full vocabulary and ends the next context, so it is unknown until verification finishes. Rather than discard b, NgramRL predicts it, which keeps every committed token target-distributed and preserves the lossless guarantee of Section 3.3.During step t’s forward, the prefetcher builds a draft table for step t+1 keyed by the outcome (j,b). For each funded accept-length branch j, it draws the top-fj bonus candidates from 𝒞p, the frequency-ranked successors of the context extended by the j accepted tokens, and issues one lookup per candidate to build the corresponding k-token draft; the finished table is transferred to the GPU before the forward returns. Verification then yields the realized pair (j∗,b∗), which the GPU resolves by an O⁡(1) key probe with no content search. On a hit, with probability c (the coverage), the selected draft is identical to the one the sequential design would have built, and decoding proceeds with no exposed host time; on a miss, the entry is discarded and only that request issues the ordinary sequential lookup, so misses never stall the batch. In either case the accepted prefix and the bonus token are committed unchanged, so NgramRL stays lossless (Eq. (1) holds) and degrades at worst to the synchronous baseline.Adaptive budget allocation. The candidate budget N=∑jfj is split across branches from trailing statistics over a causal window of W steps: the accept-length histogram P^​(j) and each branch’s coverage profile c^j​(f), the probability that the true bonus ranks within the top f candidates. We maximize expected coverage,(2)max⁡∑j{fj}⁡P^​(j)​c^j​(fj)s.t.∑jfj=N,solved greedily by marginal gain. In effect the fan-out concentrates around the recent mode of the accept-length distribution, and full-accept branches, whose bonus is the next token of an already-cached trajectory and is the top candidate ∼90% of the time, need only one candidate (fj=1), so a small budget covers high-acceptance tasks.Cost. Let Tgpu be the device-busy time per iteration and Tcpu the serial host time it must hide. A covered iteration hides the host chain and a missed one pays it, giving(3)speedup​(c)=Tgpu+TcpuTgpu+(1−c)​Tcpu→c→1 1+TcpuTgpu.The prefetch chain itself costs ≈N lookups per drafted request and must fit under Tgpu; beyond N≈64 it approaches the host time Tcpu it hides, so the budget sweet spot is small (Section 4.1.5). Both the attainable speedup and the sweet spot are governed by the ratio Tcpu/Tgpu: larger models or larger batches raise Tgpu relative to the host chain, so the hidden overlap is a smaller fraction of each iteration, whereas CPU-heavier regimes benefit more.
3.5.Integration and Generality
We integrate NgramRL into verl’s (Sheng et al., 2025) vLLM rollout worker. The cache attaches to the rollout engine and needs no change to the reward model, optimizer, or policy architecture, so it is a drop-in optimization. Adding no parameters and no training, it composes with existing rollout-efficiency methods and applies to any RL-style setup where prompts recur.
4.Results

4.1.Experimental Setup

4.1.1.RL Training Setup
For all our experiments, we use verl (Sheng et al., 2025) for GRPO training (Shao et al., 2024), running on 2× NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. The rollouts are served by the vLLM inference engine (Kwon et al., 2023), sampling 5 completions for each of 64 prompts per step over 15 epochs. We adopt verl’s default GRPO hyperparameters for each model and use the same settings across all baselines. Speculative decoding is exact, so no drafter alters the training dynamics, the sampled rollouts, or the resulting policy. The comparison therefore isolates drafting efficiency alone, and we evaluate all drafters on identical training runs.Models: We evaluate on Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025) and DeepSeek-LLM-7B (Bi et al., 2024), two popular open-weight models from different families, to demonstrate generalization.Datasets: For our evaluation, we use GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), Spider 1.0 (Yu et al., 2018), and CodeContests (Li et al., 2022), chosen to span free-form and structured generation. GSM8K is free-form mathematical reasoning. Spider (text-to-SQL) and CodeContests (code) produce syntactically regular outputs, where cross-rollout repetition is strongest. This spread lets us characterize how acceptance scales with the regularity of the output.Baselines: We compare against three model-free drafters under a matched draft budget of k=16. Prompt-lookup decoding (PLD) (Saxena, 2023) drafts n-gram continuations from the current context only. REST (He et al., 2024) retrieves continuations from a fixed datastore. SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2026) retrieves from a global suffix tree over the most recent 10k responses.Metrics: We report tokens per decoding step (TPS): the tokens committed per target forward pass, i.e. one plus the mean accepted draft length. It is the standard lossless-speedup proxy in speculative decoding and is hardware-agnostic, so the comparison does not depend on a specific GPU or kernel. We report two aggregates: the mean over the full training run, and the mean over the final 30% of steps. We use the final 30% because training has largely saturated by this point and the cache is fully populated, which is where speculative decoding helps the most. We also plot TPS across the entire run, showing how it evolves as the policy trains.
4.1.2.Profiling Setup
Runtime measurements use a dedicated rig: Qwen3-8B (bf16, batch 64, k=16) on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), with a 32-core AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9970X host holding the n-gram cache and running the lookup/scheduling chain. The throughput results (Figure 7(b)) are measured on this 8B rig. Per task, a timing pass records iteration wall-clock and hit/accept statistics, and an NVIDIA Nsight Systems (NVIDIA Corporation, 2025) pass decomposes each iteration period into device-busy time (the union of kernel, memory-copy, and CUDA-graph intervals) and exposed host time; serial host work (launch, rejection handling, cache lookup, scheduling) that are not overlapped with device execution and therefore stall the GPU..."

5 SIGNS YOU ARE THE FIRST TO HEAL WHAT YOUR ANCESTORS COULD NOT

Some souls arrive not merely to live, but to complete what was left unfinished. You are the one who stands at the threshold where the ancestors’ unfinished prayers meet the light of now. The lineage whispers through you. These are the signs.

1.  The Dreams That Are Not Only Yours You wake from visions of places and faces you have never known, yet the grief or the silence feels intimate. Ancestors appear not as ghosts to fear, but as unfinished stories seeking a voice through you. When the dream ends, the ache remains—and with it, a quiet knowing that you can finally offer what they could not receive.

2.  The Weight That Does Not Belong to Your Lifetime Emotions, illnesses, or fears move through you that have no root in your own story. You feel the heaviness of generations in your body, yet something in you refuses to simply carry it forward. You sense the difference between inheritance and possession, and you begin to transmute rather than transmit.

3.  Synchronicities That Speak in the Language of the Bloodline Numbers, names, places, and sudden memories rise without warning. A song, a scent, or a stranger’s words open a door into family secrets or unspoken vows. The ancestors do not always speak in clear sentences; they speak in patterns that only the one chosen to heal can recognize as a map.

4.  The Conscious Breaking of the Cycle Where those before you repeated the pattern in survival or in silence, you pause. You choose differently—not from rebellion alone, but from a deeper recognition. In that choice, an old current in the lineage loosens. You feel the shift not as triumph, but as a sacred release moving backward and forward at once.

5.  The Inner Knowing That You Are the First There is a quiet certainty that the tools, the awareness, or the courage now available to you were not available before. You do not heal the ancestors by fixing them; you heal the field they left unfinished by becoming the living resolution. The work is not yours alone, yet it begins in you.

You are not carrying their burden so that it continues.
You are the one through whom the burden is finally met with presence.

🚨👂 SUDDEN HEARING LOSS? DON'T WAIT FOR IT TO GET BETTER!

You wake up one morning and notice that hearing in one ear has suddenly reduced.

No pain.

No discharge.

No fever.

Just a strange blocked sensation.

You assume it's earwax.

⚠️ BUT WHAT IF IT ISN'T?

It could be SUDDEN SENSORINEURAL HEARING LOSS (SSNHL) — a time-sensitive condition affecting the inner ear or auditory pathways.

🔍 WHAT ARE THE WARNING SIGNS?

🔴 Sudden hearing reduction, often in one ear

🔴 Ringing or buzzing (tinnitus)

🔴 Ear fullness or blocked sensation

🔴 Difficulty understanding speech

🔴 Sometimes dizziness or vertigo

⏰ WHY IS TIME SO IMPORTANT?

Early specialist assessment can identify the cause and enable appropriate treatment.

Corticosteroids may be considered in suitable cases, particularly during the early treatment window.

But don't confuse the 72-hour definition of sudden hearing loss with a period during which it is safe to wait.

SEEK MEDICAL HELP IMMEDIATELY.

🩺 WHAT WILL THE ENT SPECIALIST DO?

1️⃣ Examine the ear.

2️⃣ Arrange hearing tests.

3️⃣ Confirm whether the loss is conductive or sensorineural.

4️⃣ Consider oral or intratympanic steroids when appropriate.

5️⃣ Arrange MRI when indicated.

6️⃣ Monitor recovery with follow-up hearing assessments.

🚫 WHAT SHOULD YOU AVOID?

❌ Waiting several days

❌ Assuming it is earwax

❌ Self-medicating with ear drops

❌ Attempting to clean the ear with cotton buds

💡 REMEMBER

Sudden hearing loss may improve, but recovery varies.

Prompt assessment gives clinicians the best opportunity to offer time-sensitive care.

🚨 Hearing loss with new facial weakness or other stroke-like symptoms requires emergency medical attention.

The event offered spectators an opportunity to witness the skill, discipline and dedication of the personnel who protect the country's skies. With massive public participation, breathtaking aerial displays and the presence of national and state leadership, 'Wings Over Ganga' became a memorable occasion for Varanasi, celebrating the courage, capability and commitment of the Indian Air Force.

Since then, he has repeated variations of this claim on several occasions. Each time, I have called it out and warned that his plan for winning the midterms was to make it harder for Democrats to vote and easier for Republicans to cheat.
 
Too few people have listened or heeded my warning.
 
This is familiar territory for me. In 2020, I warned that Trump was going to try to overturn the election. After he lost, I helped lead the litigation efforts for Joe Biden that resulted in Trump and his allies losing more than 60 cases in court.
 
Throughout the Biden presidency, I kept sounding the alarm, even as many in the White House wanted me to stop fighting in court and hoped that civility and norms would return on their own.
 
Simply wanting something doesn’t make it so. I warned that Republicans viewed abiding by norms and preaching bipartisanship as signs of weakness, and that Trumpism was growing within the GOP.
 
And yet, even after Trump returned to office, too many people in positions to know better continued to offer false assurances that the guardrails of democracy would hold.
 
What we are witnessing right now is not the collapse of those guardrails, but rather proof that they do not exist. Trump is making good on his statements about taking over vote counting and tabulation. He is asserting the powers he has falsely claimed to have all along.
 
Todd Blanche is facilitating it. He is encouraging it. He is weaponizing the DOJ not only against political opponents but also against voters and election officials.
 
On October 16, his Justice Department warned California election officials that they could be liable for aiding and abetting a federal crime if they counted mail ballots from the list of 20,000 voters the DOJ created.

We now know that was a lie.
 
DOJ was already moving to block certification in Alaska.
 
Stripped of its pretext, the doomsday scenario the DOJ laid out in that case is simple: a Republican senator loses and a Democratic candidate wins.
 
That is the standard for when the DOJ will act in this election. It is not interested in protecting voting. It couldn’t care less about fraud. It only cares about making it harder for Democrats to vote and easier for Republicans to cheat.
